meta.source: Meeting video transcripts (ASR, un-diarized); member attribution is name-based with per-position confidence.

cases.name: Personnel — Resignations/Retirements, Appointments, and Terminal Leave

timeline.summary: The board approved the appointment of Josephine Egan as Confidential Secretary to the Supervisor (effective January 1, 2024) and J. Carvey as Hourly Librarian (effective January 16, 2024), and accepted resignations from Susan Kramer (library, Jan 2), Kevin Mills (library, Dec 7, 2023) and Adam Woodruff (highway department, Dec 30, 2023). Members welcomed Egan warmly, with the Supervisor and colleagues expressing confidence she would be an asset to the whole board.

The board approved three personnel items by voice vote: appointing Arthur Ellis as an alternate to the Board of Ethics (5-year term to Jan 11, 2028); appointing Linda Cervich as Librarian 1 (hourly, effective Jan 29, 2024); and authorizing Finance Director Abbas to attend the 2024 NYS Government Finance Officers Association conference (April 17-19). Routine and uncontested.

Accepted the retirement resignation of Detective Sergeant Kevin Finetti (effective July 30, 2024); approved the probationary appointment of Danielle D. Thomas as Senior Office Assistant in the Building Department (effective June 13, 2024); and accepted, with regrets, the resignation of Melissa Horowitz from the Landmark Preservation Committee (effective June 23, 2024). The board noted thank-you letters are sent to departing volunteers.

The board made probationary appointments of Anna Dowing and Emma Goit as hourly clerks for the North Castle Public Library (effective October 24), received a letter of resignation from highway department mechanic Andrew Zakowinski (effective October 30), reappointed Aaron McCaffrey to the Conservation Board (two-year term to October 23, 2026), and reappointed Edward Loberman to the Board of Ethics (five-year term to October 23, 2029). All approved by voice vote. Members praised the reappointees and Rende explained the town re-interviews all willing volunteer board members regardless of tenure, thanking them for their service.

The board unanimously appointed Alfonso D'Abruzio as a seasonal road maintainer in the Highway Department, effective May 19, 2025, and reappointed Adam Barnett to the Conservation Board for a two-year term expiring May 14, 2027, thanking him for his service. The consensus agenda was also approved.

The board received the resignation of Irwin Hernandez from the Water and Sewer Department (effective June 18, 2025) and of Michael Calderola from the Police Department (effective July 1, 2025), and approved court office personnel attending the 2025 NYS Association of Magistrates Court Clerks annual conference in Albany (Sept 28-Oct 1, 2025). All approved by voice vote as routine personnel items.

The board acted on four personnel items, each by motion, second, and unanimous voice vote: appointment of Jennifer Paglieli as Librarian (effective Sept. 25, 2025); acceptance 'with regret' of Mary Jacobs's resignation as hourly Library Clerk (effective Oct. 18, 2025); reappointment of Beira Bull Tata to the Architectural Review Board for a five-year term ending Sept. 30, 2030; and appointment of Eric Bell to the Library Board for a five-year term ending Dec. 31, 2030. The consensus agenda was also approved.

The board acted on several personnel matters by voice vote: accepted the retirement/resignation of Assistant Building Inspector Michael Cromwell (eff. Jan 31, 2026, with thanks for long service) and the resignation of full-time librarian Diana Wendell; made the probationary appointments of Elizabeth Esposito (part-time assistant court clerk and part-time intermediate police clerk, eff. Jan 12) and Henry Sieno (part-time fire inspector, eff. Jan 19); and approved a terminal-leave pay plan for retiring Police Chief Peter Simonson, whom Rende reported is doing well in retirement.

cases.name: Local Law — Short-Term Rental Regulations

timeline.summary: Public hearing on a local law amending the code to require four LPC meetings per year (matching the state minimum) instead of six, while allowing additional meetings as needed. A parallel idea discussed in executive session — increasing LPC membership beyond the current 8 of 9 seats to absorb two interested applicants — was not included in the noticed law, so Roland advised adopting this amendment now and running a separate local law on membership later. The board closed the hearing and adopted the amended local law by voice vote (no roll call).

The board received the Assessor's memo recommending a local law to update the senior-citizen and disability tax-exemption income formula: raising the qualifying threshold (roughly from the mid-$30,000s to ~$58,000, about a 40% increase) and electing not to deduct IRA distributions from income. The change is expected to roughly double eligible residents (from ~30-35 to ~60). Members favored the Assessor's recommendation; Berra also asked her to report the cost borne by other taxpayers. Item received and a public hearing set for the February 14 meeting.

Public hearing on a local law (originally titled to 'prohibit' BESS, corrected to a definitional amendment clarifying that a battery energy storage system is not a 'public utility'), aimed at closing a loophole after a Mount Kisco case argued BESS qualifies as a public utility substation. Attorney Doug Worden, for Catalyze Energy, urged the board instead to adopt a durationally reasonable moratorium and develop a BESS code, citing a June 2024 PSC order targeting 6 GW of storage statewide and ESRG (the town's own engineer) approval of technologies like the Tesla Megapack 2. The board and town attorney Roland Barone rejected the need for a moratorium (the use is already not permitted) but cited volunteer-fire-service and water-supply safety fears; extended discussion also covered not inadvertently restricting normal residential EV/battery uses. The board closed the hearing but deferred the vote to a future meeting to correct the local law, neg-dec and notice documents; a confirmatory motion received the county Planning Board, town Planning Board and Snyder & Snyder letters.

The board received the draft short-term rental (STR) local law, short environmental assessment forms, and a resident email (Tan Nguyen, Dec 18, 2025), then scheduled a public hearing for January 28, 2026. Following a Zoom meeting that day with Airbnb representatives (attended by the Planner, Town Administrator and counsel), the board opted to hold the referral to the town/county planning boards until a more finalized draft exists after a follow-up Airbnb meeting, while still setting the hearing date (which may be opened and adjourned/kept open). Rende stressed the town needs a defensible law 'with teeth' to pursue offenders. A council member pressed that a standalone (non-zoning) law still requires a mandatory referral at some point.

The board received the proposed local law amending the town code definition of 'electric vehicle charging station' (Sec. 355-4) to permit level-3 charging, plus full environmental assessment forms (parts 1-3). It referred the law to the Westchester County and town planning boards and circulated to interested/involved agencies, and scheduled a public hearing for January 28, 2026 — all on voice votes. Before the item was formally stated, a council member recused himself, explaining the item originated from a request by his employer, IBM, creating an appearance of conflict; counsel recommended the recusal.

The board held a public hearing on a proposed local law creating a regulatory framework for short-term rentals, requiring a building-department permit plus an operating permit, occupancy/vehicle limits, a 120-day annual cap, noise restrictions, and a notarized affidavit or affirmation of primary residence. Town Planner Adam Kaufman summarized the draft and Attorney Roland answered questions on enforcement (police can issue violations) and affirmation forms. After public comment, the board closed the hearing, received the Planning Board memo (dated March 10), adopted a negative declaration, and adopted the local law by voice vote. Enforcement, public education, and a license-fee schedule were flagged as follow-up items.

cases.name: Ramadan Crescent Moon & Star Display at Wampus Brook Park (and Annual Display Policy)

timeline.summary: The board approved the Armonk Lions Club request to hold its annual fall folder roll at Wampus Brook Park on June 6-9, 2024, subject to receiving all required documentation. Motion, second, all in favor.

The board awarded the bid for replacement of the north bridge at Wampus Brook Park to Mega Painting and Contracting and authorized the Supervisor to sign the agreement. Members expressed relief that, after years of rebids at unreasonable prices, a sensible bid had finally come in. Approved by voice vote.

The August 14, 2024 bid award to Mega Painting & Contracting was rescinded because the contractor could not meet the town's stringent insurance requirements. The board debated whether to draw on the 5% bid bond or impose a penalty; the Town Attorney explained the options, and members agreed the contractor appeared to have acted in good faith and had not sought to lower requirements, so the board rescinded without penalty. The board then awarded the bid to the second-lowest bidder, JT Oranzio General Contracting, and authorized the supervisor to sign. Both actions passed by voice vote.

The board approved the Armonk Lions Club's request to hold the Fol-de-rol at Wampus Brook Park June 5-8, 2025. Councilman Milim recused himself as Lions Club president (deeming himself an interested officer under the ethics code) but, after discussion, spoke about the event in his individual capacity; the supervisor and Ethics Board chair questioned whether recusal was even required. Members praised Milim's revitalization of the club and noted the Lions' $20,000 donation to the Wampus North Bridge repair and other charitable giving. Adopted by voice vote.

The board approved a payment requisition to J.T. Oranzio for the Wampus Brook Park North Bridge replacement, with members praising the finished work. The board thanked the Lions Club, which committed $20,000 from folder-roll fundraising toward the project. Motion carried.

The board approved a resident request to install a crescent moon and star display at Wampus Brook Park to mark Ramadan (Feb 17-Mar 19, 2026), separate from the December holiday-season display of prior years. Because Ramadan shifts annually by the lunar calendar, the board established a protocol: the requester need only notify the Town Clerk in writing each year of the holiday's start and end dates by the last board meeting of the month prior, and directed Parks staff not to place this display during December. Discussion emphasized not burdening the resident with an in-person appearance each year.

cases.name: Gateway Residential Development — One-Year SUP Extension
cases.applicant: 45 Bedford Road, LLC (attorney Tony Veneziano; developer J.D. Soma; engineer Lauren McMahon, Lane/Langan Engineering)

timeline.summary: The board received three letters and heard the applicant's request, prompted by a Planning Board recommendation, to use the town right-of-way along Maple Avenue to create a shallower, better-landscaped stormwater/floodplain basin, to establish an easement (with HOA-maintained plantings), and to interpret or amend a one-acre deed restriction so rear patios and fences would be permitted. Town Planner Adam Kaufman supported the aesthetic benefit and applicant-maintenance arrangement, and attorney Roland advised the board could interpret the 'structures' language or hold a public hearing to amend it. Several residents spoke in opposition, including a St. Stephen's Church warden urging deferral to the ARB and a letter from Sharon Tombach urging the board not to schedule hearings, grant easements or weaken the deed restriction. The board declined to set a public hearing, requesting overlay renderings showing the deed-restriction line and comparative basin designs, and tabled the matter to reconvene in two weeks.

The board received a letter from Veneziano & Associates and revised plans (motion to receive carried) for the 34-townhouse Gateway project, then took up four related items flowing from Planning/Conservation/ARB review: a license to use the Maple Avenue right-of-way for expanded floodplain/stormwater storage, a license to use town land behind the annex (Cornell-Birdsall House) for 2-to-1 wetland-buffer mitigation, an amendment to the community benefit agreement adding $250,000, and a proposed amendment to the town's deed restriction to allow patios and screening fences in the deed-restricted area. Town Attorney Roland advised the deed-restriction change legally requires a public hearing (the licenses and CBA do not); the board leaned toward scheduling that hearing for May 22 and discussed whether to also let the Landmarks Preservation Committee weigh in. Extensive discussion covered future Maple Avenue widening options, density, and the historic meaning of the deed restriction; no final vote on the licenses/CBA is captured in the transcript.

The applicant asked the board to amend a deed restriction (barring 'structures') on land the town conveyed, to permit seven six-foot privacy fences and eight roughly 225 sq-ft at-grade stone/paver patios on the eastern side of the 34-townhouse Gateway project — placements driven by the planning board's request to spread the units out. Town Attorney Roland explained the 1962-63 New York City deed restriction (tied to watershed/flood-control protection since rendered obsolete by the Route 22 realignment) and that the town later conveyed to Winkler intending mainly to protect the church viewshed. Residents (Julie DeFilippo of Wampus Close HOA, Ed Woodyard, and Sharon Combach by Zoom) urged denial or continuance, arguing the restriction runs with the land and can only be modified by NYC and warning against a 'camel's nose' precedent. The transcript ends mid-hearing during Combach's statement; no final vote is captured.

Request for a one-year extension of the special use permit granted June 28, 2023; the Planning Board had just granted site plan approval two nights earlier. The board approved the extension. Milim noted he had opposed the project all along but saw no basis to deny the extension and voted in favor reluctantly.

cases.name: Public Comment — Tributes to Tony Futia

timeline.summary: Resident Ed Loberman detailed New York's new credit-card surcharge law (Gen. Business Law Art. 29-A §518, effective Feb 11, 2024), which allows municipalities/town attorneys to enforce penalties, and urged the town to take up enforcement locally rather than defer to the county. Rende responded that the enforcement 'onus' concerned him given the town's limited staff and suggested complaints route to the county Department of Consumer Affairs, while noting the law limits vendors to passing through their actual processing fees. Loberman pushed back that local enforcement is the law's intent. No action taken; matter to be reviewed with counsel.

Resident Tony Voutier (89) used the public comment period to describe his 25-year effort challenging the federal income tax and his correspondence with Donald Trump, unrelated to town business. The board took no action; Supervisor Rende thanked him, and Town Attorney Roland cautioned the public not to rely on tax advice given in the room without consulting a tax professional.

During public comment and community announcements, residents raised several matters. Ed Loberman urged the board to restore the public speaking time limit from three minutes to five and to allow public comment on all agenda items in person (not just via Zoom or at public hearings). Ed Woodyard updated on the 250th-anniversary documentary screenings and historic-site preservation efforts (Sands Mill, Miller Hill), prompting Rende to float purchasing a replica cannon for the Miller Hill battlefield. The town-wide cleanup (April 26, 9 a.m.–1 p.m.) was promoted by sustainability liaison Jose Berra. No formal action taken.

During public comment several residents (Mike Shaliro of 14 Orchard Drive and a longtime resident/judge) offered tributes to the late Tony Futia, a passionate civic gadfly and former water superintendent who died in April, recalling his ward-vote petition, his primary runs, and his dedication to the town despite frequent disagreements. Supervisor Rende and Councilwoman DiGiacinto responded warmly with their own recollections. No action taken.

cases.name: Special Permit — Troy's Nursery Garden Design LLC (Easter Event & Fall Festival)

timeline.summary: The board received a special event permit application from Troy's Nursery / Garden Design LLC for an Easter event on April 24, 2024 at 97 Bedford Banksville Road, and scheduled a public hearing for March 20, 2024 by voice vote. A council member flagged that the application stated no parking arrangements had been made, to be resolved at the hearing along with police-department requirements and insurance certificates.

Public hearing on a special-event permit for a fall festival (pumpkin/face painting, petting zoo, possible band) on October 6th. The board opened the hearing, read correspondence, adopted a negative declaration, and adopted the approving resolution, all by unanimous voice vote. Applicant Maria Cece asked whether repeat events could avoid the recurring permit process; the board and Town Planner Adam Kaufman explained a blanket approval covering multiple pre-dated events for the year could be possible.

A single consolidated special-event permit was sought for an Easter event (April 13, 2025) and two fall festivals (October 5 and 12, 2025), streamlining the applicant's prior year-by-year filings. The board opened the hearing, received PD/fire district/building inspector recommendations, heard the applicant and complimentary board comments, adopted the neg dec and the resolution, and closed the hearing. The board discussed possibly enacting a future local law to allow low-impact, repeat on-premises events with only building-inspector/PD/fire sign-off; special counsel noted that would require a town-code change and could not be done now.

The board received and approved a special-permit application from Troy's Nursery for an Easter event (March 29, 2026) and a fall festival (Sundays in October 2026). Under the town's new streamlined policy, such applications are pre-reviewed by staff so applicants no longer need individual public hearings, which the board praised as a customer-friendly improvement.

cases.name: Reappointment — George Tropeau to the Conservation Board (term to March 11, 2028)

timeline.summary: The board reappointed Vincent Giordano to the Conservation Board for a two-year term expiring October 9, 2026, with members commending his service. Approved by voice vote.
The board reappointed Diane Borgia to the Library Board for a five-year term expiring December 31, 2029. Motion made and seconded, adopted by voice vote.

The board reappointed Craig Benedict to the Conservation Board for a two-year term ending April 23, 2027. Members described him as an experienced and important member of the board. Adopted on a voice vote.
The board reappointed George Tropeau to the Conservation Board for a two-year term expiring March 11, 2028. The motion was made 'with appreciation and thanks,' seconded, all in favor.

cases.name: Receipt of Ferrari Companies Petition to Rezone 333 Main Street for Residential Use

timeline.summary: Supervisor Rende gave a lengthy explanation of exploring the purchase of 333 Main Street (the 'Boys/Du Bois Schiller' building) to consolidate town hall, police, court and staff under one roof, citing 2007 strategic-plan findings, ADA/code and egress deficiencies, sewage backups in the police locker room, and 30-year 'temporary' water/sewer trailers; the building owner proposed a 'friendly eminent domain' process, an appraisal and bond counsel are engaged. The board voted to authorize the supervisor to sign an Arconnex agreement for a test-fit/feasibility study, which staff said mainly pays for work already done. Town Historian Sharon Tombach objected the property sits in Landmarks Preservation District No. 1 and the two-page agreement read like an open-ended 'blank check'; the board pointed to its stated scope and hourly rates. It passed 4-1 by roll call (Milim, Berra, Hussain, Rende aye; DiGiacinto no, calling it premature). The board also adopted a companion bond-counsel resolution allowing all professional fees from that date forward to be captured into any future financing.

The board received a SEQR short-form EAF Part 1 and the appraisal (BS F&F LLC / Mike Ferrari, dated Nov. 18, 2024) and adopted an order calling a public hearing on February 12, 2025 for the friendly eminent-domain acquisition of 333 Main Street to house all town offices, the police department, and the water/sewer staff currently in 30-year-old trailers. Supervisor Rende laid out the deficiencies (cited since a 2007 study) — flooding police locker rooms, inadequate holding cells, ADA non-compliance, an unsafe farmhouse annex — and urged an outright referendum from the start rather than the minimum permissive referendum. Members broadly supported pursuing the opportunity but urged cost scrutiny, at least two public hearings, a parallel study of the existing town-hall campus, and aggressive public outreach. Special counsel Bob Spolzino explained why condemnation benefits the town (it brackets/forces the negotiation and forecloses competing buyers).

The 333 Main Street property (the Boyes law-firm building, owned in part by presenter Michael Ferrari) had been targeted a year earlier by the town for possible eminent-domain acquisition as a new town hall, drawing opposition; Ferrari included it in his RFEI concept as a conversion to ~40 residential units and disclosed he is separately filing a rezoning petition (to be completed the next day) to change it from commercial to residential, independent of any town-hall decision. Board members clarified this is a separate matter a future town board would decide, and that a private rezoning is not protected by permissive referendum — the board can grant or deny it. Whippoorwill Hills residents (a 150-home HOA adjacent via Log Cabin Way) voiced concern about traffic, construction disruption, and sightlines. No action was taken; the petition was not yet before the board.

The board voted only to RECEIVE (not consider or refer) a petition from Ferrari Companies to rezone 333 Main Street to permit residential use, after special counsel Bob Spolzino distinguished the ministerial act of receiving from the discretionary act of considering. The receipt passed on a roll call (DiGiacinto, Hussain, Milim, Rende aye; Berra abstained). Milim, who is leaving the board, opined that the rezoning does not fit the comprehensive plan given already-approved units (Airport Campus 175, Mariani 34, Lumberyard 20, Summit Club). Berra's abstention triggered a sharp exchange with Rende over whether a member may abstain without stating a reason under Robert's Rules.

cases.name: Resignation — Judy Kitt from Open Space Committee

timeline.summary: The board accepted the resignation of Mitzy Weissman from the Beautification Committee, effective January 13. Councilwoman DiGiacinto praised her contributions as a master gardener and environmentalist and her family's long town history. Accepted by voice vote with appreciation for her service.

The board received the resignation of Planning Board member Jim Jensen, effective March 27, 2025, after 11 years of service. DiGiacinto read Jensen's stated reason — that the town bypassed site-plan review for the IBM community park (turf-field) project, which he viewed as an ethical issue — triggering a heated exchange over whether the project was handled properly. Rende and Milim defended the process (engineer and DEC review, no shortcuts) and argued the Planning Board review was not required, while DiGiacinto maintained a public hearing/planning review should have occurred; Berra, the Planning/Conservation liaison, had not objected to skipping review. The board voted to accept the resignation with thanks. Motion carried.

The board accepted a letter of resignation from Austin Farkas of the building maintenance department, effective April 11, 2025. Members praised him as an exceptional employee in the newly formed maintenance department who left for the private sector, and noted resumes for a replacement are already coming in. Adopted on a voice vote.
The board accepted, with regret, Judy Kitt's letter of resignation from the Open Space Committee effective July 22, 2025, noting she had been a good member. Motion carried.

cases.name: Street Naming & Addressing — Airport Campus, 113 King Street (E-911 Referral)
cases.applicant: Airport Campus (attorney Chris Fisher, Cuddy & Feder; Jeff Ringler; Kevin Moses, Toll Brothers)

timeline.summary: As required by its August SEQRA findings and rezoning, the applicant filed a petition and map/plan/report (prepared by the town's engineer D&B) to extend Water District No. 8 by running a main up King Street over I-684 to the site, with a 300,000-gallon storage tank and pump station. Attorney Roland advised adopting the order calling a public hearing while negotiating a water-contribution agreement and referring the ~$3 million cost estimate to the Kellard firm for review. Members raised questions about inflation and cost escalation (DiGiacinto), tank sizing discrepancies and coordination with a possible future combined million-gallon tank and Water District 4 extension (Milim/Rende, with Water/Sewer Superintendent Sal). The board voted by roll call to refer the map/plan to Kellard and to adopt the order calling a public hearing for February 14, 2024 (DiGiacinto, Hussain and Supervisor Rende recorded aye).

A public hearing under Town Law was opened on a petition to extend Water District 8 to bring municipal water to the former MBIA campus (redevelopment), replacing on-site wells via a 12-inch main from New King Street over I-684 to the site, an oversized 297,000-gallon tank and pump station sized to also serve a future District 4. The applicant, building privately at 30-40% below public-bid cost, said it is not seeking action yet pending a D&B basis-of-design report (expected end of month) and a water-contribution/capital agreement. The board received the revised map, plan and report, then adjourned the hearing without a specific date, anticipating a follow-up work session.

The board received a January 13, 2025 memo from KSCJ Consulting on the assignment of new street names and addresses for the Airport Campus and referred it to the Town E-911 Coordinator. The naming committee had to revisit the plan because it had not accounted for the amenities building (senior/older housing) remaining on site. Received by voice vote.

cases.name: Terminal Leave Payment — Lisa Larson, Parks & Recreation Department

timeline.summary: The board approved a terminal leave payment for Liz Duffy, senior recreation leader in the Senior Citizens Recreation Department, by voice vote. A council member noted she has been working part time remotely and will continue in a part-time in-person role starting in April, calling it a good solution for everyone.
The board approved the terminal leave payment for retiring Police Department member Kevin Finateri, with members wishing him well. Approved by voice vote.
The board approved a terminal leave payment to Lisa Larson of the Parks and Recreation Department. Routine personnel item, moved and seconded, all in favor.

cases.name: Probationary Appointments — Water & Sewer and Parks & Recreation

timeline.summary: The board approved, by individual motions and votes, the probationary appointments of Anthony Stevens (effective June 3, 2024), Joseph D. Santesis, and Andrew Sigenga as skilled laborers filling open positions in the Water & Sewer Department. Town Administrator Kevin said he was impressed with the candidates interviewed and glad to fill the openings under superintendent 'Sal.' All appointments adopted unanimously.

The board made two probationary appointments effective December 11, 2025: William Segmuller as Assistant Building Inspector and Yvonne Henriquez as Office Assistant (Automated System). Both passed unanimously by voice vote.

The board approved a series of probationary appointments by voice vote: Brian Kidoff as skilled laborer in Water & Sewer (effective April 13), Leroy Crawley as skilled labor in Water & Sewer (effective April 27), Nicholas Champagne as skilled labor in Water & Sewer (effective April 27), and Jorge Hodaro as groundskeeper in Parks & Recreation (effective April 13). Each passed on a motion, second, and aye vote.

cases.name: Receipt of Resignation — Brendan Malloy, Parks & Recreation Advisory Board

timeline.summary: The board accepted, with regret and thanks, the resignation of Allison Miller from the Sustainability Committee effective April 27, 2024. The Supervisor noted the town clerk's office sends a formal thank-you letter to departing volunteers on behalf of the board.
The board received the resignation of Jane Rothschild from the North Castle Public Library, effective January 16, 2025, and wished her well. Accepted by voice vote.
The board received the letter of resignation from Brendan Malloy from the Parks and Recreation advisory board, effective February 14, 2026, and thanked him for his service. Accepted by voice vote.

cases.name: Special Use Permit — 23 Bedford Banksville Road (wood/metal manufacturing)
cases.applicant: Greenwich Realty Group, LLC (counsel Tony Veneziano)

timeline.summary: Received county and town Planning Department letters on a proposed zoning text amendment to permit light industrial use (woodworking and iron/aluminum assemblage) by special use permit in the GB General Business district; the Planning Board gave a positive recommendation. The board scheduled the public hearing for June 26. Members flagged that the drafted use language is broad and asked to tour the site before the hearing, citing an observed active/disturbing operation and environmentally sensitive wetlands to the rear. Barbara DiGiacinto recused herself (her husband owns 25% of Band Monk Realty, which holds a mortgage on the property).

A noticed public hearing on 23 Bedford Banksville Road was opened and immediately adjourned to a date uncertain because the applicant felt they were not fully ready. DiGiacinto recused herself due to a family financial interest — her husband John DiGisono owns 25% of Ban Monk Realty, which holds a mortgage on the property. The board opened and adjourned by voice votes.

Following a rezoning to CBB at the prior meeting, the board held a public hearing on a special-use permit to legalize existing specialized wood-product and metal-assemblage manufacturing, with conditions limiting occupancy to 20, keeping storage inside, and requiring proper handling/ventilation of chemicals and fumes. A resident (Jen) questioned why a permit would be granted before the building inspector confirmed safety; counsel and the board explained the operating/building permit review follows the use approval. The board adopted the neg dec and resolution and closed the hearing. A late redline of the conditions circulated the day of the meeting prompted a board member's objection to '11th hour' document changes.

cases.name: AI Engineers Proposal — Water District No. 9 Quarry Heights Water Main Extension Distribution System

timeline.summary: The board authorized the Supervisor to sign an agreement with Westchester Joint Water Works (WJWW) to begin extending public water to the long-troubled Quarry Heights neighborhood, where wells have dried and been contaminated. WJWW, under a DOJ/DEC consent order, earmarked ~$1.1 million in lieu of penalties to extend mains and make roughly 14 connections; the agreement commits the town to later form a water district (in reverse of the usual order) to absorb those and remaining properties, buy water from WJWW, and resell it. Sal Misisti explained plans to install three master-meter interconnection points and later extend districtwide, pursuing grants given the high rock-excavation cost. Residents Diana Kandrea and Nico Marino pressed for equitable connection of all homes and possible cost recovery from the contaminator; the board committed to a special public informational meeting. Approved by voice vote.

The board held a public hearing on extending Water District No. 9 to the Quarry Heights area under Article 12A of Town Law, addressing chronic well-water/PFAS problems among roughly 48 homes. Town Attorney Roland explained that two preliminary resolutions would let the town apply to the State Comptroller and better position the project for grant funding, with a worst-case per-home cost around $46,700 over the life of the bond. Residents spoke strongly in favor (a signed petition and letter were submitted into the record), and the board adopted a 21-day open comment period before both preliminary resolutions passed 5-0 by roll call (Berra, Vitaj, DiGiacinto, Hussain, Rende all aye). Board members voiced unanimous, emphatic support and commitment to pursue grants.

Under agreements, the board approved receipt of a proposal from AI Engineers for the Water District No. 9 Quarry Heights water main extension distribution system (design work supplementing the map/plan/report). Approved by voice vote.

cases.name: Tony Castell Inc. — Kent Place Parking Lot (Former Verizon Property) Final Payment
cases.applicant: Town of North Castle (bid documents by Kellard)

timeline.summary: The board approved authorizing a bid for improvements to the Kent Place parking lot, a new downtown parking addition, with an 18-month completion date. Bid documents prepared by Kellard were ready to release. Approved by unanimous voice vote of the members present.

The board approved payment requisition No. 4 to Tony Casale Inc. for the completed Kent Place parking-lot improvements, already cleared by the town's engineer. Members praised the finished lot (now open and in use) and discussed remaining holdback, extra fence work, and fall overseeding, plus plans to encourage Main Street business owners/employees to use the new lot and to advance a future parking-district effort.

The board accepted the contractor's affidavit of release of liens and a one-year guarantee bond and approved final payment requisition number five to Tony Castell Inc. for the Kent Place parking lot improvements. Councilwoman DiGiacinto recused herself because her family owns commercial property on the west side of Main Street. Motion made and all in favor.

cases.name: Interim MS4 Stormwater Reports (period ending January 2, 2026)

timeline.summary: The board accepted the interim MS4 stormwater reports for the period ending September 1, 2024, prepared by town engineer KSCJ Consulting, detailing routine compliance activities such as catch-basin cleaning, street sweeping, and education/training. Approved by voice vote as a standard annual filing.

The board accepted the interim MS4 stormwater reports for the period ending January 2, 2025, prepared by town engineers KSCJ, and authorized the supervisor to sign. Described as annual housekeeping to promote stormwater safety practices and reduce pollution. Councilwoman DiGiacinto moved it; adopted by voice vote.

The board accepted the interim MS4 stormwater reports for the period ending January 2, 2026 from the town engineer and authorized the supervisor to sign the reports. Routine compliance item, moved and seconded, all in favor.

cases.name: Resolution — NYS Archives Local Government Records Management Improvement Fund Grant Application (up to $75,000)

timeline.summary: The board adopted a resolution authorizing the Town Court to apply for a Justice Court Assistance Program grant in the 2024-2025 cycle for up to $30,000, primarily to scan and preserve criminal case files the court is required by law to retain (some dating to the 1800s). Rende praised the court staff for identifying the opportunity and asked the administrator to have the town's grant writer keep pursuing similar grants. Adopted by voice vote.

The board adopted a resolution requesting North Castle be officially included in the federal Highlands boundary (U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service) to qualify for Highlands Conservation Act grant funding and technical assistance. Members raised concerns about whether joining could bind the town to federal environmental regulations, but Attorney Roland and materials from Kerry Kasak clarified that merely joining imposes no obligation and only enables the town to apply for grants (with any accepted grant to be reviewed closely for conditions). Adopted by voice vote.

The board adopted a resolution authorizing a New York State Archives Local Government Records Management Improvement Fund grant application for the conservation of historical records in an amount not to exceed $75,000, and authorized the supervisor to sign the application. Moved, seconded, all in favor.

cases.name: Public Hearing — Acquisition of 333 Main Street via Eminent Domain

timeline.summary: Continued public hearing on whether to acquire 333 Main Street via eminent domain procedure law to relocate town hall, police and court from the deficient 15 Bedford Road campus. About two dozen residents spoke, nearly all opposed or urging a pause: they objected to an open-ended 'blank check,' warned the ~$7M appraisal would balloon in court (owner's counsel already disputes it), demanded a full cost comparison with renovating/expanding 15 Bedford Road, and voiced fears the historic 10-acre town hall site would be sold for development. The board received a batch of letters/emails into the record and Supervisor Rende announced an ad hoc concept study committee and a commitment to a public referendum. No vote to close was taken; the hearing was adjourned and continued to the March 12 meeting.

The board reconvened the continued public hearing on acquiring 333 Main Street by eminent domain procedure law to relocate Town Hall, citing deteriorated, non-ADA-compliant, and unsafe conditions in the current facilities (police basement flooding, mold, undersized space per a 2007 study). Dozens of residents spoke or submitted letters; a clear majority opposed or expressed concern about eminent domain, traffic, historic-district loss, potential development of the current town parcel, and lack of cost information, while some developers argued the purchase is financially sound. The board repeatedly stressed no decision would be made without full cost studies of multiple options and a town-wide referendum, and committed to an FAQ, a process one-pager, and possible mailings. The board received several resident letters into the record and voted to recess/adjourn the hearing to April 23, 2025 (with the option to postpone further by public notice). No acquisition decision was taken.

The board reconvened the public hearing to consider acquiring 333 Main Street under the Eminent Domain Procedure Law. As noticed, the hearing was opened and immediately adjourned to an undetermined future date because the board is still gathering information. Resident Andrew Lester spoke against the acquisition, calling the property undesirable and urging a holistic, process-driven review before proceeding.

cases.name: IMA with Westchester County — Grasslands Firing Range Training

timeline.summary: Approval of an intermunicipal agreement with Westchester County (via a NYSERDA/Con Ed incentive program) to install EV charging stations at no cost to the town, with authorization for the Supervisor to sign. Construction is slated for Hergenhan and Community Park, then Town Hall and Clove Road. Members discussed pricing/time-limit enforcement to avoid overcrowding and logistical timing around other park work. Approved on a voice vote.

Approval of an intermunicipal agreement for the STOP-DWI patrol project (reimbursement up to $8,400/year for overtime checkpoint work), with authorization for the Supervisor to sign. DiGiacinto voiced concerns about the reimbursement cap, overtime rates by rank, and the many procedural steps required to be reimbursed, but supported the long-running program. Approved on a voice vote.

Approval of an intermunicipal agreement with the Westchester County Department of Public Safety Services for police training at the Grasslands Reservation firing range, with authorization for the Supervisor to sign. A recurring year-end renewal; approved on a voice vote.

cases.name: Extension of Special Use Permit — St. Nersess Armenian Seminary, 486 Bedford Road
cases.applicant: St. Ursula's Armenian Seminary (architect Robert Stanzial; Dean Father Maderos)

timeline.summary: Public hearing on a special use permit to modify the 5.5-acre R-2A seminary campus with a two-room/two-story guest addition to the married-students building and a new two-bedroom single-family dean's residence. Coverage remains well under limits (7% building, 15.5% land); a 30-foot side-yard setback requires a variance, and Planning Board, ARB and neighbor screening/lighting concerns were noted for follow-up. Residents (Historical Society) spoke in strong support, praising the seminary as gracious neighbors. The board closed the hearing and adopted the negative declaration and the resolution by voice vote (5-0).

The board received a letter and adopted a resolution granting a one-year extension of a special use permit for building modifications at the St. Nersess Armenian Seminary, giving the applicant additional time to address conditions of approval. No applicant appeared (a routine extension); passed by voice vote.

cases.name: Armonk Close (Lumberyard) — Reduce AFFH Units from Four to Two

timeline.summary: Developer Mike Ferrari asked (bifurcating off a separate future request to relocate units to 470 Main Street) that the board amend the zoning code so his 20-unit condo project could immediately reduce its affordable requirement from four units (20%) to two (10%), rather than waiting for the code's existing incentive that automatically drops it to two upon obtaining COs/75% completion by June 30, 2025. His stated need was to finalize a condo offering plan now (his attorney said the unit-count uncertainty prevents filing). The board debated whether the uncertainty truly blocks marketing; Berra opposed advancing it (fearing it as leverage for the later relocation request), Hussain said he would hold at 20%, and Milim viewed it as only a marketing-convenience with no real delay. Ferrari, frustrated, withdrew the request after concluding the votes were not there; no action taken.

Developer sought confirmation that, having reached over 80% completion (verified by the building inspector), the affordable (AFFH) requirement drops from 20% (four units) to 10% (two units), so its offering plan can be filed with the Attorney General. Hussain and Berra objected that the justification rested on the applicant's own attorney's letter rather than a direct AG statement, and that the letter's '0?' reference was confusing; Hussain wanted a commitment this was the last AFFH request. DiGiacinto and Milim held the reduction was clearly earned and appropriate. Adopted 3-2 by roll call (Milim aye, DiGiacinto aye, Hussain no, Berra no, Rende yes), with an added recital that the developer is well beyond 80% complete.

cases.name: Proclamation — Adoption of the IHRA Working Definition of Antisemitism

timeline.summary: Supervisor Rende read a proclamation declaring May 2024 Jewish American Heritage Month in the Town of North Castle, developed together with Councilman Matt Milim. The board moved to authorize the Supervisor to sign and date it effective May 8, 2024. Adopted unanimously by voice vote.

The board read and adopted a proclamation recognizing the growing problem of antisemitism and adopting the International Holocaust Remembrance Alliance (IHRA) working definition, including its 11 contemporary examples, and directing town agencies (including the police department) to make it available as an educational resource. A council member gave an impassioned statement citing FBI hate-crime and ADL statistics and a recent neo-Nazi rally in nearby Greenwich. Adopted unanimously by voice vote effective May 8, 2024.

cases.name: Residential Contract of Sale to Oliver and Samantha Baranovic (0.334 acres)
cases.address: Town-owned parcel contiguous to 101 Old Hickory Way, Bedford (Crossroad)

timeline.summary: The board received a request from the Bonistalls to acquire a vacant town-owned lot the town obtained through an in rem tax foreclosure (roughly $12,000 in tax arrears accumulated over ~10 years) that the owner wishes to merge into his residence under a covenant against further subdivision. Town Attorney Roland explained the history and noted the assessor should value the parcel with and without the restriction and that any sale cannot be a gift of town funds. The board referred the matter to the town attorney, the assessor, and the Planning Board (highway foreman deemed unnecessary) by motion and vote.

The board approved a residential contract of sale of a 0.334-acre town-owned parcel contiguous to 101 Old Hickory Way for a private, non-gated driveway, authorizing the Supervisor to sign. The buyers had spent since 2022 obtaining RPRC, Conservation Board, wetland, and culvert-mitigation approvals, and the contract includes a covenant surviving closing that keeps the passageway open for town emergency-vehicle access. The price was reviewed by the assessor and is stated in the contract. The board first received a related letter from an interested neighbor into the file, then approved the sale, which is subject to permissive referendum by statute. Passed by voice vote.

cases.name: Breezemont Day Camp (HZBR LLC) — Special Use Permit (Schedule Public Hearing)

timeline.summary: Received the LPC recommendation to landmark the historic Armonk barber pole and scheduled a public hearing for July 10, 2024. Members confirmed the business owner is enthusiastic and asked that owner consent/maintenance documentation be delivered to the Town Attorney before the hearing; the designation is understood to cover the pole itself.

Received the special use permit application and short-form EAF (Part 1) for operation of a summer day camp, now permitted after the town recently legalized day camps. The board scheduled the public hearing, coordinating with the Planning Board (July 8) and setting the town board hearing for July 10, 2024; not time-sensitive since operation would begin next summer.

cases.name: New Street Address Assignment — 100 Business Park Drive Condominium Units
cases.applicant: WMG Armonk Warehouse Owner LLC / KSCJ Consulting

timeline.summary: Received the KSCJ Consulting recommendation to establish a new wetland mitigation bond followed by a five-year monitoring/maintenance bond, and (per a June 5, 2024 letter) authorized the Supervisor to sign the wetland mitigation planting, maintenance and monitoring bond agreement with WMG Armonk Warehouse Owner LLC. Approved routinely.

The board received a KSCJ Consulting memo on assigning new street addresses to base-space commercial condominium units, changing 100 Business Park Drive to 100, 112, 114 and 116 Business Park Drive, and referred the matter to the town E-911 coordinator by unanimous voice vote.

cases.name: Special Use Permit — Little Sparrows Nursery School Expansion (Hillside Church of Christian Ministry Alliance)
cases.applicant: Hillside Church of the Christian Missionary Alliance (attorney Stephen Veneruso)

timeline.summary: The board received the application to modify an existing special use permit to legalize the Little Sparrows nursery school operating six classrooms when the permit only allowed two — discovered during interior renovation permitting. The school (~60 children) also needs one likely variance for outdoor-recreation-space square footage (code requires 200 sq ft per child). The board scheduled a public hearing for July 24 and referred the application to the town and county planning boards, coordinating timing with the ZBA (meeting July 11) so the applicant can resolve everything before the September school year.

Public hearing on a special use permit to legalize enlargement of the Little Sparrows Nursery School from two to six classrooms, which the school had been operating for years under an old two-classroom permit. Attorney Veneruso explained a needed outdoor-recreation-space variance (code requires 200 sq ft/child; ~800 sq ft available for a typical max of 11-12 children) would still be sought from the ZBA. The board adopted a negative declaration and then a resolution granting a one-year special use permit conditioned on the ZBA variance, building-department sign-off and fire approval, and closed the hearing. Members praised the school as a good neighbor; Berra flagged a deteriorating retaining wall at the parking lot as a safety housekeeping item.

cases.name: Two-Way Radio Communications Satellite Receiver System — Metrocom Wireless Proposal
cases.applicant: Metrocom Wireless Incorporated (via Town Administrator Kevin)

timeline.summary: The board approved and authorized the Supervisor to sign a Metrocom Wireless proposal (off state bid, meeting procurement policy) to replace the town's 20-year-old analog police radios with an encrypted digital system, funded from general-fund balance. The system brings the Highway Department onto the same network so police and highway can communicate directly during storms and emergencies, and eliminates dead spots where cell service fails. Approved by voice vote.

At the police chief's request, the board approved funding a two-way radio communications satellite receiver system and a Metrocom Wireless Inc. proposal of roughly $14,000 to replace older equipment and eliminate communication dead spots. The expandable system will also serve highway, water and sewer and enable cross-department coordination in emergencies. Adopted by voice vote.

cases.name: Agreement with Arc Westchester — Main Street Armonk Maintenance 2026

timeline.summary: Following a recommendation from the Landmark Preservation Committee, the board opened and held a public hearing to landmark the roughly 100-year-old Armonk Barber Pole (a Made-in-Chicago Koch No. 909), which the property-owning family enthusiastically supported. Board members discussed only the pole (not the building) and debated adding a future designation plaque, to be placed on the building with owner permission. The hearing was closed and the board unanimously adopted the landmark designation by voice vote.
The board authorized the supervisor to sign a 2026 agreement with Arc Westchester for maintenance of Main Street, Armonk. Passed unanimously by voice vote.

cases.name: Discussion — Allocation of Funds for Capital Projects / Capital Reserve Funds

timeline.summary: Prompted by the new Road Naming Committee liaison appointment, DiGiacinto asked the board to clarify what a liaison position entails, noting members are neither chair nor committee member but a bridge to the town board. Rather than a formal work session, the board reached consensus to have staff (Eliana, via Administrator Hay) draft guidelines, with members submitting their own input, referencing Barone's recollection that liaisons historically served as an information bridge.

At DiGiacinto's request the item was discussed in public session. Town Administrator Kevin Hay explained the two types of state capital reserve funds (specific vs. type, each with capital-improvement and equipment subcategories), the resolutions and permissive-referendum rules to establish or expend them, and the state comptroller's guidance that the town's healthy fund balance should be designated to specific projects (roughly no more than 15% of tax revenue undesignated). The board reached consensus to have the administrator and finance office refine project cost estimates (salt dome, turf fields, radio system, North Bridge, town-building maintenance) and then hold a work session before adopting establishing resolutions. DiGiacinto asked that library/town-building maintenance needs be folded in.

cases.name: Special Use Permit Extension — Additional Horses at 263 Bedford Banksville Road
cases.applicant: Hackerman, Tortorella & Weckstein LLP (Jerry Tortorella) for the property owner

timeline.summary: Counsel requested a first extension of a special permit (originally granted September 13, 2023) for additional horses as a personal accessory equestrian use, after delays obtaining Westchester County Health Department approvals. Nothing about the application had changed. The board found it straightforward and adopted the extension resolution by voice vote.

The board received a letter and adopted a resolution granting a one-year extension of a special use permit for additional horses, given ongoing construction of equestrian buildings and a new residence that will not be completed by the 9/13/2025 expiration. The applicant's attorney reported construction is proceeding smoothly with no issues. Received and extension granted to September 13, 2026 by unanimous voice vote.

cases.name: 45 Hurlingham LLC — Wetland Mitigation Planting Bond Extension and 5-Year Maintenance/Monitoring Bond Extension

timeline.summary: On the town engineer's (KSCJ/Kellard) recommendation, the board approved extension of a wetland mitigation planting bond and a five-year extension of the maintenance and monitoring bond. The applicant said most work is complete and did not object to the town continuing to hold security. Added to the agenda late; approved by voice vote.

On the town engineer KSCJ's recommendation, the board approved a one-year extension of the wetland mitigation planting bond plus a corresponding five-year maintenance and monitoring bond extension. KSCJ had not yet verified all plantings were complete; attorney Jerry Tortorella explained plantings were done but a contractor changeover delayed the as-built certification, after which a town inspection would start the five-year monitoring clock. Members confirmed the bonds are de minimis cash amounts. Approved.

cases.name: Eagle Ridge (3 North Castle Drive) — Declaration of Covenants and stormwater easement/maintenance agreement
cases.applicant: Summit Club / Mad Madonna Armonk LLC & IBM (Gary Rosen for Corey Salomon)

timeline.summary: A package of documents for a school-bus easement/dedication over an IBM-owned private road (to allow Byram Hills buses into the Eagle Ridge subdivision) plus a related utility easement. The board received one letter but tabled items 2-5 (motion to table passed unanimously) because of unresolved issues: an incorrect IBM corporate name, typos, an over-broad indemnity, questions about the town plowing scope and the map's hash-marked area extending to the security gate, and Councilman Berra's lost markup. Counsel and members will circulate corrections (edits due by close of business Tuesday) before it returns to a future agenda.

The board received a November 6, 2024 letter from Zarin & Steinmetz regarding Eagle Ridge and authorized the supervisor to sign the Declaration of Covenants and Restrictions and the Stormwater Control Facility Easement and Maintenance Agreement. Councilman Berra questioned whether the easement (town right to inspect and default obligation to perform maintenance) imposed liability on the town; the Town Attorney explained roughly 30 such DEC-designed agreements exist, the town is the default performer and charges back the HOA, with no undue liability. Rende reacted with mild impatience to the questions. Receipt and signature authorization both passed by voice vote (one board member recused).

cases.name: Special Use Permit — Gavi Restaurant Mixed-Use Building

timeline.summary: The board considered receipt of a special-use-permit application to add a 5,000 sq ft mixed-use building with first-floor retail plus two one-bedroom first-floor apartments and two two-bedroom second-floor apartments (four units total). The written application erroneously described the apartments as being only on the second floor; the applicant clarified the layout orally and will submit an amendment letter. The board referred the revised submission to the town and county planning boards and scheduled a public hearing for November 20, 2024 (moved one week from the originally noticed November 13 to allow adequate county/planning-board review time).

Public hearing on a special use permit for a new 5,000 sq ft mixed-use building with two ground-floor retail spaces and four apartments (two 1-bedroom on the first floor, two 2-bedroom on the second), with basement garages for tenants. County and Planning Board correspondence and the SEQRA short form were received; Town Planner Adam Kaufman confirmed no unusual county comments and that site-plan details return to the Planning Board. No residents spoke. The board closed the hearing, adopted a negative declaration, and adopted the resolution granting the permit (all by voice vote). Board members suggested (non-binding) bike racks and more permeable parking surfaces.

cases.name: Local Law Amending Chapter 60 (Officers & Employees) — Residency for Assistant Building/Fire Inspector Titles

timeline.summary: The board considered receipt of a proposed local law amending Chapter 60 to change the residency requirement for the assistant building inspector (and fire inspector) from residing within the town to residing in New York State, matching the existing standard for the building inspector. Town Administrator Kevin explained Westchester County Human Resources requires this change in connection with a recent appointment. The board received the local law and scheduled a public hearing for October 23, 2024.

The board opened, held, and closed a public hearing on a local law amending Chapter 60 to exempt the assistant building inspector and fire inspector titles from the state residency requirement for officers who take oaths of office, using the home-rule workaround that lets such employees live anywhere in New York State rather than in-town. Town Attorney Roland gave a brief overview; no one from the public or board raised objections and members called it 'pretty clear cut.' The board closed the hearing and adopted the local law by voice vote (motion, second, all in favor).

cases.name: Map Clarification — New Town Roadways and Names, Airport Campus Subdivision
cases.address: Airport Campus Subdivision (Weber Farm / Fieldstone Knoll / Cove View), North Castle

timeline.summary: The board approved the Road Naming Committee's recommendations for new roads in the Toll Brothers airport campus subdivision (Weber Farm Road, Cove View Way, and Fieldstone Knoll), with notification to the E911 coordinator, because tax lot numbers must be assigned before the plat can be filed. Members objected to the committee attaching conditions/stipulations (preserving historic field stones and requesting a WWII commemorative plaque), agreeing that naming a road is a town responsibility that cannot be bartered; those requests will be passed to the developer only as non-binding suggestions. The board also directed staff (via Kevin/Adam) to build developer notification into the future road-naming process. Approved by voice vote.

The board adopted a corrected configuration of new roadways in the airport campus subdivision. The road names recommended by the Road Naming Committee were unchanged; only the road configuration was clarified so the entrance road to the 50-unit senior housing has a proper address consistent with 911/emergency addressing, verified with the builder and police department. On the Town Attorney's advice the board voted to adopt the sketch map.

cases.name: Probationary Appointment — Jose Sala, Highway Department Mechanic

timeline.summary: The board approved the probationary appointment of Paul Taft as assistant building inspector, effective October 10, 2024, contingent on setting the Chapter 60 residency public hearing per Westchester County HR requirements. The position was budgeted and is part of a transition ahead of an expected retirement in the building department. Approved by voice vote with best wishes to Taft.
The board approved the probationary appointment of Jose Sala as a mechanic in the Highway Department, effective January 9, 2025, by voice vote.

cases.name: Conference Attendance — Kevin Neely, Assistant Assessment Clerk (NYS Assessors Cornell Conference)

timeline.summary: The board approved a request from Highway General Foreman Jamie Norris to attend the League of Municipalities Conference in Atlantic City, November 14-17, 2024, with lead mechanic Matthew Hirsch, using a town vehicle. The Supervisor encouraged board members and staff to treat such conferences (including the upcoming Association of Towns convention) as continuing education. Approved by voice vote.

The board approved Assistant Assessment Clerk Kevin Neely's attendance at the New York State Assessors Association Cornell Conference on July 14 and 15, 2025. Rende highlighted that Neely received a scholarship of up to $1,200, making the roughly $700 conference cost effectively no cost to the town, and noted its focus on artificial intelligence. Approved by voice vote with congratulations.

cases.name: AI Engineering Proposal — Quarry Heights Water District #9 Extension (Map, Plan & Report)
cases.applicant: Resident (Rob Kanana) / Westchester Joint Water Works

timeline.summary: During public comment, resident Rob Kanana (69 James Street) said the town board had not responded to his email about the Quarry Heights water-line project and voiced community anxiety over contamination, drought, temporary above-ground hookups freezing, and whether homes will be connected before the $1.1 million (DOJ consent-order-funded, Westchester Joint Water Works) money runs out in the rocky terrain. Supervisor Rende explained the process is unusually 'backwards' (no map-plan-report because the work is capped by available funds), apologized for missing his email, said the town knows little more than residents, and committed to a community meeting once next steps and cost-sharing are known. No vote; discussion only.

The board approved AI Engineering's proposal for the required map, plan and report to extend Water District No. 9 (Quarry Heights), the first legal step toward bringing water service to remaining area residents. The firm, already familiar with the terrain from prior feasibility and sewer work, will follow with a separate design/construction-management proposal; the town is also researching grant funding. A member confirmed any out-of-scope work would require board approval before payment. Motion carried.

cases.name: Alcohol Permit Application — Armonk Outdoor Art Show Closing Reception

timeline.summary: The board approved an alcohol permit application from Michelle Falkenstein for an opening reception for an art exhibit at the North Castle Public Library on December 7, 2024. Approved by voice vote with no discussion.

The board approved an alcohol permit application for the Armonk Outdoor Art Show 'Armonk Has a Heart' closing reception at the North Castle Public Library on October 9, 2025. Approved by voice vote with no discussion.

cases.name: Zoning Text Amendment / Local Law — 23 Bedford Banksville Road light-industrial special use (CB-B)
cases.applicant: Greenwich Realty Group LLC (attorney Tony/Anthony Veneziano; owner Mark Masiello)

timeline.summary: Attorney for Greenwich Realty asked the board to reset a public hearing to legalize two interior industrial uses (wood processing and iron/aluminum assemblage) at a split-zoned CBB/GB property. Councilman Milim strongly objected that rezoning the whole parcel to GB (as originally proposed) would expand the potential for a warehouse/self-storage use that neighbors had opposed. After a brief executive session for counsel's advice, the board directed that instead the entire parcel be zoned CBB with the two uses added by special-use permit, and voted to schedule the public hearing for February 12, 2025, pending a re-referral to the county. DiGiacinto recused herself (her husband owns 25% of Band Monk Realty, which holds a mortgage on the property).

A local law/zoning text amendment to create a narrowly-tailored light-industrial special use (wood processing and pre-cut metal/aluminum assemblage) applicable essentially only to this one 10.8-acre, 15,500 sq ft pre-1990 building, legalizing existing tenant operations while dropping a previously proposed self-storage use. Framed by the board as a compromise (worked out with planner Adam Kaufman and in executive session) to protect the Banksville hamlet from larger uses. The board opened and closed the public hearing, adopted a SEQRA negative declaration, and adopted the local law. Councilman Berra secured amendments requiring indoor storage, ventilation of fumes/odors, a 'not subsequently expanded' building limit, and town-board review/approval of the operation plan; a formal special-permit application will follow at a later meeting. DiGiacinto recused herself.

cases.name: North Castle Public Library Hourly Staff Salary Increases (effective Jan 1, 2026)

timeline.summary: The board approved hourly staff salary increases for library employees Diana Cunningham (hourly librarian), Karen Prophet (hourly librarian), Susan Medico (hourly clerk), and Nicholas Shallcross (hourly clerk), effective January 10, 2025. Passed by voice vote.

The board approved salary increases for the North Castle Public Library's hourly staff, effective January 1, 2026, consistent with the library director's memo and the budget. Adopted by voice vote after brief confirmation that the figures were budgeted.

cases.name: Alcohol Permit — Katona Classic Stage (Whippoorwill Hall)
cases.address: Whippoorwill Hall, North Castle Public Library, Armonk
cases.applicant: North Castle Revolutionary War 250 Steering Committee

timeline.summary: The board approved an alcohol permit application from the North Castle Revolutionary War 250 Steering Committee for a reception at Whippoorwill Hall on April 4, 2025 (7 PM), with a waiver of the permit fee. Members thanked committee members, including Ed Woodyard, for their work. Adopted by voice vote.
The board approved an alcohol permit application from Katona Classic Stage for theatrical performances at Whippoorwill Hall, April 24 to May 4, 2025. Routine motion carried.

cases.name: Purchase of Two Storage Container Units for IBM Community Park (Connex West)
cases.address: IBM Community Park (near the turf fields)
cases.applicant: Town of North Castle (Derosa Sports Construction via Sourcewell co-op)

timeline.summary: The board received the Westchester County DPW and NYS DEC lead-agency circulation responses, adopted a negative declaration, and approved the roughly $4.1 million agreement (via Sourcewell cooperative purchasing with Derosa Sports Construction) for artificial turf fields at IBM 1 and 2, plus a Hydro Environmental Solutions proposal for soil-fill testing. Councilman Milim championed the project with survey and park-and-rec data showing turf as the top-requested capital project; the supervisor and Councilman Hussain strongly supported paying from the ~$25M fund balance rather than bonding. Councilwoman DiGiacinto urged bonding instead and raised concerns about not doing soil testing first given possible contamination and about future capital needs (town hall, pool, water lines). Numerous residents spoke in strong support, and all items were adopted by voice vote.

The board considered a request to purchase two new green storage container units for equipment near the IBM Park turf fields, to be paid from fund balance, replacing rotted existing containers. Vitaj strongly objected that metal containers cheapen a multimillion-dollar turf investment (his "Ferrari with used tires" analogy) and pushed for a prefab garage-style structure, while DiGiacinto defended the containers as utilitarian, secure, and cost-conscious but asked for full all-in cost comparisons of any alternative. With no motion made, the item was tabled to the next meeting for staff to bring back options.

cases.name: Personnel Actions — Appointments and Terminal Leave

timeline.summary: The board approved a slate of personnel items by successive voice votes: probationary appointment of Thomas Farrington as skilled laborer in Water & Sewer (eff. March 31, 2025); salary adjustments for Library Director Kathryn Feely and Assistant Library Director Angela Cook (eff. Jan 1, 2025); terminal leave payments for William Gallagher (Water & Sewer) and Angel Morales (Police); and authorization for Patrick Ritchie to attend a NYS tax receivers/collectors training in Lake George (June 8-11, 2025). The consensus agenda was then approved.

The board approved three personnel actions by voice vote: the probationary appointment of William Etzel as Librarian 1 at the North Castle Public Library (eff. March 16, 2026), the probationary appointment of Jeffrey (Highway Department, eff. March 16, 2026), and a terminal-leave payment to Michael Cromwell of the Building Department. A consensus agenda was also approved.

cases.name: Public Hearing — 2026 Town and Special Districts Preliminary Budgets

timeline.summary: Public hearing on Board of Ethics-recommended amendments: barring a town board member/candidate from voting on matters involving anyone who contributed over $500 in the aggregate (effective no earlier than Jan 1, 2026), an apportionment rule for committee contributions, a failure-to-file-disclosure violation, applicant disclosure for real-property applications (27.6F), a bar on land-use committee members representing third parties (27.10), and a prohibition on electeds/department heads serving as political party officers (27.22-C). Supervisor Rende voiced strong opposition to the party-officer ban and mandatory contribution-based recusal as a First Amendment overreach, while other members largely supported the package with reservations. After extensive debate the board adjourned the public hearing (no adoption) and, by roll-call vote, referred both the Board of Ethics recommendations and Councilman Berra's redline changes to legal counsel for a written opinion, targeting reopening by roughly June 11.

Comptroller Abbas Sura presented the $43.7 million 2026 preliminary budget (about 3% appropriations increase), which produces a 4.81% property-tax-rate increase, uses about $3.2 million of fund balance, and overrides the state tax cap by roughly $600,000. Numerous residents objected to exceeding the tax cap and to reliance on reserves, arguing for deeper spending cuts; the board defended the plan as a fiscally responsible pivot away from years of over-hoarded reserves and deferred maintenance (citing one-off 2025 costs for roofs, salt domes, police radios, and lawsuits). No vote was taken; the board adjourned the public hearing to December 10 and agreed to hold additional public budget work sessions to look for cuts.

cases.name: Final Payment Requisition No. 1 — Southern Industries Corp. (Water District No. 4 / School Street Extension)

timeline.summary: The board awarded the construction bid for the Water District No. 4 School Street extension to Southern Industries Corp., following evaluation of 11 bids and a recommendation from the engineer's office. Members emphasized holding a pre-construction meeting as was successfully done on the prior (Casale) project. Motion carried.

The board considered the final payment requisition (~$33,900, including ~$11,600 miscellaneous additional-work allowance and a mobilization charge) to Southern Industries for the Water District No. 4 (School Street) extension, plus receipt of a general release. Councilman Berra questioned paying a mobilization charge to a contractor the town released for underperformance when a replacement contractor also had to be paid to mobilize. Supervisor Rende and Attorney Roland explained the release was a negotiated arrangement to separate quickly before winter and avoid a surety dispute. The requisition was approved by voice vote.

cases.name: Purchase of F-350 Pickup Truck for Parks Department

timeline.summary: The board approved purchasing a new Ford F-150 and F-250 for the water and sewer department through the Sourcewell cooperative contract, paid from the 2025 operating budget. The Supervisor confirmed with Sal that the vehicles were budgeted, came in under budget by over $2,000, and replace vehicles due for replacement. Adopted on a voice vote.

The board approved purchasing a Ford F-350 for the parks department from the National Auto Fleet Group through the Sourcewell contract, funded by the 2025 operating budget, at roughly a 3.5% discount. The Administrator confirmed it replaces a vehicle coming out of service. Adopted on a voice vote.

cases.name: Local Law amending Chapter 325 (Vehicles & Traffic), Section 325-55, Schedule 13 — No Parking Anytime on Old Mount Kisco Road
cases.address: Old Mount Kisco Road, Armonk (near Main Street / Wago Avenue)

timeline.summary: The board received a memo from Police Chief Simonson recommending an amendment to Chapter 325 (Vehicles and Traffic), Section 325-55, Schedule 13, to establish no-parking-anytime restrictions on portions of Old Mount Kisco Road, and scheduled a public hearing on the local law for June 11, 2025.

Amends the town code to prohibit parking on portions of Old Mount Kisco Road (east side from Main Street north to Crossroad; west side from Main Street to Wago Avenue) in response to years of resident complaints about hazardous parking by commercial employees on a narrow, curving residential road with heavy pedestrian use. Lt. McCormick presented photos and a safety analysis, noting NYSDOT had also agreed to add a stop sign at the Main Street intersection. A public hearing was opened, several residents spoke, and it was closed; the board adopted the local law (motion by Jose Berra, seconded by Barbara DiGiacinto), to be filed with the Secretary of State. Board members flagged a possible 'whack-a-mole' displacement of parked cars to be revisited if it arises.

cases.name: Payment Application No. 5 — Papatito Construction (Water District No. 4 New Well)

timeline.summary: The board awarded the bid to Papatito Construction Co. Incorporated for the Water District No. 4 new well site work and authorized the Supervisor to sign the agreement, by unanimous voice vote (water/sewer superintendent 'Sal' present and satisfied).

The board approved payment application number five to Papatito Construction for site work on the Water District No. 4 new well project. Town Administrator Kevin Hay reported strong progress, with the tank backfilled and the building expected early February. Motion made and all in favor.

cases.name: Receipt of Long Pond Dam 2025 Dam Safety Inspection Report

timeline.summary: The board approved a WSP USA proposal for engineering services for the Long Pond dam safety inspection, an obligation because DEC requires Class B dams to be inspected every four years. Supervisor Rende recused himself (a person had once consulted him about the matter in his capacity as a lawyer). Approved.
The board voted to receive the Long Pond Dam 2025 dam safety inspection report. Supervisor Rende recused himself as he has in the past. Received.

cases.name: Personnel Appointments — Librarian, Library Clerk, and Recreation Supervisor

timeline.summary: The board approved the probationary/provisional appointment of Irwin Hernandez as a Water and Sewer maintenance worker and the appointment of Luke Wynn Land as a seasonal road maintainer in the Highway Department, both effective June 16, 2025. Members welcomed the additions while noting the water/sewer department still needs more staff.

The board adopted three personnel actions effective November 10, 2025: the probationary/promotional appointment of Diana Wendell to full-time Librarian; the provisional promotional appointment of Michelle McDavid to full-time Library Clerk; and the provisional appointment of Kimberly Williams to Recreation Supervisor (Senior Citizens). Rende wished Williams luck and acknowledged the work of the outgoing Liz Duffy (staying on part-time). The librarian and clerk positions were noted as budgeted for 2025. All passed by voice vote (aye).

cases.name: Mianus River Gorge — Special Use Permit for Scientific Research Center

timeline.summary: The board received a request from Mianus River Gorge Inc. for a special use permit for a scientific research center in a residential zone and scheduled the public hearing for August 13, 2025 (moved up from a proposed September 10). Executive Director Rod Christie explained the preserve has operated at the site since the 1950s and only recently learned a special use permit was needed in connection with a building project; it has already been through zoning and planning with no objections. Approved by voice vote to set the hearing.

The board opened and closed a public hearing on a special-use permit letting Mianus River Gorge, in operation since 1953, formalize/expand its scientific research center on ~960-1,200 protected acres in a residential zone. No neighbors spoke in favor or opposition. The board adopted a negative SEQRA declaration and the resolution granting the permit; site-plan approval to follow at the Planning Board. Motions carried unanimously by voice vote.

cases.name: KSCJ Consulting Memo — New Street Names/Addresses for Eagle Ridge; Referral to E911 Coordinator

timeline.summary: The board approved the road naming committee's recommendation to name the new Eagle Ridge subdivision roads 'Kesper Crossing' and 'Parkview Road,' with notification to the town's E-911 coordinator. Councilman Hussain recused himself because he works for IBM, which is adjacent to the property, then returned. Passed by voice vote as a routine item.

The board received a KSCJ Consulting memo (dated Jan. 13, 2025) assigning new street names and addresses for the Eagle Ridge development and referred it to the town E911 coordinator. Councilman Berra recused himself, citing his association with IBM and consistency with prior Eagle Ridge recusals. Passed with Berra recused.

cases.name: Ethics Code Amendments — Work Session

timeline.summary: The Ethics Board chair asked, during public comment, to resume the ethics-code public hearing (commenced April 9) on September 24. The board discussed that special counsel Bob Spolzino delivered his opinion May 28 but no board member has yet submitted written comments to counsel; the Supervisor and members set August 27 as the deadline for member comments. Counsel (Roland) advised that if substantive changes are made the existing hearing must be closed and a new hearing re-noticed and republished. No formal vote; targeted for the September 24 meeting.

Continuation of a multi-year effort to revise the town Ethics Code, held as a work session on a rewritten draft prepared by special counsel Bob Spolzino with Board of Ethics input. Key debates: adding a sentence so a campaign loan (even if repaid) is treated as a contribution; broadening the 'interest' definition to cover an applicant's relative, partner, or business associate (with concern that 'business associate' is undefined and legally vague); the effective date of a new $500 contribution-triggered recusal rule; and Section 5, which would force land-use applicants to disclose campaign contributions to board members.
