Sitting Town Attorney; advised closing the Summit hearing with a 10-day comment period, framed the AFFH reduction as a self-executing confirmation the standard was met, negotiated the 12 Maple CBA transfer/lease provisions and reviewed the confidential parking leases, confirmed the salt-dome emergency requires a written justification letter, and clarified the Middle Patent leaf-only authorization.
Provided fund-balance transfer detail for paving/drainage and the salt-dome emergency work; furnished Middle Patent Yard removal invoices; coordinated site access.
Comptroller/Finance Director; reported strong fund balance (~$23M net after commitments), thanked the auditors, and flagged that ARPA funds must be committed by year-end.
External auditors presented the FY2023 audit with an unmodified (clean) opinion, no new GASB, and no management disagreements; Town Justice Court agreed-upon-procedures report still pending.
Water/Sewer superintendent; by email/conversation provided the Middle Patent Yard's purchase history (bought by the water district) and described how the composting footprint grew over the years.
Acting/filling in for Town Clerk Allison Simon; handled motions receipt, records, and correspondence for the meeting.

meetings.attributionNote: Raw ASR with no speaker labels; the Supervisor's presiding voice (Joseph Rende, mangled as 'Rendezvous/Endy/Randy') and roll-call votes anchored attribution. Two roll calls disambiguated members: AFFH 3-2 (Milim aye, DiGiacinto/'Digacinto' aye, Hussain/'Hussein' no, Berra/'Bera/Barra' no, Rende yes) and the 12 Maple CBA 3-1 (Milim aye, Berra aye, DiGiacinto no, Rende yes; Hussain dropped off Zoom at 12:50 a.m.). Saleem Hussain participated remotely and was intermittently cut off. Some Summit public-hearing remarks by residents (e.g., a lawyer citing ROWI general-counsel history) were kept in publicComment rather than risk mis-attributing them to a member. No Sonny Vitaj (2026 only). Non-members Adam Kaufman, Roland, Kevin, Abbas, Sal and the Bonadio auditors were routed to staffInput.

meetings.meetingSummary: The Town Board opened with a lengthy work session on the Summit Club (formerly Brynwood) permanent special use permit, working through areas of concern with the developer and town planner Adam Kaufman one at a time: guest-cottage ownership, event noise, public golf-course use during construction, membership numbers, parking, day camp, pickleball, water sampling and Audubon certification. The regular meeting then handled a recused public hearing on 23 Bedford Banksville Road, amended and approved the June 12 minutes, authorized a wetland-mitigation license/bond for the Levine property, scheduled July 24 public hearings for the Hillside Church/Little Sparrows nursery school and a local law prohibiting battery energy storage systems, named a new town road, sold a landlocked town parcel, and approved a police/highway radio system and a Westchester Joint Water Works agreement. It closed with resignations, committee appointments, liaison updates, an executive session and a memorial for community volunteer David Ashliff.
meetings.durationNote: Meeting began 5:30 PM, adjourned immediately into a Summit Club work session, then resumed the regular meeting; all five members present (Rende, DiGiacinto, Hussain, Milim, Berra). DiGiacinto recused herself from the 23 Bedford Banksville Road public hearing (family financial interest via Ban Monk Realty). Board went into executive session at the end for real-estate/advice-of-counsel matters.

cases.name: Summit Club (formerly Brynwood) — Permanent Special Use Permit Work Session
cases.address: Route 22 / Upland Avenue, Armonk (Summit Club golf course)
cases.applicant: Summit Club / developer 'Jeff' (Metropolitan Golf Group), attorney Mark Weingarten
cases.summary: Extended work session (no vote) to resolve outstanding conditions for the permanent special use permit covering the maintenance building, guest cottages and continued public golf-course use during construction of 73 residential units. The board reached near-consensus on most items: no-kitchen guest cottages limited to 20 bedrooms, a 9 PM amplified-music curfew until the amenities building is built (then the standard town noise ordinance, with events sited behind the building), public play ending October 2026 with yearly extensions, a 100-per-day day camp, deferred pickleball, water sampling per SEQRA findings, and Audubon certification applied for by April 1. The unresolved item was cottage ownership — the developer wants to pre-sell/lease units to members or passive investors placed in a management-company rental pool, while DiGiacinto and Berra worried about losing control; a no-public-posting restriction was floated as a compromise. Noise was the most contentious: Berra pushed for a stricter 'no distinctly audible noise beyond the property line' standard while the applicant and Milim argued that was legally unworkable and singled the club out. Formal action (Old Business B) was tabled for the town attorney and planner to codify the discussed terms into a resolution for a future meeting; the developer's late request to revive 88 (vs. 73) residential units was ruled out of scope.
cases.publicComment: Public hearing already closed; a few residents present but no public comment taken. Supervisor noted written comments received from Ed Woodyard, Kevin Devaney Jr., Stephen Condon, Sue Scheimer (excluded as late), Garrett Kennedy and Elon/Lon Keller. Developer disparaged neighbor Garrett Kennedy as a serial complainer, prompting a decorum reminder from Hussain.

memberPositions.evidence: Presided and steered toward resolution; thanked the applicant for removing parking-lot materials and argued 'nothing has changed in 60 years' of club use; kept the 88-unit request out of scope.

Moderated the session and played 'devil's advocate' for the applicant — argued the club-as-manager protects against bad guests regardless of who owns the cottages, and as police liaison said fears of hourly noise complaints were unrealistic.

Most resistant on noise — pressed for a stricter 'no distinctly audible noise beyond the property line' standard because the club is a for-profit venue holding frequent events, and shared DiGiacinto's unease about investor ownership of cottages.
Preferred the planner's club-owned-cottages language, worried about 'losing control' if investors buy and lease units; but found the applicant's 9 PM music limit acceptable and 'part of summer.'

Asked repeated clarifying questions on membership/guest/cottage definitions and proposed the no-public-posting compromise; publicly urged the developer to stay respectful of residents in the public forum.

cases.name: Public Hearing — 23 Bedford Banksville Road
cases.summary: A noticed public hearing on 23 Bedford Banksville Road was opened and immediately adjourned to a date uncertain because the applicant felt they were not fully ready. DiGiacinto recused herself due to a family financial interest — her husband John DiGisono owns 25% of Ban Monk Realty, which holds a mortgage on the property. The board opened and adjourned by voice votes.

memberPositions.evidence: Recused herself, citing that her husband owns 25% of Ban Monk Realty which holds a mortgage on the property.

cases.name: Approval of Town Board Minutes — June 12, 2024
cases.summary: Milim objected to minutes language stating the board 'resolved to confirm that the applicant has met the standard' to reduce the AFFH affordable-unit count from 20% to 10% (4 units to 2) on the Mock Glen project. He stated he had said clearly the applicant did NOT meet the standard but that the board was making a reasonable accommodation because the project was over 80% complete. The offending language was struck so the minutes read that the board 'agreed to allow the developer to reduce the number of AFFH units from 4 to 2.' Amended minutes approved by voice vote.

memberPositions.evidence: Refused to vote until minutes were corrected — 'I don't want the record to say that we believe they met the standard. I said clearly that they did not meet the standard,' while accepting the accommodation.
Agreed with Milim's correction and framed the change as making an accommodation based on the project being over 80% complete.

cases.name: Levine Residential Project — Wetland Mitigation License Agreement & Bond, 11 Piping Brook Lane
cases.summary: The board received the town engineer's (KSCG/J) recommendation to establish a wetland mitigation bond and a five-year monitoring/maintenance bond after an encroachment of roughly 23,680 sq ft into a conservation easement abutting the Levine property. It authorized the Supervisor to sign a license agreement (already signed by Levine and the abutting owner) allowing remediation work, with the Conservation Board having approved at least 2-for-1 mitigation. Approved by voice vote.

memberPositions.evidence: Asked whether mitigation was at least 2-for-1 and confirmed Conservation Board approval before stating he was satisfied.

cases.name: Hillside Church / Little Sparrows Nursery School — Special Use Permit Modification
cases.applicant: Hillside Church of the Christian Missionary Alliance (attorney Stephen Veneruso)
cases.summary: The board received the application to modify an existing special use permit to legalize the Little Sparrows nursery school operating six classrooms when the permit only allowed two — discovered during interior renovation permitting. The school (~60 children) also needs one likely variance for outdoor-recreation-space square footage (code requires 200 sq ft per child). The board scheduled a public hearing for July 24 and referred the application to the town and county planning boards, coordinating timing with the ZBA (meeting July 11) so the applicant can resolve everything before the September school year.

memberPositions.evidence: Worked to sequence the referral, ZBA and public hearing so the school could be legalized before September, emphasizing avoiding snags for the applicant's time constraint.

cases.name: Local Law to Prohibit Battery Energy Storage Systems (BESS)
cases.applicant: Town Board / Town Planner Adam Kaufman & Town Attorney Roland
cases.summary: The board received a draft local law (with short EAF parts 1-3, a negative declaration and lead-agency intent) to strengthen the definition of 'public utility' so that battery energy storage systems cannot be claimed as public utilities and thus effectively prohibited, prompted by a dispute in neighboring Mount Kisco. The attorney flagged that a stronger version (modeled on the Town of Evans) should also define the different BESS levels. The board declared itself lead agency, referred the law to planning boards, and scheduled a July 24 public hearing. Extended discussion centered on fire risk (volunteer fire departments cannot safely fight BESS fires) versus renewable-energy benefits; the board consensus is that the risks currently outweigh the benefits.

memberPositions.evidence: Stressed the fire departments' request not to allow BESS and that a for-profit arbitrage facility offers minimal town benefit against a fire that 'can last a month or more.'

Fully backed denying BESS but asked repeatedly to see 'the other side of the argument' — examples of towns with significant installations — before the public hearing, to be sure the record covers both risks and benefits.

As a former power-utilities analyst explained BESS economics (off-peak/on-peak arbitrage, better paired with wind), concluding the reward is real but minimal and not captured by North Castle while it bears all the risk.
Recounted the prior King Street application and fire-department opposition and urged moving forward to prohibit BESS now, revisiting the code in the future.

cases.name: Road Naming — Israel Townsend Hill (Orchard Road Subdivision)
cases.summary: The board considered the Road Naming Committee's first-choice recommendation to name a new road 'Israel Townsend Hill,' honoring a Quaker patriot buried on the property whose family were town founders. Hussain objected on principle to naming roads after individuals (citing unknown historical complexities and the risk of later reappraisal) and urged instead the committee's agreed second choice 'Townsend Farm Hill,' plus a referral to the Conservation Board and board guidance/liaison for future namings. Milim, Rende and Ed Woodyard resisted micromanaging the committee. Milim moved to adopt 'Israel Townsend Hill'; it passed 4-1 on a roll call with Hussain voting no. The board agreed to appoint Hussain as liaison to the Road Naming Committee.

memberPositions.evidence: Voted NO; argued for 'Townsend Farm Hill' to honor the family rather than one man, wanted rigorous character vetting and Conservation Board input, and warned people read road signs by literal interpretation, not intent.

Made the motion for 'Israel Townsend Hill,' opposed referrals as micromanaging the committee, and argued a historically significant figure should be recognized despite the impossibility of perfect vetting.
Voted aye and cautioned against micromanaging committees, saying a knowledgeable Road Naming Committee plus a board liaison suffices without Conservation Board referral.
Voted aye ('I'm fine with the Israel Townsend Hill').
Voted aye while noting mild reservation about 'Hill' and saying Hussain's ideas could be considered in future liaison work.

cases.name: Offer to Purchase ~1 Acre Town-Owned Property Contiguous to 21 Windmill Road
cases.address: Lot 101.42-2-8, contiguous to 21 Windmill Road, Armonk
cases.summary: The board accepted an offer (over $50,000, against ~$12,000 in back taxes) from the Bonistalls to purchase a landlocked ~1-acre town parcel acquired via in-rem foreclosure that the family had always believed they owned. The buyer will merge it into their residence lot and sign a covenant against future subdivision, avoiding a 'house behind a house' scenario; the Planning Board recommended the merger 5-0. Resolution adopted subject to permissive referendum. Berra supported this unique, sympathetic case but insisted the town develop a fair, transparent process (notifying residents/neighbors) for any future sales of town property.

memberPositions.evidence: Supported this 'unique, sympathetic' sale but pressed that in future the town should notify residents/neighbors and follow a rational, fair process rather than deciding on its own.
Agreed the parcel is unique and sympathetic (buyer thought he owned it; over $50K price vs. ~$12K taxes) and supported the merger-plus-covenant while agreeing to improve the process.

cases.name: Two-Way Radio Communication System — Metrocom Wireless (Police & Highway)
cases.applicant: Metrocom Wireless Incorporated (via Town Administrator Kevin)
cases.summary: The board approved and authorized the Supervisor to sign a Metrocom Wireless proposal (off state bid, meeting procurement policy) to replace the town's 20-year-old analog police radios with an encrypted digital system, funded from general-fund balance. The system brings the Highway Department onto the same network so police and highway can communicate directly during storms and emergencies, and eliminates dead spots where cell service fails. Approved by voice vote.

memberPositions.evidence: Highlighted that highway and police currently cannot communicate directly during storms and that the system removes communication dead spots; called it overdue.
As police liaison relayed Chief Simonson's view that it is important and necessary public safety, moved/seconded approval, noting the newest current equipment is 20 years old.

cases.name: Westchester Joint Water Works Agreement — Water District No. 8 (Airport Campus Extension)
cases.applicant: Town / Westchester Joint Water Works (Town Attorney Roland, Superintendent Sal)
cases.summary: The board approved and authorized the Supervisor to sign the Westchester Joint Water Works agreement creating Water District No. 8 (Airport Campus extension), described as the final piece securing a water supply for the airport campus property. Approved by voice vote; Supervisor thanked the attorney, Sal and others.

memberPositions.evidence: Called the agreement 'the final piece of the puzzle' giving the town a water supply — 'this is big' — and thanked staff who worked on it.

cases.name: Resignations and Committee Appointments
cases.summary: The board received resignations from James Worthman (Highway Department, eff. June 25) and Alec Tobia (Police Department, eff. June 24) — with the Administrator confirming exit interviews are conducted — and made several appointments: Ed Woodyard and Nora Manueli to the Landmark Preservation Committee (three-year terms), and Elisa (surname uncertain), Doug Mancinelli and Kate Hall to the Open Space Committee. The Landmarks appointments were expedited to ensure a quorum could bless the wording of a memorial plaque for Becky (gazebo dedication targeted for an August summer concert). All approved by voice vote.

themes.note: Dominated by the Summit Club special use permit work session, plus Hillside Church, road naming and the town-parcel sale.
Special use permits for the Summit Club and the Little Sparrows nursery school.
Cottage-ownership control and event-noise impacts on Summit Club neighbors were the sharpest disputes.
Battery-storage prohibition, Levine wetland mitigation, Audubon certification and water supply.
Minutes correction, road-naming committee guidance/liaison, and calls for a fair process on town-property sales and elections/voting information.
Police/highway radio upgrade and volunteer fire-department concerns driving the BESS ban.
Water District No. 8 airport-campus extension approved; Summit Club water withdrawal permit; sewer-line jetting.
Metrocom radio system and Westchester Joint Water Works agreement.
Two resignations and five committee appointments.
Summit Club Airbnb-style guest cottages and the Mock Glen AFFH affordable-unit reduction in the minutes.
Memorial for volunteer David Ashliff, Becky memorial plaque, and Modern Barn wine award.

staffInput.summary: Town Planner; framed each Summit Club issue with a staff-recommended solution, drafted the battery-storage local law and the road-naming/land-use referrals, and coordinated the nursery-school review timeline.

Advised on the noise-ordinance limits and special-permit standards for the Summit Club, drafted and recommended strengthening the BESS 'public utility' definition (Town of Evans model), and explained the permissive-referendum mechanism and in-rem foreclosure background for the town-parcel sale.

Presented the Metrocom radio proposal (off state bid, encrypted digital, bringing highway onto the network), reported paving on Route 128 and Virginia Road, sewer-line jetting in District 2, a maintenance-mechanic opening, and confirmed exit interviews are conducted.

Gave a community announcement on primary-election logistics and voter-information resources on the town website, and assisted the nursery-school applicant with scheduling; will handle referral and document execution.
Water/Sewer superintendent acknowledged for work on the Westchester Joint Water Works Water District No. 8 agreement.

meetings.attributionNote: Speakers were identifiable with high confidence despite the label-free ASR. The Supervisor's presiding voice = Joseph Rende (Joe). Roll-call on the road naming confirmed member identities: DiGiacinto aye, Berra (ASR 'Vera') aye, Milim (ASR 'Milam') aye, Hussain (ASR 'Hussein') no, Supervisor Rende aye — a 4-1 vote. Jose Berra (Councilman, present all of 2024) was disambiguated from Supervisor 'Joe' Rende by role: Berra was the member pushing for a stricter noise standard and questioning the parcel-sale process, addressed as 'Jose.' Non-members correctly routed out of memberPositions: developer 'Jeff'/Mark Weingarten (applicant), Adam Kaufman (planner), Roland (attorney), Kevin (administrator), Allison Simon (clerk), Ed Woodyard (Road Naming Committee, not the councilman), and attorneys Hollis, Veneruso. Sonny Vitaj not attributed (joined 2026). All five members present; DiGiacinto recused from the 23 Bedford Banksville Road public hearing.

meetings.meetingSummary: The North Castle Town Board swore in new police officer Matthew Giannella, heard a county update from Deputy County Executive Ken Jenkins, and held public hearings on the Breezemont Day Camp special use permit and a landmark designation for the Armonk Barber Pole. The board's longest debates concerned the Summit Golf Club (formerly Brynwood) temporary and permanent special use permits, both adopted 3-1, and two legal-services retainer agreements — the assignment of Roland Barone's firm to Abrams Fensterman and special counsel to fight a Greenwich CT development — which drew sharp transparency and standing objections. The board also handled a salt-dome grant application, a highway pickup-truck purchase, several personnel appointments, and routine consensus items.
meetings.durationNote: Meeting ran 5:30 PM (executive session) to about 10:15 PM. Councilman Saleem Hussain absent (celebrating his mother's 80th birthday; attempted but could not join by Zoom). Quorum of four present.

cases.name: Appointment of Police Officer Matthew Giannella
cases.applicant: North Castle Police Department (Chief Peter Simon)
cases.summary: Chief of Police Peter Simon presented Matthew Giannella, a six-year NYPD transfer with EMT and field-training credentials, as a candidate for police officer effective July 13, 2024. Chief Simon detailed the background investigation and panel interview and recommended appointment in light of an upcoming retirement and a resignation. The board approved the appointment unanimously by voice vote and the Supervisor administered the oath of office.
cases.publicComment: Officer's family present; celebratory tone, no formal public comment.

memberPositions.evidence: Called swearing in new officers 'one of the most enjoyable opportunities' of being supervisor and welcomed the officer's family.

cases.name: Westchester County Update — Deputy County Executive Ken Jenkins
cases.applicant: Westchester County (Deputy County Executive Ken Jenkins)
cases.summary: Deputy County Executive Ken Jenkins, standing in for County Executive George Latimer, gave a mid-year update covering sales-tax stabilization, a new civil-service role easing NYPD transfers, airport flight-path concerns, free Bee-Line transit for the summer, and the Route 22 crosswalk in North White Plains. Board members asked about sales-tax impacts on town revenue and pressed for county help on the crosswalk, Health Department pool-permit delays, and roadside invasive-species trimming on county roads. No action taken; the exchange was informational and cooperative.

memberPositions.evidence: Asked Jenkins to explain the sales-tax outlook and noted it also impacts the towns that share sales-tax revenue.
Urged the county to expedite the North White Plains Route 22 crosswalk, calling it 'very, very dangerous' for residents going to the community center and ball fields.
Thanked Jenkins for coming out and updating the board and for the partnership; had no questions.
Credited county HR cooperation, asked for Health Department help expediting upcoming water projects and pool inspections, and county help trimming invasive growth on county roads.

cases.name: Community Announcements — Passport Unit, Shredder, Summer Concerts
cases.applicant: Town Clerk / Town of North Castle
cases.summary: Town Clerk Allison Simon announced a county mobile passport renewal unit at Town Hall on August 28 and a mobile shredder event on September 17, both 10 AM-1 PM. She and board members also promoted the Armonk summer music concerts at the Gazebo and Music in the Square, and reminded residents to sign up for E-News and Nixle alerts. Informational only.

memberPositions.evidence: Announced the passport unit, shredder, and concert schedule and thanked the Clerk for arranging the county events.

cases.name: Special Use Permit — Breezemont Day Camp (HZBR LLC)
cases.address: Breezemont Day Camp, Armonk (Cox Avenue / Rose Hill area)
cases.summary: The board opened and held a public hearing on Breezemont Day Camp's application for a special use permit to operate a summer day camp, made permissible under a recently adopted local law allowing day camps as a special use in residential districts. Town Planner Adam Kaufman explained the planning board gave a positive recommendation, with the applicant to update plans for required 15-foot perimeter screening and parking, and to limit the PA system/bullhorn to emergencies only (no amplified music). No public spoke in opposition; board members praised the camp and its historic-building preservation. The hearing was closed with adoption of the resolution deferred until updated plans are submitted, targeting the July 24 meeting.
cases.publicComment: Camp owner Gordon Josie and director Walter Kowalczyk spoke; supportive tone. A neighbor's letter (Bonnie) found children's play sounds 'delightful' but objected to the PA system, which the applicant agreed to limit to emergencies.

memberPositions.evidence: Said the camp has never presented a traffic or noise problem for him and that residents love it; effectively made a commercial for them.
Called Breezemont a cornerstone business and 'such a good member of the community.'
Glad the applicant agreed not to use the PA/bullhorn except in emergencies, citing the neighbor's letter; praised the camp as a wonderful business.
Praised the camp's historic-building designation and work, calling it a tremendous asset, and looked forward to wrapping up the permit.

cases.name: Landmark Designation — Armonk Barber Pole
cases.address: Main Street, Armonk (in front of Manny's)
cases.summary: Following a recommendation from the Landmark Preservation Committee, the board opened and held a public hearing to landmark the roughly 100-year-old Armonk Barber Pole (a Made-in-Chicago Koch No. 909), which the property-owning family enthusiastically supported. Board members discussed only the pole (not the building) and debated adding a future designation plaque, to be placed on the building with owner permission. The hearing was closed and the board unanimously adopted the landmark designation by voice vote.
cases.publicComment: LPC representative (Ed) presented history; family (Vivian Utko, Jerry Hendricks) supportive. No opposition.

memberPositions.evidence: Called it great to landmark, praised the actively involved family, and raised adding a designation plaque so future owners know it is protected.
As LPC liaison explained landmarking only affects a building's exterior and cited Breezemont as an easy, win-win partner.
Moved to establish the landmark designation 'with gratitude' to all parties involved.

cases.name: Temporary and Permanent Special Use Permits — Summit Golf Club (formerly Brynwood)
cases.address: Summit Golf Club (formerly Brynwood), off Evergreen
cases.summary: The board considered separate resolutions for a temporary special use permit (allowing public use of the golf course during residential construction, plus a proposed maintenance building) and a permanent special use permit for the Summit Golf Club. Debate centered on the town noise ordinance (Chapter 210): Councilman Milim analyzed the code and concluded it already suffices with the added 9 PM restriction, while Councilman Berra wanted a stricter 'not distinctly audible beyond the property line' standard (matching the town planner's original staff position) and a 350-member cap, calling the project speculative. Residents on Evergreen (via attorney Garrett) asked that no amplified sound exceed the property boundary. Amendments were added, including no valet parking on public streets and broader material-storage language. Both resolutions passed 3-1 (DiGiacinto aye, Milim aye, Berra no, Rende yes; Hussain absent), the permanent one adopted with conditions including a pending zoning variance.
cases.publicComment: Residents Garrett (attorney), Jill O'Dell and Susan Youngblood of Evergreen asked that amplified sound not exceed the property line, citing an open-air facility, a nearby school, and a recent 6:30 AM lawnmower noise complaint.

memberPositions.evidence: Voted no on both permits; wanted a 'not distinctly audible beyond the property' noise standard and a 350-member cap, and called the project speculative, citing the 88-units-for-financing remark.
Seconded and voted aye; argued Chapter 210 plus the 9 PM limit is sufficient given ~250 ft to the road and ~1,000 ft to the school, and deviating from it sets a high bar.

Made the motions and voted aye but pushed successfully for a no-valet-parking-on-public-streets condition and clarifications, and argued Chapter 210 addresses noise well without holding Summit to a different standard.
Voted yes, invoked Robert's Rules to keep debate to the motion, and pushed back on characterizing the project as speculative.

cases.name: 2024 Standard Workday and Reporting Resolution (NYS Retirement System)
cases.summary: The board adopted the annual standard workday and reporting resolution required by the New York State and Local Retirement System for elected and appointed officials not on hourly payroll, who must certify hours worked (via a three-month sample, recertified each four-year term) to participate. The Clerk explained the mechanics and it passed by voice vote. Members joked about the roughly $11.85/hour effective stipend.

cases.name: NYS DEC Water Quality Improvement Grant Application — Salt Storage Domes
cases.applicant: Town of North Castle (Administrator Kevin Hay; grant writers)
cases.summary: The board took two actions on a NYS Consolidated Funding Application / Water Quality Improvement Program grant to help fund demolition of the failing existing salt storage dome, installation of a new 72-foot-diameter dome, and re-roofing/repair of the second dome, at 75% grant with a 25% town match. It authorized the Supervisor and Town Attorney to sign the grant application and adopted a resolution of support, both by voice vote. Administrator Hay and the Supervisor clarified for a resident that one dome is in jeopardy of collapse and has been shut down.
cases.publicComment: A resident asked for clarification on which structures were involved; answered by the Administrator and Supervisor.

memberPositions.evidence: Said he'd sign for a 75% grant 'any day of the week' and clarified the collapsing dome for residents.

cases.name: Purchase of 2024 Chevrolet Pickup Truck for Highway General Foreman
cases.applicant: Highway Department (General Foreman Jamie Norris); Sourcewell contract
cases.summary: The board considered purchasing a 2024 Chevrolet pickup (via Sourcewell contract, from general fund balance) for Highway General Foreman Jamie Norris, whose current Ford Explorer would move into the shared fleet to replace a 20-plus-year-old vehicle no longer roadworthy. Councilman Berra objected that the unbudgeted purchase was a hefty expense, preferred a smaller/hybrid replacement, and wanted two weeks to explore alternatives; DiGiacinto, Milim, and Rende argued a pickup better fits a working foreman's duties and a fleet vehicle is needed regardless. After debate Berra withdrew his tabling request, and the motion carried on a roll call (DiGiacinto aye, Milim aye, Berra aye, Rende yes).

memberPositions.evidence: Called it a hefty, unbudgeted purchase, wanted a smaller hybrid replacement and two weeks to review options, then relented and voted aye rather than debate further.
Relayed that Foreman Norris finds a pickup far more useful than the Explorer for carrying equipment, and that a fleet vehicle is needed regardless.
Thought a pickup a reasonable request for a highway foreman since a vehicle must be bought anyway, but was fine tabling two weeks if desired.
From business experience preferred a foreman with a work truck over a passenger vehicle, warned of losing the on-lot vehicle, and quoted his father against endless tabling.

cases.name: Assignment of Legal-Services Retainer — Stevens Barone Riley & Lewis to Abrams Fensterman LLP
cases.summary: The board considered authorizing the Supervisor to sign an assignment of the legal-services retainer from Town Attorney Roland Barone's firm to Abrams Fensterman LLP (effective Sept 1-Dec 31, 2024), as Barone merges his practice into the larger firm to create a long-term exit strategy while continuing to serve the town. Councilwoman DiGiacinto abstained, reading a prepared statement demanding full disclosure of Supervisor Rende's monetary and legal relationship with Abrams Fensterman and raising transparency and future-fee questions. Rende disclosed he has no monetary relationship but was represented by firm partner Bob Spolzino (whom he has known 30+ years) in his post-election absentee-ballot case, and stressed the merger was Barone's decision affecting all his municipal clients. Milim and Berra defended the process and criticized DiGiacinto for not raising concerns in executive session; the motion passed with DiGiacinto abstaining.

memberPositions.evidence: Abstained and read a prepared statement demanding disclosure of Rende's 'complete monetary and legal relationship' with Abrams Fensterman, questioning transparency and future fees.
Commended Barone's exit strategy, took issue with DiGiacinto for making it seem shady and political rather than raising it beforehand, and voted aye.
Voted yes; disclosed no monetary relationship, detailed the Spolzino election-case history, and called it offensive to turn the matter into a political football.
Thanked and commended Barone for looking out for long-term clients and passing on institutional knowledge; said he checked fees with the firm and got satisfactory answers.

cases.name: Special-Counsel Retainer — Greenwich American Center / King Street Development (Tishman Speyer)
cases.address: King Street (Greenwich American Center, Greenwich CT)
cases.applicant: Town of North Castle (via Town Attorney Roland Barone)
cases.summary: As an add-on item, the board considered a retainer agreement with Connecticut special counsel (subject to Barone's final review) to follow the Tishman Speyer / Greenwich American Center development on King Street in Greenwich, now proposing 198 townhouse units, to protect North Castle's interests and possibly negotiate community-benefit funding for downtown Armonk impacts. Both the motion to add the item to the agenda and the motion to approve the retainer passed 3-1, with Councilwoman DiGiacinto opposed on both, saying she was not confident the town has standing or that she understood the value well enough to commit funds. Councilman Berra championed the item and Rende joined a conference call with the proposed counsel.

memberPositions.evidence: Voted no on both the add-on and the retainer, saying she was concerned about the project's impact on Armonk but did not understand it well enough or feel confident the town had standing to commit to paying.
Championed the retainer, vetted the qualified special counsel, and urged moving expeditiously to protect the town's interests on the Greenwich development.
Voted 'definitely aye' on the retainer.
Thanked Berra and Barone, framed the goal as negotiating possible community-benefit funding, and said he was impressed by counsel on a conference call.

cases.name: Personnel Appointments, Resignation, and Liaison Assignment
cases.summary: The board unanimously approved probationary appointments of Alex Cornev and Jeffrey Osciello as Highway Department road maintainers (eff. July 15) and Kaylee Castillo as an hourly library page (eff. July 11), accepted with regret the resignation of library custodian Felix Barrios (eff. Aug 2), and appointed Councilman Saleem Hussain (absent) as liaison to the Road Naming Committee, a role he had volunteered for. All passed by voice vote.

cases.name: Discussion — Role and Guidelines for Town Board Liaison Positions
cases.summary: Prompted by the new Road Naming Committee liaison appointment, DiGiacinto asked the board to clarify what a liaison position entails, noting members are neither chair nor committee member but a bridge to the town board. Rather than a formal work session, the board reached consensus to have staff (Eliana, via Administrator Hay) draft guidelines, with members submitting their own input, referencing Barone's recollection that liaisons historically served as an information bridge.

memberPositions.evidence: Asked for a shared understanding of the liaison role, describing it as a bridge between a committee and the town board.
Suggested tasking staff to draft liaison guidelines and having members submit input rather than holding a formal work session.

cases.name: Consensus Agenda (Town Clerk Report Tabled)
cases.summary: The board approved consensus agenda items A and C by voice vote but tabled item B, the Town Clerk report, to the next meeting because the document had not appeared in members' Civic Clerk/Civic Plus portal (an ongoing software glitch). Members noted the clerk report is informational (fees/receipts) that they receive rather than approve.

cases.name: Administrator Update — Route 128 Paving and Water/Sewer Generator RFP
cases.summary: Administrator Kevin Hay reported that NYS DOT paving of Route 128 remains on schedule to begin at the end of July, with the town coordinating equipment staging, and that the Water and Sewer Department has an RFP out for annual servicing of emergency generators, due back at month's end for board adoption. Informational only.

themes.note: Two contested legal-retainer items (Abrams Fensterman assignment; Greenwich special counsel) dominated the back half of the meeting.
Summit Golf Club permits, Breezemont day camp, and barber-pole landmarking; Summit noise standard was contested.
Transparency clash over the Abrams Fensterman retainer plus liaison-role and consensus-agenda procedure.
Police officer swearing-in, road maintainers, library page, and liaison assignment all passed smoothly.
County update from Deputy County Executive Jenkins and cross-border concern over a Greenwich CT development.
Salt-dome grant, Route 128 paving, and water/sewer generator RFP.
Evergreen residents' noise concerns about the Summit golf course; Route 22 crosswalk safety.
Salt-dome project, upcoming water projects needing Health Dept expediting, and generator RFP.

staffInput.summary: Read into the record correspondence for both public hearings, announced county passport/shredder events and concerts, and explained the NYS retirement standard-workday reporting mechanics.

Explained his firm's merger into Abrams Fensterman as a long-term exit strategy affecting all his municipal clients, and recommended engaging Connecticut special counsel for the Greenwich American Center development; advised on resolution mechanics.
Explained the salt-dome grant application (75/25), justified the highway pickup-truck purchase and fleet needs, and reported on Route 128 paving and the water/sewer generator RFP.

Town Planner: relayed the planning board's positive recommendation and outstanding screening/parking items for Breezemont, drafted and clarified the Summit Golf Club permit conditions, and confirmed landmark-mapping for the barber pole.
Chief of Police: presented and recommended appointment of Officer Matthew Giannella after a comprehensive background investigation.

meetings.attributionNote: Speakers were identifiable via roll-call votes and the presiding-voice/role heuristic. ASR mangled surnames: 'Rendezvous/Randy/Rundy/Andy' = Joseph Rende; 'Digacinto/Digicinto/Digiocinto/Jacinto' = Barbara DiGiacinto; 'Millam/Millen/Milam/Miller/mounts' = Matt Milim; 'Barra/Bera/Baer/Barron' = Jose Berra. Saleem Hussain was absent (mother's 80th birthday). On the Abrams Fensterman roll call the ASR captured only Milim (aye), DiGiacinto (abstain), and Rende (yes); Berra's vote was not clearly transcribed but the motion carried and he spoke in support. Non-member speakers (Chief Simon, Deputy County Executive Ken Jenkins, attorney Mark Weingarten, resident Garrett, camp owners) were kept out of memberPositions.

meetings.meetingSummary: The Town Board opened after an executive session and handled a full agenda dominated by a bitter public dispute between Supervisor Rende and Councilwoman DiGiacinto over Rende's campaign contributions from the Abrams Fensterman law firm and related ethics/disclosure questions. Substantive business included a work session with the Open Space Committee, Conservation Board and Westchester Land Trust on exploring a community preservation plan/fund; the appointment and swearing-in of a new police officer; a public hearing granting a conditional special use permit for the Little Sparrows Nursery School expansion; a public hearing on a local law clarifying that battery energy storage systems (BESS) are not a public utility (vote deferred to fix documentation); discussion of creating capital reserve funds and committing ARPA money; approval to bid a new Water District 4 water source; and a resolution supporting renewal of the Westchester County airport terminal use agreements. The meeting closed with an emotional discussion of tree-hazard safety on state Routes 128 and 22 following a resident fatality.
meetings.durationNote: Opened 5:30 pm, immediately adjourned to executive session (advice of counsel, real estate), then reconvened. All five board members participated: Rende, DiGiacinto, Hussain and Berra in person; Milim by remote from an outside location. Quorum present.

cases.name: Supervisor's Disclosure Statement — Abrams Fensterman Campaign Contributions / Ethics
cases.summary: Rende opened by reading an email/statement disclosing that, contrary to his answers at the July 10 meeting, he had received $1,000 campaign contributions each from Abrams Fensterman LLP, attorney Robert Spolzino and attorney Albert Pirro, after having voted to assign the town's legal-services retainer to Abrams Fensterman. He asserted he had satisfied the ethics code's after-the-fact disclosure requirement and that the Ethics Board chair (Brett Summers) was satisfied. DiGiacinto, who had abstained on the underlying vote, accused him of a possible ethics violation, of citing executive-session discussion, and of orchestrating the timing to silence her; a lengthy, hostile exchange revisited the matter at the end of the meeting. Milim and Berra defended Rende, criticizing DiGiacinto for 'playing politics on camera.' No vote; resident Ed Loberman also questioned the Ethics Board timeline (meeting set for Aug 5).
cases.publicComment: Resident Ed Loberman (North White Plains) asked for clarification on Rende's contacts with Ethics Board chair Brett Summers; noted the Ethics Board's first meeting on the matter would be Aug 5.

memberPositions.evidence: Read a prepared disclosure, insisted he met full-disclosure requirements once made aware, and pushed back hard on DiGiacinto's 'lie' and ethics-violation accusations.
Alleged a possible ethics-code violation, said he disclosed executive-session content, urged him to review all his donations, and said the timing 'muzzled' her.
Confirmed the tax matter was first raised in executive session so Rende 'did not lie,' and accused DiGiacinto of turning meetings into 'a Jerry Springer show' instead of governing.

Backed Rende, called DiGiacinto's criticism 'appropriate criticism' aimed back at her, and pointed to her own family/LLC campaign contributions and his own practice of recusing on DiGiacinto-related items.

cases.name: Work Session — Community Preservation Plan / Fund (Open Space Committee, Conservation Board, Westchester Land Trust)
cases.summary: The Open Space Committee (chair Carrie Kzak), Conservation Board (Adam Barnett) and Westchester Land Trust (VP Janelle Robbins) presented land-preservation tools, focusing on a community preservation plan and an associated fund financed by a small real-estate transfer tax on home sales above the county median. They cited North Castle's 2004 open-space bond and the recent 63-acre Erico acquisition, and requested board permission to work with town professional staff (planner, attorney, assessor, clerk) to gather data and run a resident survey. The board gave informal consensus/directive (no formal vote) to let the committees proceed with staff, with survey wording to be reviewed by Adam Kaufman, counsel and the board before release. Town planner Adam Kaufman flagged state-mandated plan requirements, TDR study, five-year updates and cost/benefit considerations.
cases.publicComment: Presenters Carrie Kzak (Open Space chair), Janelle Robbins (Westchester Land Trust) and Adam Barnett (Conservation Board) advocated strongly; a sizable, supportive audience of committee members attended and nodded in agreement.

memberPositions.evidence: Said 'in concept, you got my support,' praised the committees as parsimonious with residents' money and cited the Orchard Street property as an example worth preserving.
From his remote location said he was 'fully supportive,' arguing a transfer tax would likely raise long-term property values more than its cost and preserve quality of life.
Facilitated the directive to let the committees work with staff, agreed no formal agenda vote was needed, and set up the survey-review process through the planner and counsel.

cases.name: Probationary Appointment of Matthew Greevey — Police Officer
cases.applicant: North Castle Police Department (Chief Pete Simonson)
cases.summary: Chief of Police Pete Simonson presented Matthew Greevey, a nearly nine-year NYPD officer (28th Precinct, Central Harlem) with prior Manhattan DA and National Guard experience, for a probationary police officer appointment effective July 27, 2024, tied to an upcoming retirement/transfer. The board unanimously approved the motion and Rende administered the oath of office, with a swearing-in and family photos. Sentiment was warm and celebratory.

memberPositions.evidence: Called these appointments 'the most fun and enjoyable things to do,' swore in the officer and thanked the chief for seeking qualified candidates.

cases.name: Special Use Permit — Little Sparrows Nursery School Expansion (Hillside Church of Christian Ministry Alliance)
cases.applicant: Hillside Church of Christian Ministry Alliance (attorney Steven Veneruso)
cases.summary: Public hearing on a special use permit to legalize enlargement of the Little Sparrows Nursery School from two to six classrooms, which the school had been operating for years under an old two-classroom permit. Attorney Veneruso explained a needed outdoor-recreation-space variance (code requires 200 sq ft/child; ~800 sq ft available for a typical max of 11-12 children) would still be sought from the ZBA. The board adopted a negative declaration and then a resolution granting a one-year special use permit conditioned on the ZBA variance, building-department sign-off and fire approval, and closed the hearing. Members praised the school as a good neighbor; Berra flagged a deteriorating retaining wall at the parking lot as a safety housekeeping item.
cases.publicComment: Applicant's attorney Steven Veneruso presented and answered questions; no opposition from residents.

memberPositions.evidence: Supportive but pressed that all six classrooms and egress be inspected/approved by the building and fire departments before final sign-off.

Backed the permit but raised concern about the failing railroad-tie retaining wall near where children are dropped off and asked the applicant to address it; also thanked the church for good-neighbor parking.
'Full support,' noted friends' children attended Little Sparrows and he had observed no issues with classrooms or the playground.
Supportive; raised a housekeeping point about the record confusingly referring to 'daycare' vs. 'nursery school' to avoid future confusion.

cases.name: Local Law — Clarifying That Battery Energy Storage Systems Are Not a Public Utility
cases.summary: Public hearing on a local law (originally titled to 'prohibit' BESS, corrected to a definitional amendment clarifying that a battery energy storage system is not a 'public utility'), aimed at closing a loophole after a Mount Kisco case argued BESS qualifies as a public utility substation. Attorney Doug Worden, for Catalyze Energy, urged the board instead to adopt a durationally reasonable moratorium and develop a BESS code, citing a June 2024 PSC order targeting 6 GW of storage statewide and ESRG (the town's own engineer) approval of technologies like the Tesla Megapack 2. The board and town attorney Roland Barone rejected the need for a moratorium (the use is already not permitted) but cited volunteer-fire-service and water-supply safety fears; extended discussion also covered not inadvertently restricting normal residential EV/battery uses. The board closed the hearing but deferred the vote to a future meeting to correct the local law, neg-dec and notice documents; a confirmatory motion received the county Planning Board, town Planning Board and Snyder & Snyder letters.
cases.publicComment: Attorney Doug Worden (Snyder & Snyder, for Catalyze Energy) urged a moratorium and BESS code rather than a de facto ban, arguing the technology is here now and can be deployed safely; his client attended. The board was unpersuaded on the moratorium.

memberPositions.evidence: Stressed the town's all-volunteer fire service is 'scared to death of these things' and the risk to the water supply from a thermal runaway, and rejected making policy on press releases while backing the definitional clarification.
Wanted to stay focused on the agenda item (the definitional change), said she was not comfortable with a moratorium, and wanted the documentation corrected before voting.
Questioned Worden's use-variance argument (use variances are rare/hard to get) and pressed on not restricting normal consumer/residential EV and home-battery uses when defining Type 1-3 systems.

cases.name: Approval of Town Board Minutes — July 10, 2024
cases.summary: Under old business, the board approved the minutes of the July 10, 2024 meeting. Councilman Hussain abstained because he was not present at that meeting. Otherwise routine.

memberPositions.evidence: Abstained on the July 10 minutes because he had not attended that meeting.

cases.name: Discussion — Allocation of Funds for Capital Projects / Capital Reserve Funds
cases.summary: At DiGiacinto's request the item was discussed in public session. Town Administrator Kevin Hay explained the two types of state capital reserve funds (specific vs. type, each with capital-improvement and equipment subcategories), the resolutions and permissive-referendum rules to establish or expend them, and the state comptroller's guidance that the town's healthy fund balance should be designated to specific projects (roughly no more than 15% of tax revenue undesignated). The board reached consensus to have the administrator and finance office refine project cost estimates (salt dome, turf fields, radio system, North Bridge, town-building maintenance) and then hold a work session before adopting establishing resolutions. DiGiacinto asked that library/town-building maintenance needs be folded in.

memberPositions.evidence: Supported the exercise but wanted the administrator and finance office to sharpen project numbers first, then hold a work session; stressed designations are 'not carved in stone.'
Asked to discuss publicly and pressed that significant library/town-building maintenance and upgrade needs be included in the reviewed list.
Deferred, saying he thought the topic had been fully covered.

cases.name: Q2 2024 Finance Report and ARPA Fund Commitment
cases.applicant: Director of Finance (Abbas, via Town Administrator Kevin Hay)
cases.summary: The board received the Director of Finance's July 11 memo on second-quarter 2024 revenues, expenses, budget reports and bank reconciliation (presented by Kevin Hay in the comptroller's absence). Discussion centered on roughly $1.2 million in American Rescue Plan (ARPA) funds that must be committed/spent on eligible water-and-sewer infrastructure; Milim corrected the deadline to Dec 31, 2026 (not 2025). Rende and Milim stressed urgency to designate projects and 'not mess this up.'

memberPositions.evidence: Urged getting the ARPA process moving 'ASAP' given the size of the funds, and correctly identified the Dec 31, 2026 spend deadline.
Called committing the ARPA money 'an absolute top priority' so the town does not forfeit the ~$1.2M.

cases.name: New Water Source, Water District 4 — DOH Approval and Authorization to Bid Construction
cases.summary: Water & Sewer superintendent Sal reported that, after roughly eight and a half years of work (since 2016), the county Department of Health approved a new ~350-gpm well water source in Water District 4 and authorized going to bid for a prefabricated pump house, storage tank, booster/well pumps and DOH-required treatment, at an estimated ~$1.5 million. The board received the memo and adopted a motion approving the new source and authorizing the bid (hoped out to bid by late fall). Members tied the project to potentially committing ARPA funds, given water/sewer eligibility.

memberPositions.evidence: Praised Sal, wanted to commit ARPA money to the project once numbers firm up, and pushed to notify the funding agency now that the project is identified.
Supportive; pressed on the spend deadline/risk of delay and correctly established the Dec 31, 2026 ARPA deadline gives some breathing room.
Asked when the long-running project would actually be completed and whether the timeline fit funding constraints.

cases.name: Request to Purchase Town-Owned Property at 533-535 Main Street, Armonk (Frank Madonna Sr.)
cases.summary: The board received a letter from Frank Madonna Sr. seeking to buy the ~0.06-acre town-owned former oil-depot parcel (acquired via in-rem foreclosure, ~$353K spent on tank cleanup), evidently to relocate two AFFH affordable units from the Byram condominium project there. A majority of the board expressed no interest in rezoning the tight, CB-Armonk-zoned parcel to residential or moving the affordable units off-site; Berra and Milim opposed on principle (AFFH integration and 'moral hazard' of bailing out a developer's economics), while DiGiacinto was more open/empathetic to the developer's post-COVID financial hardship. No action beyond receiving the letter; the board left the parcel's for-sale status essentially unchanged and discussed possible future parking uses.

memberPositions.evidence: Said he had 'no interest whatsoever' in the proposal, called it 'a horrible place' for residential use (wouldn't even put a dog park there).
Okay to sell the parcel but opposed rezoning it residential; invoked 'moral hazard,' warning against one-off exceptions that bail out developers who overpay and then seek density.
Argued the AFFH goal fails if affordable units can be relocated wherever a developer wants; said consistency matters and he'd shared this position with residents.

Empathetic to the developer's post-COVID financial difficulty and open to considering the sale, citing existing separate affordable units (near the Beehive) that fostered community, while respecting the majority.

Criticized AFFH as a 'one size fits all' concept ill-suited to high-land-cost suburban parcels and, via a 'Mr. Deeds' analogy, noted developers never return profits, showing little interest in the specific request.

cases.name: Resolution Supporting Renewal of Westchester County Airport Terminal Use Agreements
cases.applicant: Intermunicipal Airport Master Plan Task Force
cases.summary: The board received the Airport Master Plan Task Force's July 10 request and adopted a resolution recommending Westchester County renew and reaffirm, with updates, the terminal use agreements of the commercial airlines operating at Westchester County Airport. Members praised town representatives Larry Ruozzi and Michael Pollack, noted the airport would not expand and that commercial flights are only ~15% of airport traffic, and adopted the resolution as the task force's document.

memberPositions.evidence: Called it a sensible, practical agreement, made the motion to adopt, and warmly thanked reps Larry Ruozzi and Michael Pollack for their volunteer work.
Said he could 'tinker at the edges' but by and large agreed, deferring to the town's two capable airport representatives.
Agreed with the airport representatives after reading the document through.

cases.name: Authorization of Leave of Absence — Employee No. 003937
cases.summary: The board authorized a leave-of-absence request for employee number 003937, a Unit 2 contract requirement that the board authorize the extent of the leave. Routine; questions were answered offline and the motion carried unanimously.

memberPositions.evidence: Confirmed his questions on the leave request had already been answered before voting yes.

cases.name: Liaison Update — Pool Renovation and Turf Field Projects
cases.summary: Milim gave a liaison update that the pool renovation and turf field projects (with Kellard consultants, Kevin Hay and Recreation Superintendent Matt Traynor) are progressing well. The turf field can use a state bidding co-op system to shorten timelines and save money, with detailed, near-executable cost figures expected within a couple of months; pool renovation options will be brought back to the board.

memberPositions.evidence: Reported good progress and highlighted the state bidding co-op as a way to save time and money on the turf field.
Praised the state-bidding approach ('great idea, great fit') and asked how it applies to turf-field square footage and labor.

cases.name: Tree-Hazard Safety on State Routes 128 and 22 — Letter to State Officials
cases.summary: Prompted by a fatal accident (resident Kathy Tuziani killed April 4 when a tree fell on her car on Route 128) and a recent large branch fall near the same site that damaged power lines and caused a fire, the board discussed tree-hazard safety. Rende read a letter he was sending to Senator Mayer, Assemblyman Burdick and DOT officials urging proactive state tree assessment and trimming along Routes 128 and 22, and directed the highway foreman to trim aggressively with additional funds if needed. DiGiacinto conveyed the Tuziani family's plea for urgency. Kevin Hay noted state DOT paving on Route 128 begins around July 28.
cases.publicComment: Concerns relayed on behalf of resident Michael Tuziani, whose wife died in the April tree-fall accident, urging immediate action.

memberPositions.evidence: Drafted and read a letter to state legislators and DOT urging aggressive tree assessment/trimming and directed the highway foreman to prioritize trimming.
Emotionally relayed the Tuziani family's plea, stressed the corridor must be a priority, and pressed that the town act before another tragedy.

themes.note: Dominated by the hostile Rende-DiGiacinto ethics/disclosure dispute over campaign contributions and executive-session conduct.
Strong support for exploring a community preservation plan/fund; caution and safety fears on battery energy storage systems.
Capital reserve fund creation and urgency to commit ~$1.2M ARPA money by end of 2026.
Little Sparrows permit approved; board resisted rezoning the Madonna parcel and relocating AFFH units; BESS definitional change.
Long-awaited new Water District 4 well source approved to bid at ~$1.5M.
New police officer sworn in; volunteer-fire safety fears drove BESS caution; tree-hazard road safety after a fatality.
Police officer appointment and a Unit 2 leave-of-absence authorization.
Letter to the state urging tree assessment/trimming on Routes 128 and 22.
Board largely opposed relocating AFFH affordable units to the Madonna parcel.
Resolution supporting renewal of Westchester County airport terminal use agreements.
Pool renovation and turf field projects advancing via state bidding co-op.

staffInput.summary: Explained the two types of state capital reserve funds and the resolution/permissive-referendum rules; presented the Q2 finance report in the comptroller's absence and flagged the ~$1.2M ARPA commitment; provided a state DOT Route 128 paving-start update; supported the water and recreation project timelines.

Advised on parliamentary procedure and the chair's discretion; clarified the BESS local law is a definitional change (BESS already not a permitted use, no moratorium needed) and that documentation should be corrected before voting; advised on the Little Sparrows conditional permit and on the town-owned Madonna parcel's history and sale process.

Town Planner: flagged state-mandated requirements, TDR study, five-year updates and cost/benefit analysis for a community preservation plan; explained the three-stage Little Sparrows approval path and BESS Type 1-3 (NYSERDA) definitions and residential-accessory-use questions; described the Madonna parcel's zoning and prior sketch plan.

Water & Sewer superintendent: reported county DOH approval of the new ~350-gpm Water District 4 well after 8.5 years, detailed the ~$1.5M prefab pump-house/treatment scope, and urged tying ARPA funds to shovel-ready water/sewer projects without jeopardizing grants.

Gave community announcements (Nixle alerts, E-News, summer concerts, mobile passport unit Aug 28, shredder truck Sept 17) and advised on public-hearing procedure (receiving recommendations, opening/closing hearings).
Chief of Police: presented Officer Matthew Greevey's background and recommended his probationary appointment.

meetings.attributionNote: No speaker labels in the ASR; speakers were identified via role (presiding/supervisor voice = Rende), direct address ('Matt,' 'Barbara,' 'Jose,' 'Mr. Hussein'), motion/second patterns and context. Roll-call-style votes were mostly voice votes ('all in favor, aye') without named tallies, limiting per-member vote attribution. All five members participated (Milim by remote from an outside location); Berra attributed as councilman ('Jose') distinct from Supervisor Rende. ASR manglings normalized: DiGiacinto (Digacinto/DeJacinto/Digisono), Hussain (Hussein; also rendered 'Celine'/'Selena'/'Salim'), Rende ('Rendez/Rendezvous/Randy'), Berra ('Jose'). Some extended BESS (EV/consumer-use) and Madonna-parcel AFFH exchanges were hard to pin to a specific councilman and were attributed at lower confidence (notably the AFFH-consistency remarks tentatively to Hussain).

meetings.meetingSummary: The North Castle Town Board opened after executive session, promoted Police Officer Christopher Costa to Sergeant, and dedicated the Armonk gazebo to former board member Becky Kidrich. The board adopted a local law clarifying that battery energy storage systems (BESS) are not public utilities, received a basis-of-design report for interconnecting Water Districts 8 and 4 (a new booster station and eliminated 1-million-gallon tank), and authorized the Westchester Joint Water Works agreement to begin extending public water to Quarry Heights. The most contested item was floodplain mitigation for artificial turf at IBM Community Park, approved 4-1 with Councilwoman DiGiacinto opposed. The board also handled numerous bonds, permits, appointments, an alcohol permit, event requests, and set two September 11 public hearings.
meetings.durationNote: Full board present: Supervisor Rende, DiGiacinto, Hussain, Milim, and Berra. Meeting opened at 5:30 with an executive session on interviews, personnel, and real estate before the public session.

cases.name: Probationary Appointment of Christopher Costa to Police Sergeant
cases.summary: The Police Chief requested promotion of Officer Christopher Costa, a nine-year veteran, field training officer and EMT, to the budgeted, vacant patrol sergeant position effective August 17. The vacancy arose from Sergeant Sabatella's transfer to detectives following Detective Sergeant Finoteri's retirement. Board members offered congratulatory remarks praising Costa's finance background and record, and the probationary promotion was adopted by voice vote. Costa introduced his family, who were seated in the audience.
cases.publicComment: Costa's family attended in support; celebratory tone.

memberPositions.evidence: Praised the department as 'no finer police department in Westchester County' and thanked the chief before making the promotion motion.
'I couldn't agree more. Congratulations.'
Recalled hiring Costa from the finance world and said he was 'not surprised' at the promotion.
'Fully support this and really excited for you, Chris.'

cases.name: Dedication of Armonk Gazebo to Becky Kidrich
cases.summary: The Supervisor announced completion of a long-delayed dedication of the gazebo to former deputy supervisor and board member Becky Kidrich, prompted originally by resident Sue Miller. A plaque was made and mounted to a stone taken from Kidrich's former garden, with help from the Landmark Preservation Board, Parks & Rec Board, Highway Department, and the Supervisor's confidential secretary Josephine Egan. The unveiling was scheduled for the final outdoor gazebo concert on Saturday. This was an announcement, not a vote.
cases.publicComment: Referenced resident Sue Miller's earlier advocacy; positive.

memberPositions.evidence: Credited as a longtime advocate for the dedication and praised Josephine Egan's work: 'if it weren't for Josephine, we would not be having this ceremony.'
Led the effort to completion and expressed pleasure at finally making it a reality.

cases.name: Board of Ethics Statement Regarding Supervisor's Disclosure
cases.summary: During public comment, Board of Ethics chair Brett Summers read a statement, authorized by the full Ethics Board at its August 5 meeting, correcting Supervisor Rende's July 24 work-session assertion that the Ethics Board had found he satisfied full disclosure requirements under Section 276. Summers stated he had only provided informal guidance on July 12 and could not speak for the board absent a formal meeting. No board action was taken; the item was informational/critical public comment.
cases.publicComment: Ethics Board chair Brett Summers delivered a formal correction of the Supervisor's prior public characterization; measured but pointedly critical tone.

cases.name: Approval of Town Board Minutes — July 24, 2024
cases.summary: The board approved the minutes of the July 24, 2024 meeting by voice vote with no discussion.

cases.name: Local Law Amending Definition of Public Utility to Address Battery Energy Storage Systems (BESS)
cases.summary: Following a public hearing closed in July, the board adopted a corrected local law amending the definition of 'public utility' to make clear that a battery energy storage system (BESS) is excluded and cannot claim public-utility status as a zoning loophole; only Level 1 and Level 2 systems are covered, with Level 3, Tesla chargers, solar, and cars excluded. The board adopted a negative SEQRA declaration and then the local law by voice vote. Members framed it as a temporary stopgap pending safety-technology maturation and discussed proactively identifying appropriate zones (avoiding sensitive environmental areas and areas without public water). The Town Attorney noted the state could still preempt via an override law.
cases.publicComment: Hearing already closed; no residents spoke. An applicant had earlier hinted at possible litigation.

memberPositions.evidence: Raised detailed concerns about residential capacities exceeding Level 2 (reverse-charging cars), supported it 'as a band-aid fix' but urged revisiting it, warning the restriction could push residents into less-safe home installs and 'endanger our town more than it helps.'
Agreed it is a stopgap and suggested proactively considering permitted zones, excluding sensitive environmental areas and areas without public water.
Asked clarifying questions about whether a state preemption or a defined term in town code could override the local law.

cases.name: Extension of Special Use Permit for Additional Horses — 263 Bedford Banksville Road
cases.applicant: Hackerman, Tortorella & Weckstein LLP (Jerry Tortorella) for the property owner
cases.summary: Counsel requested a first extension of a special permit (originally granted September 13, 2023) for additional horses as a personal accessory equestrian use, after delays obtaining Westchester County Health Department approvals. Nothing about the application had changed. The board found it straightforward and adopted the extension resolution by voice vote.

memberPositions.evidence: 'We had scrubbed it pretty carefully back then... this is one of the easier things.'

cases.name: Extension of Wetland Mitigation Planting Bond and Monitoring Bond — 45 Hurlingham Drive
cases.summary: On the town engineer's (KSCJ/Kellard) recommendation, the board approved extension of a wetland mitigation planting bond and a five-year extension of the maintenance and monitoring bond. The applicant said most work is complete and did not object to the town continuing to hold security. Added to the agenda late; approved by voice vote.

cases.name: Basis of Design Report — Water Storage Tank, Booster Station, and Interconnection of Water Districts 8 and 4
cases.applicant: Water & Sewer Dept (Sal Misisti); D&B Engineers & Architects
cases.summary: The board received (by voice vote) a July 2024 basis-of-design report evaluating interconnection of Water District 8 (New King Street / Airport Campus, sourced from Westchester Joint Water Works) with Water District 4 to secure an additional water source for downtown Armonk. Engineer Andrew Grundy presented the history and options; the selected approach eliminates the previously proposed 1-million-gallon Cooney Hill tank (saving ~40% of cost) in favor of drawing WJWW water on demand via a booster station on an Airport Campus parcel to be dedicated to the town. Members discussed grant pursuit, coordination timing with Airport Campus, rehabilitating the Miller Circle tank, and future extension toward Water District 2 and the high school. A member briefly moved to recuse over IBM being a District 4 customer but withdrew after the Town Attorney advised there was no special benefit to IBM.
cases.publicComment: No residents spoke.

memberPositions.evidence: Praised the evolving, cheaper design, pressed on grant availability and Airport Campus coordination timing, and called it 'a very prudent thing to do' given climate-driven water scarcity.
Emphasized the townwide benefit and the added water capacity 'well above what we needed,' and questioned coordination and legal document status.
Asked how District 4 would balance the new well with WJWW supply and about extension logic/cost allocation toward District 2.

cases.name: Armonk Close (former Lumberyard) — Sanitary Sewer Main Dedication and Maintenance Bonds — 154 Bedford Road
cases.summary: The board acted on the town engineer's recommendations to accept dedication of the sanitary sewer main extension into Sewer District No. 2 and to establish related maintenance bonds for the Armonk Close project. Because the applicant had submitted only electronic drafts, the Town Clerk lacked original ink documents; the board approved the acceptances and bonds contingent on receipt of original documents satisfactory to the Town Attorney, to avoid delaying the building's certificate of occupancy. Approved by voice vote.

memberPositions.evidence: Questioned whether a bond is absolute and whether the board can ever waive it; accepted the answer given repaving timing.

cases.name: Summit Club at Armonk (former Brynwood) — SPDES Permit and Paper Sewer District
cases.summary: The board received (by voice vote) Summit Club's draft SPDES discharge permit, permit fact sheet, and NYSDEC notice of complete application for a resized wastewater treatment plant Summit will operate. The Town Attorney explained that a transportation-corporation 'paper' sewer district petition (for ~73 homes) will come next meeting and sit dormant unless the private operator defaults, in which case the town would step in with an operating district funded by those residents. Treated as a formality/notification.

cases.name: Local Law Amending Chapter 336 (Water) — Hydrant Fees and Final Water Meter Reading Fee
cases.summary: The board received a memo, short environmental assessment form, and lead-agency declaration for proposed local laws to collect hydrant fees in Water Districts 1, 2, 4, 5, and 8 via quarterly customer water bills, and a final water meter reading fee in all districts. Items one through four were approved by voice vote and a public hearing was scheduled for September 11, 2024. The Supervisor noted the change lets fire districts avoid budgeting for hydrant costs.

cases.name: IBM Community Park Turf Field Improvements — Floodplain Mitigation Approval
cases.summary: The board considered a memo requesting approval to use a portion of the Water/Sewer superintendent's adjacent property to mitigate 100-year floodplain storage lost by adding up to 3 inches of fill and a short retaining wall behind the outfields of Fields 1 and 2 (a step toward possible artificial turf, which has not yet gone to bid). The plan was developed with NYSDEC. Councilwoman DiGiacinto sought to table and refer it to the Conservation Board, objecting that costs were unknown and the floodplain is environmentally sensitive; Councilman Milim countered that approval carries no cost and characterized the referral as an unnecessary delay tactic, leading to a sharp exchange. The approval passed 4-1 on a roll call, with DiGiacinto opposed.

memberPositions.evidence: Moved to table and refer to the Conservation Board; 'I just can't see approving something that I have absolutely no idea what it's going to cost'; voted No.
'There is no cost of agreeing to do this part'; said referral would be burdening a project with 'unnecessary administrative things'; noted the fields were dry when he visited; voted Aye.
Framed it as a DEC-directed mitigation of existing ball fields, mediated the exchange, and voted Yes.
Voted Aye on the roll call.
Voted Aye on the roll call.

cases.name: Hidden Oak Subdivision (Kevin McKenna) — Recommendation on Bond Amounts
cases.summary: The board considered KSCJ/Kellard recommendations for construction performance bond amounts for the subdivision road, water main extension, and stormwater drainage system. Because no actual bonds had been drafted or reviewed by counsel, the board declined to establish the bonds and only received Kellard's recommended amounts, opting for a two-step process with the actual bonds to return on a future agenda. Received by voice vote.

memberPositions.evidence: 'I don't feel comfortable without... voting on something that hasn't been seen by and approved by town counsel'; pushed for a two-step process.

cases.name: Purchase of Salt Spreader from Sourcewell Contract
cases.summary: The board approved a request to purchase a slide-in salt spreader (with brine tanks) via Sourcewell contract, paid from the highway fund balance, repurposing a truck chassis whose dump body was damaged rather than discarding the truck. Approved by voice vote.

cases.name: Extension of Construction Performance Bond — Subdivision, 7 Pine Ridge Road
cases.summary: On the town engineer's recommendation, the board approved a seven-year extension of a construction performance bond. A member had worried inflation over seven years would leave the original amount inadequate, but confirmed with JMC and Kellard that most construction is complete, so the existing bond is sufficient; a future bond reduction was anticipated. Approved by voice vote.

memberPositions.evidence: Raised an inflation concern, then relayed Kellard's memo confirming the bond remained adequate and seconded.

cases.name: Rosenthal Residence — Wetland Mitigation and Monitoring Bonds — 10 Creamer Road
cases.summary: On the town engineer's recommendation, the board approved establishment of a wetland mitigation bond and a five-year monitoring/maintenance bond. The Town Attorney had seen a draft and confirmed no contingency was needed. Approved by voice vote.

cases.name: Armonk Cider and Donut Festival, Jamie's 5K Run, and Byram Hills Carnival — September 22, 2024
cases.applicant: Armonk Chamber of Commerce and Byram Hills Preschool Association
cases.summary: The board approved the annual festival, 5K run, and preschool carnival for September 22. Discussion focused on road markings after a past event used non-removable paint; the board reaffirmed only non-permanent directional signage may be used and directed the Town Administrator to permanently update the permit form accordingly. Approved by voice vote with that modification.
cases.publicComment: Event organizers present but did not formally address the board.

memberPositions.evidence: Made the motion and raised the road-marking/signage question to protect town roads.

cases.name: Alcohol Permit — Burke Neurological Institute Retreat at Lombardi Park
cases.address: Lombardi Park Pavilion and Clark Field
cases.summary: The board approved an alcohol permit for a staff retreat on September 5, 6, and 12, subject to updated indemnity and release language matching corrections made on other recent permits to better protect the town. Approved by voice vote.

cases.name: Donation to Recreation and Parks Department from Byram Hills Preschool Association
cases.summary: The board accepted, with appreciation, a donation to the Recreation and Parks Department. Approved by voice vote with no debate.

cases.name: Special Event Permit — Jewish Board of Family and Children Services Cycling Fundraiser at Congregation B'nai Israel
cases.applicant: Jewish Board of Family and Children Services
cases.summary: As a late addition, the board received a special event permit application for a September 15 cycling fundraiser relocating its base to Congregation B'nai Israel (tents, breakfast/lunch, vendors) because of construction at Purchase College. The board received the application and scheduled a public hearing for September 11, 2024, pending fire, police, and town planner review. Councilman Milim recused himself as a member of the congregation.

memberPositions.evidence: Recused himself as a member of Congregation B'nai Israel; abstained from the vote.

cases.name: Bid Award — Wampus Brook Park North Bridge Replacement
cases.summary: The board awarded the bid for replacement of the north bridge at Wampus Brook Park to Mega Painting and Contracting and authorized the Supervisor to sign the agreement. Members expressed relief that, after years of rebids at unreasonable prices, a sensible bid had finally come in. Approved by voice vote.

memberPositions.evidence: Noted it 'amazes me' the project finally got a reasonable bid after years of 'crazy numbers.'

cases.name: Annual Emergency Generator Service — Peak Power Systems (Water & Sewer)
cases.summary: The board approved a proposal from Peak Power Systems for annual emergency generator service of 15 units in the Water and Sewer Department and authorized the Supervisor to sign. Treated as straightforward; approved by voice vote.

cases.name: Indoor Sports Facility Operation Agreement — CDC Development (Tech Track Sports Center)
cases.applicant: CDC Development Program Properties Inc. (Tech Track Sports Center)
cases.summary: The board approved a proposal for continued operation of the indoor sports facility by CDC Development (Tech Track Sports Center) for another year and authorized the Supervisor to sign. Approved by voice vote.

cases.name: Westchester Joint Water Works Agreement — Quarry Heights Water Infrastructure Extension
