cases.summary: The board authorized the Supervisor to sign an agreement with Westchester Joint Water Works (WJWW) to begin extending public water to the long-troubled Quarry Heights neighborhood, where wells have dried and been contaminated. WJWW, under a DOJ/DEC consent order, earmarked ~$1.1 million in lieu of penalties to extend mains and make roughly 14 connections; the agreement commits the town to later form a water district (in reverse of the usual order) to absorb those and remaining properties, buy water from WJWW, and resell it. Sal Misisti explained plans to install three master-meter interconnection points and later extend districtwide, pursuing grants given the high rock-excavation cost. Residents Diana Kandrea and Nico Marino pressed for equitable connection of all homes and possible cost recovery from the contaminator; the board committed to a special public informational meeting. Approved by voice vote.
cases.publicComment: Residents Diana Kandrea (69 James) and Nico Marino (9 William St.) spoke, frustrated by delays and confusion, seeking assurance all homes will be connected and that contamination-responsible parties help fund the work; cautiously hopeful overall.

memberPositions.evidence: Committed the town to resolving the problem 'cost effective for all,' urged cautious optimism, and proposed a special informational meeting for affected residents.
Shared his own neighborhood's phased sewer experience, saying neighbor cooperation 'advances the ball quite a bit.'
Pressed that connections be equitable: 'I want to make sure it's not just some people... we all need water here, not just some people.'

cases.name: Probationary Appointment of Jake Terenzi — Maintenance Mechanic
cases.summary: The board approved the probationary appointment of Jake Terenzi as maintenance mechanic effective August 15, 2024. The Supervisor praised Terenzi's trade skills, especially fence work that has saved the town outside-contractor costs, in support of the new maintenance department. Approved by voice vote.

memberPositions.evidence: Made the motion, calling Terenzi 'a very skilled person.'

cases.name: Probationary Appointment of Jim Loewenburg — Parks Groundsman
cases.summary: The board approved the probationary appointment of Jim Loewenburg as parks groundsman in the Parks and Recreation Department effective September 3, 2024, by voice vote with no discussion.

cases.name: Terminal Leave Payment — Kevin Finateri, Police Department
cases.summary: The board approved the terminal leave payment for retiring Police Department member Kevin Finateri, with members wishing him well. Approved by voice vote.

cases.name: Annual $500 Stipend for Deputy Supervisor Jose Berra
cases.summary: The board approved a $500 annual stipend for Deputy Supervisor Jose Berra, retroactive to January 1, correcting a reorganization oversight; the Supervisor noted past deputy-supervisor stipends ran much higher and that Berra himself asked only for $500. Councilwoman DiGiacinto explained her history of voting for and against such stipends and endorsed the modest amount as a fitting token of appreciation. Approved by voice vote.

memberPositions.evidence: Called the $500 'a token of appreciation... the right amount... save the town a little bit of money,' recounting her prior votes on the stipend.

cases.name: Court Office Personnel Attendance at NYS Magistrates Court Clerks Conference
cases.summary: The board approved attendance by court office personnel (Nancy and Elizabeth) at the New York State Association of Magistrates Court Clerks conference, a budgeted expense. Approved by voice vote.

cases.name: Consensus Agenda (Items A-E)
cases.summary: The board adopted the consensus agenda (items A through E) in a single voice vote without individual discussion.

cases.name: Liaison Update — Community Pool Facility Planning
cases.summary: In liaison updates, the board discussed the ongoing planning for the town pool, addressing four interrelated categories: the pool and its mechanicals, the building, the decking, and overgrown former tennis courts. Members stressed that biweekly consultant calls have not yet produced firm options or a budget, cautioned residents against circulating misinformation, and clarified the intent is to keep the pool open next year while planning a multi-year overhaul with possible year-round building use. No vote taken; a future work session with Matt Traynor was proposed.
cases.publicComment: Referenced widespread resident questions and rumors that the pool would close next year.

memberPositions.evidence: Requested a work session with Matt Traynor, urged transparency about 'what we don't know,' and explained the interrelated planning cadence.
Cautioned against premature numbers, called the site beautiful with 'a lot of potential,' and aimed for the best long-term facility.
As pool liaison, described the four planning categories and their interdependencies.

cases.name: Liaison Update — Armonk Fire Department / Bristol EMS Transport Agreement
cases.summary: In a liaison update, the Supervisor reported that the Armonk (volunteer) Fire Department, fire commissioners, the Bristol senior facility, the Town Attorney, Town Administrator, and the planning board reached an agreement resolving the misuse of volunteer firefighters for non-emergency transports from the Bristol. The agreement obligates the Bristol to maintain EMTs and eliminate inappropriate calls, with a backstop enforcement mechanism. Informational; no vote.

memberPositions.evidence: Praised the multi-party effort producing a workable agreement with an enforcement backstop, calling it 'good for the town.'

meetings.meetingSummary: The North Castle Town Board opened with a work session on a proposed dog park at IBM Community Park, then swore in two new police officers and promoted a detective sergeant. It held a public hearing approving a special-event permit for a nursery fall festival, adopted an order scheduling a sewer-district public hearing, and tabled a set of Eagle Ridge school-bus easement documents that were not ready. The board also discussed a subdivision address-change notification law (scheduling a November public hearing), granted a resident a grace period on an address-change enforcement fine, approved going to bid on the Kent Place parking lot, accepted a $20,000 Lions Club donation, and waived permit fees for an October 7th memorial vigil.
meetings.durationNote: Councilman Saleem Hussain absent (traveling on business); four of five members present, quorum met. Sonny Vitaj not yet on board (2026).

cases.name: Proposed Dog Park at IBM Community Park
cases.address: IBM Community Park, 205 Business Park Drive, Armonk
cases.applicant: Recreation & Parks Department (Matt Traynor) / residents Molly Weinrock & Juliet
cases.summary: A work session on creating a roughly 105-by-90-foot fenced dog park at IBM Community Park, championed by Rec Superintendent Matt Traynor and residents Molly and Juliet Weinrock. The board debated rules, permits, fees, vaccinations, and a hold-harmless agreement, with the consensus favoring a streamlined single process run through the Town Clerk with no separate fee and no separate permit. Next steps: firm cost numbers, possible ARPA funding, a check with Town Planner Adam Kaufman on wetlands/buffer, and a later public hearing to codify rules and amend the dog code. No vote was taken.
cases.publicComment: Residents Molly and Juliet Weinrock presented and thanked the board; tone enthusiastic and appreciative. Board praised the young resident's civic involvement.

memberPositions.evidence: Backed the project, favored keeping rules simple and free ('this is what a municipality does, we provide parks'), suggested using ARPA funds and allowing non-residents.
Strongly supportive of a dog park but pushed an extensive Bedford-model rule set: permits, additional vaccinations, hold-harmless agreements, spay/neuter, no toys, cameras, resident-only initially.
Introduced the resident proponents; favored an 'enhanced license' recommendation over a separate permit, wanting the process kept practical.
Repeatedly urged a streamlined, single process through the clerk's office and no second permit; comfortable with ARPA funding.

cases.name: Police Appointments — Officers James Lucas & Reynaldo Pena; Promotion of Anthony Sabatella to Detective Sergeant
cases.summary: Chief Simonson presented James Lucas (veteran NYC DEP police officer) and Reynaldo Pena (former NYPD/Danbury officer) for appointment as police officers, and Sergeant Anthony Sabatella for promotion to Detective Sergeant, all effective September 28, 2024. All three were approved unanimously (motions made and seconded, 'all in favor — aye') and the two officers were sworn in. The board noted the department is now at its budgeted officer strength for the first time in years.
cases.publicComment: Officers' families attended for the swearing-in; celebratory tone.

memberPositions.evidence: Called swearing in officers 'one of my favorite things to do' and praised the department's professionalism at length.
'I have never had one resident say anything but positive things about our police officers and our police chief.'
Noted officers had been working heavy overtime due to being short-staffed and thanked them for keeping residents safe.
Made the motion (joking he would do it 'in Spanish') to appoint Reynaldo Pena.

cases.name: Special Event Permit — Troy's Nursery Garden Design LLC Fall Festival
cases.applicant: Troy's Nursery Garden Design LLC (Maria Cece)
cases.summary: Public hearing on a special-event permit for a fall festival (pumpkin/face painting, petting zoo, possible band) on October 6th. The board opened the hearing, read correspondence, adopted a negative declaration, and adopted the approving resolution, all by unanimous voice vote. Applicant Maria Cece asked whether repeat events could avoid the recurring permit process; the board and Town Planner Adam Kaufman explained a blanket approval covering multiple pre-dated events for the year could be possible.
cases.publicComment: Applicant Maria Cece spoke, generally satisfied but frustrated by the recurring administrative burden (~8 hours per event); board sympathetic.

memberPositions.evidence: Explained the permit exists mainly for public-safety/traffic control and that the town rarely denies such applications.
Had previously spoken up for the applicant; asked how many staff hours the process took, sympathetic to easing it.

cases.name: Order Calling Public Hearing — Summit Club Sewer District & Sewage Works Corporation
cases.summary: The board adopted an order calling a public hearing for October 9, 2024 on the petition, map and plan to form the Summit Club Sewage Works Corporation and establish the Summit Club sewer district. Town Attorney Roland Barone explained the district would 'sit on a shelf' until needed and that the order required a roll-call vote under the Transportation Corporations Law, tied to the applicant's financing and imminent plant construction. Roll call passed 4-0 (Milim, DiGiacinto, Berra, Rende aye; Hussain absent).

memberPositions.evidence: Asked why the roll-call order was required now; satisfied by counsel's explanation and voted aye.

cases.name: Eagle Ridge (3 North Castle Drive) — Declaration and School Bus Easement / Dedication Agreements
cases.applicant: Summit Club / Mad Madonna Armonk LLC & IBM (Gary Rosen for Corey Salomon)
cases.summary: A package of documents for a school-bus easement/dedication over an IBM-owned private road (to allow Byram Hills buses into the Eagle Ridge subdivision) plus a related utility easement. The board received one letter but tabled items 2-5 (motion to table passed unanimously) because of unresolved issues: an incorrect IBM corporate name, typos, an over-broad indemnity, questions about the town plowing scope and the map's hash-marked area extending to the security gate, and Councilman Berra's lost markup. Counsel and members will circulate corrections (edits due by close of business Tuesday) before it returns to a future agenda.
cases.publicComment: Applicant's counsel Gary Rosen appeared (remotely) and agreed to make the requested changes.

memberPositions.evidence: Not ready to approve; questioned the indemnity's breadth, the town incurring plowing expense on North Castle Drive, and map/document inconsistencies; his markup had been lost.
Frustrated at the lack of preparation ('I hate when stuff comes on the agenda and there's a lack of preparation'); insisted the town attorney have all correct information before it returns.
Flagged the incorrect IBM corporate name and that a 7-day notice requirement was impractical for the water department maintaining/repairing the water main.

cases.name: Proposed Amendment to Code Sec. 275-15.1 — Subdivision Notice / Address-Change and Mailing Reforms
cases.applicant: Town Board / Town Planner Adam Kaufman
cases.summary: Discussion of amending the code so subdivision public-notice mailings alert neighbors that a subdivision could trigger an address change, prompted by resident Matt Sorrell whose address was changed (April Road / Whippoorwill) without his prior knowledge after a neighbor's subdivision. The board declined to reverse the change or use alphanumeric (A/B) addresses, deferring to Police Chief Simonson and county 911 on public-safety grounds. Councilman Berra also proposed switching notices to trackable certified mail, requiring a copy of the addressed envelope as proof, and widening the notification radius. The board voted unanimously to schedule a public hearing on the amended law for its first November meeting.
cases.publicComment: Resident Matt Sorrell (and his wife Becky) spoke at length, upset about the un-noticed address change and fearing school-bus/navigation mishaps for their young children; tone earnest and pointed but civil.

memberPositions.evidence: Sympathetic on notice and timing but firm that the board must defer to public-safety experts and would not reverse the change or adopt A/B addressing.
Agreed the resident should have been noticed but said the board is not a public-safety expert and would not overrule the police chief; did not share the fear about kids being misdropped.
Understood both sides but sided with police/county professionals, saying she'd feel guilty if a lettered address delayed a 911 response.
Drove the notification reforms: certified (trackable) mail, envelope-copy proof, and a wider/clearer notice radius for anyone whose address could change.

cases.name: Resolution — Non-Enforcement Grace Period on Address-Change Mailbox Requirement (Sorrell)
cases.summary: To relieve the Sorrell family from the code's daily fine for not updating their changed mailbox address, the board adopted a resolution (unanimous voice vote) suspending enforcement until July 1, 2025, letting the school year end before the change takes effect. The neighbor whose subdivision caused the change is to be notified and given an additional grace period. Town Attorney Barone will draft the resolution with the specific names/addresses.
cases.publicComment: Residents Matt and Becky Sorrell participated in shaping the timeline; appreciative of the accommodation.

memberPositions.evidence: Said it was not the town's wish to levy fines over how much time a resident needs; supported the extension.
Proposed the end-of-June/July 1 timeline so the change avoids the school year and gives a buffer for maps to update.

cases.name: Authorization to Go to Bid — Kent Place Parking Lot (Former Verizon Property) Improvements
cases.applicant: Town of North Castle (bid documents by Kellard)
cases.summary: The board approved authorizing a bid for improvements to the Kent Place parking lot, a new downtown parking addition, with an 18-month completion date. Bid documents prepared by Kellard were ready to release. Approved by unanimous voice vote of the members present.

memberPositions.evidence: Glad to get the downtown-parking project moving forward; made the motion to go to bid.
Recused herself out of caution because the DiGiacinto family owns commercial property on the west side of Main Street.

cases.name: Acceptance of $20,000 Armonk Lions Club Donation — Wampus Brook North Bridge Replacement & Fence
cases.address: Wampus Brook Park / Hunter Field, Armonk
cases.summary: The board accepted a $20,000 Armonk Lions Club donation toward the Wampus Brook North bridge replacement and a fence along the Wampus Brook Park/Hunter Field border, approving the conditions in the donation letter (including a commemorative plaque). The donation offsets part of the ~$56,000 bridge cost and funds fence material, with removable panels for the Folderol festival; town labor is to be used. DiGiacinto raised process questions about whether the fence sits on town or school property and possible union concerns, which counsel addressed. Adopted by voice vote.

memberPositions.evidence: Grateful for the donation but pressed on process/fence location (school vs. town property) and potential union issues for town labor on school land.
Praised the Lions and the town-school collaboration to save money; explained the panel/plaque arrangement.
Credited as having revived the Lions Club; a Lions member who thanked the fundraising effort.

cases.name: Waiver of Permit Fees — Congregation B'nai Israel October 7th Memorial Vigil
cases.summary: The board approved waiving permit fees for a memorial vigil for the victims of October 7th at the Wampus Brook Park gazebo, consistent with past practice of waiving such fees. Approved by unanimous voice vote.

memberPositions.evidence: Thanked resident Michelle for spearheading the vigil and the Town Clerk for coordinating; called it important.

cases.name: License Agreement — 4 Trip Lane (Right-of-Way Driveway Gate and Stone Masonry Piers)
cases.summary: The board approved a single license agreement (for both spouses, Anna and David) covering the right-of-way area by the driveway entrance gate and stone masonry piers at 4 Trip Lane. A duplicate agreement mistakenly on the agenda was excluded. Approved by voice vote.

cases.name: Town Administrator / Council Updates — Route 128 Paving, Salt Domes, Route 22 DOT Meeting
cases.summary: Closing updates: Route 128 paving is essentially complete (final checklist items remaining) and salt-dome construction is expected to begin the first week of October. Supervisor Rende noted a late-September/early-October DOT meeting on lower Route 22, with attendance limited to avoid an Open Meetings Law quorum; other members were invited to submit written comments. The board also flagged a property-maintenance/mowing issue and offered condolences to Kevin Hay on the loss of his brother.

memberPositions.evidence: Raised the Route 22 DOT meeting and the Open Meetings Law limit on how many members could attend; asked for a code remedy requiring property maintenance after approvals.

Two officer appointments and a detective-sergeant promotion; police-chief deference drove the address-change decision.
Recurring friction over notice, preparation, certified-mail reform, and tabling unready documents.
Subdivision address-change law, Eagle Ridge easement, special-event and license agreements.
Sorrell address-change dispute and dog-park quality-of-life framing.

Kent Place parking-lot bid authorization; nursery special-event process.
Summit Club sewer-district order and the Eagle Ridge water-main easement notice issue.
Lions Club $20,000 donation and possible ARPA funding for the dog park.
Nursery fall festival, October 7th memorial vigil, outdoor art show.
Route 128 paving, salt domes, and Route 22 DOT meeting updates.

cases.name: Summit Club Sewage Works Corporation & Standby Summit Club Sewer District
cases.summary: Public hearing on the petition, map/plan/report to form the Summit Club Sewage Works Corporation and establish a standby Summit Club Sewer District serving the approved residential golf-course community, whose privately owned sewage plant must be structured under NY Transportation Corporations Law so the town can take over only in the event of a default. After extensive questioning driven by the town's water/sewer superintendent and clarifications from town counsel and the applicant's engineer, the board closed the hearing and, by roll-call votes recorded 4-0 (Milim, Hussain, DiGiacinto, Rende aye), consented to form the Sewage Works Corporation and adopted the resolution establishing the standby district. The board agreed to increase the operation-and-maintenance bond term from at least five years to at least ten years. The stock escrow, O&M, and easement agreements were held for redline revisions to be presented at the next meeting.
cases.publicComment: No general public spoke; Sal (town water/sewer superintendent) raised detailed concerns about the document wording seeming to set the town up to take over the plant and about inspection/reporting obligations.

memberPositions.evidence: Initially read the documents as setting the town up to take over the plant, but after counsel's explanation supported it and successfully moved to extend the O&M bond term from five to ten years.

Reviewed the documents closely, submitted comments/typo corrections to counsel (accepted, including reducing required town insurance from $5M to $2M) and to the applicant; Rende noted 'I actually agreed with your comments.'
Pressed technical/financial due-diligence questions about how the plant is financed (debt vs. equity), what would trigger insolvency/default, and whether the bond amount adjusts for inflation.
Sought clarification on what triggers a town inspection, which five-year references applied to the bond, and confirmation that each of Sal's concerns had been addressed.

cases.name: Gavi Restaurant Special Use Permit — mixed-use building
cases.summary: The board considered receipt of a special-use-permit application to add a 5,000 sq ft mixed-use building with first-floor retail plus two one-bedroom first-floor apartments and two two-bedroom second-floor apartments (four units total). The written application erroneously described the apartments as being only on the second floor; the applicant clarified the layout orally and will submit an amendment letter. The board referred the revised submission to the town and county planning boards and scheduled a public hearing for November 20, 2024 (moved one week from the originally noticed November 13 to allow adequate county/planning-board review time).
cases.publicComment: Applicant representative present and clarified the apartment layout; no residents spoke.

memberPositions.evidence: Questioned how an error like the apartment-location mistake could get through vetting before reaching the agenda without correction.

cases.name: Tabled matter(s) pending map/plan/report redline revisions
cases.summary: Following the minutes, the board tabled a matter (and its associated items) after discussion with the town attorney and Councilman Berra pending redline changes to the documents, with Councilman Hussain abstaining. A related item (referred to as Item B) requiring changes to a map/plan/report was likewise tabled by motion. Counsel indicated the revisions would be worked out at a Monday meeting already scheduled.

cases.name: Local Law amending Chapter 60 (Officers & Employees) — residency requirement for Assistant Building Inspector
cases.summary: The board considered receipt of a proposed local law amending Chapter 60 to change the residency requirement for the assistant building inspector (and fire inspector) from residing within the town to residing in New York State, matching the existing standard for the building inspector. Town Administrator Kevin explained Westchester County Human Resources requires this change in connection with a recent appointment. The board received the local law and scheduled a public hearing for October 23, 2024.

cases.name: Local Law amending Chapter 146 (Dogs) — dog park rules and regulations
cases.summary: The board considered receipt of a local law adding dog-park rules and regulations to Chapter 146 and scheduled a public hearing for November 20, 2024. Councilwoman DiGiacinto disclosed via a letter that the project's lead proponent, Molly Meyer, is a non-resident (Mount Pleasant), arguing transparency required acknowledging the board was acting on a non-resident's request; other members strongly pushed back, calling residency irrelevant to a community benefit and defending the project. Members cited the 2022 Parks & Recreation survey (dog park the second-most-requested project) and a low estimated cost (~$25,000-$30,000 per Rec Superintendent Matt Traynor). The exchange grew heated over whether DiGiacinto's letter implied wrongdoing; the board ultimately agreed to receive the law, schedule the hearing, and send a message welcoming Meyer and her daughter's continued involvement.

memberPositions.evidence: Wrote to the board that the lead proponent is a non-resident and that transparency required disclosing the town was 'acting on the request of a non-resident'; wanted rule changes and felt mischaracterized as trying to block the project.
Said the dog park was originally his idea, cited the survey (second-most-selected project) and low ~$25-30k cost as 'greatest bang for the buck,' and called the non-resident letter 'distasteful.'

Argued a proponent whose child attends a town school is part of the community, proposed the board formally welcome Molly and her daughter's continued involvement, and wore a dog-themed tie in support.

Framed the dog park as a quality-of-life issue comparable to a public playground, criticized the town's history of studying projects 'to death,' and disputed that raising the proponent's residency served any legitimate purpose.

cases.name: Road naming for new roads in the Airport Campus subdivision
cases.summary: The board approved the Road Naming Committee's recommendations for new roads in the Toll Brothers airport campus subdivision (Weber Farm Road, Cove View Way, and Fieldstone Knoll), with notification to the E911 coordinator, because tax lot numbers must be assigned before the plat can be filed. Members objected to the committee attaching conditions/stipulations (preserving historic field stones and requesting a WWII commemorative plaque), agreeing that naming a road is a town responsibility that cannot be bartered; those requests will be passed to the developer only as non-binding suggestions. The board also directed staff (via Kevin/Adam) to build developer notification into the future road-naming process. Approved by voice vote.

memberPositions.evidence: Preferred 'Cove View Way' over the developer's 'Lakeview Place' because the water was historically Weber's Cove, and helped drive the point that stipulations attached to road names should be removed.

cases.name: Interim MS4 stormwater reports (period ending September 1, 2024)
cases.summary: The board accepted the interim MS4 stormwater reports for the period ending September 1, 2024, prepared by town engineer KSCJ Consulting, detailing routine compliance activities such as catch-basin cleaning, street sweeping, and education/training. Approved by voice vote as a standard annual filing.

cases.name: Wetland mitigation bond, monitoring bond & cash bond agreement — Guadalupe Real Estate residence, 41 Mead Road
cases.applicant: Marcella Yeps & Nicholas Quadros / Guadalupe Real Estate NY, LLC
cases.summary: On the town engineer's (KSCJ Consulting) recommendation, the board approved establishment of a wetland mitigation bond and a five-year monitoring and maintenance bond for the residence at 41 Mead Road, then separately approved the related cash bond agreement (item G1). The agreement had been submitted late and was not properly posted on the agenda; the Supervisor used the occasion to reiterate the rule that agenda items be finalized at the Wednesday agenda meeting to avoid last-minute errors. Both approved by voice vote.
cases.publicComment: Applicant's attorney (Geraldine Tortorella) was present.

memberPositions.evidence: Emphasized his rule against adding items to the agenda after the Wednesday agenda meeting, noting the late, incorrectly-numbered submission caused the board to rush.

cases.name: Wetland mitigation bond & five-year monitoring bond — Fort Trip Lane residence
cases.summary: On the town engineer's (KSCJ Consulting) recommendation, the board approved establishment of a wetland mitigation bond and a five-year monitoring and maintenance bond for the residence project at Fort Trip Lane. Approved by voice vote with no discussion.

cases.name: Retroactive filming permit — Miracle-Gro commercial
cases.summary: The board granted retroactive approval of a filming permit for World War 7 to film a Miracle-Gro commercial on October 8, 2024. Because the location is on a narrow road, the police reviewed and approved traffic arrangements before the expedited shoot; the full $3,000 fee (including the $1,000 application fee) was confirmed paid. Approved by voice vote.

cases.name: Friends of Frosty — Frosty Day parade & tree lighting road/park use
cases.address: Wampus Brook Park / Wampus Brook Park South
cases.summary: The board approved the Friends of Frosty's request to use town roads and Wampus Brook Park (and Park South) for the annual Frosty Day parade and holiday tree lighting on Sunday, December 1, 2024. Approved by voice vote.

cases.name: Alcohol permit — Katonah Classic Stage opening-night reception
cases.address: Whippoorwill Hall, 19 East Whippoorwill Road, Armonk
cases.summary: The board approved an alcohol permit for Katonah Classic Stage to hold a reception on the opening night of its play at Whippoorwill Hall on October 25, 2024. Members praised the theater as a community asset that helps drive the local economy, noting strong ticket sales. Approved by voice vote.

cases.name: License agreement — Saglimbini, 2 Trip Lane right-of-way encroachment
cases.summary: The board approved a license agreement with Martha Saglimbini regarding the right-of-way area at 2 Trip Lane for driveway entrance gates and stone masonry piers, and authorized the Supervisor to sign; it is identical to an agreement previously approved for 4 Trip Lane. The Supervisor urged residents to check with the planning department before erecting improvements that may fall within an easement. Approved by voice vote.

cases.name: Probationary appointment — Paul Taft, Assistant Building Inspector
cases.summary: The board approved the probationary appointment of Paul Taft as assistant building inspector, effective October 10, 2024, contingent on setting the Chapter 60 residency public hearing per Westchester County HR requirements. The position was budgeted and is part of a transition ahead of an expected retirement in the building department. Approved by voice vote with best wishes to Taft.

cases.name: Conference attendance — Highway foreman & lead mechanic, League of Municipalities
cases.summary: The board approved a request from Highway General Foreman Jamie Norris to attend the League of Municipalities Conference in Atlantic City, November 14-17, 2024, with lead mechanic Matthew Hirsch, using a town vehicle. The Supervisor encouraged board members and staff to treat such conferences (including the upcoming Association of Towns convention) as continuing education. Approved by voice vote.

cases.name: Reappointment — Vincent Giordano, Conservation Board
cases.summary: The board reappointed Vincent Giordano to the Conservation Board for a two-year term expiring October 9, 2026, with members commending his service. Approved by voice vote.

cases.name: Resignations — library clerk and Board of Assessment Review member
cases.summary: The board accepted the resignation of Cheryl Cheramella as library clerk at the North Castle Public Library (effective October 2, 2024) and the resignation of Stuart Breezeblatt from the Board of Assessment Review (effective September 30, 2024). Both accepted by voice vote.

themes.note: Summit Club sewer district public hearing dominated the meeting alongside MS4 stormwater and wetland bonds.
Dog-park local law drew a long, contentious debate over process and a non-resident proponent.
Recurring friction over late/incorrect agenda items, application errors, and transparency of the dog-park proposal.
Special permit referral, road naming, license agreements and tabled map/plan matters.
Assistant building inspector residency law and appointment, conservation board reappointment, resignations, conference attendance.
Wetland mitigation and monitoring bonds and stormwater compliance.
Frosty Day parade, theater alcohol permit, historical society fundraiser.

Explained that NY Transportation Corporations Law requires the corporation/bond/standby-district structure and that inspection rights protect the town without obligating it; advised extending the bond term to ten years is permissible, that road-naming stipulations should not be conditions, and handled the tabling of matters pending redlines.

Provided background on the Chapter 60 residency local law (required by Westchester County HR) and the Paul Taft appointment; reported on the Maple Avenue collapsed-pipe emergency repair and salt-dome construction progress; tasked to improve developer notification in road naming.

Town water/sewer superintendent; at the public hearing raised extensive concerns that the sewer-district documents' wording seemed to obligate the town to inspect, report on, and potentially take over the private plant, and questioned the five-year bond references and timeline; ultimately satisfied by counsel's explanation of the governing law.

Town Planner; had flagged the Gavi application's apartment-location discrepancy in his memo to the board and referred the applicant to the town board; to relay road-naming suggestions to the developer.
Recreation & Parks Superintendent; cited (referenced) as estimating the dog park would cost roughly $25,000-$30,000 and as having worked on the proposed rules.

meetings.attributionNote: Raw ASR with no speaker labels. The Supervisor (Joseph Rende) and Councilwoman DiGiacinto were the most reliably identifiable (Barbara moved the 5-to-10-year bond change and authored the dog-park non-resident letter). Jose Berra identified as the member reviewing/commenting on the sewer documents ('the escrow agreement that Jose is referring to'; 'Hear that, Jose? I actually agreed with your comments'); attributed only in this 2024 meeting. Names normalized from ASR (Milam/Millam→Milim, Hussein→Hussain, Digicento/Digento→DiGiacinto, Vera/bearer→Berra, Rendy/Rende→Rende). meetings.meetingSummary: The Town Board opened with an extended work session in which the North Castle Revolutionary War 250th steering committee presented its plans for the July 2026 semiquincentennial celebration (refurbished historic signs, a documentary video, an art competition, reenactors, concerts, a school monologue project, a trolley tour, a parade, merchandise, and beautification) and appealed for community funding. In the regular session the board held and closed a public hearing and adopted a local law amending Chapter 60 to relax residency requirements for assistant building/fire inspectors, approved routine minutes, received the tentative budget and set its hearing for November 20, and received the Lombardi Park water district extension map/plan/report while planning notice to seven affected residents. The board also approved a pool filter media replacement contract, a library alcohol permit, a suite of Eagle Ridge (IBM) easement agreements (Supervisor recused), and Summit Club sewer agreements subject to counsel resolving a superintendent's redline, plus several personnel appointments and reappointments. It closed with liaison updates, get-out-the-vote reminders, and concern over political lawn signs being removed around town.
meetings.durationNote: Reconvened from executive session (personnel and contracts); quorum present with all five members; Supervisor Rende recused himself from the Eagle Ridge easement items due to his IBM association.

cases.name: North Castle Revolutionary War 250th Committee Work Session
cases.applicant: North Castle Revolutionary War 250 Steering Committee
cases.summary: The four-co-chair 250th steering committee gave a series of presentations on plans for the nation's semiquincentennial celebration culminating July 4, 2026, including refurbished 1976 historic markers plus new signs at Mount Misery/Miller Hill and a Revolutionary War soldiers monument, a documentary film for residents and schools, an 'Art in North Castle' competition open to artists and Byram Hills/Valhalla students, reenactor encampments, colonial-era concerts, a student monologue history project, a Historical Society trolley tour, merchandise/swag, town-wide bunting and flags, and a community parade. Presenters repeatedly noted the town's generosity in funding signs and video and urged local businesses and residents to donate. No formal action was taken; the board discussed logistics such as siting the Mount Misery marker with the highway foreman, obtaining property boundary maps, coordinating with Westchester County on county-owned Miller Hill, and purchasing flag brackets for poles across all three hamlets.
cases.publicComment: Extensive input from committee members and presenters (Ed Woodyard, Judge Sue Scheimer, Sharon, Rich Rosen, George Drapeau, reenactors Eric and Eliza Lychak, student Gavin Raddus, others); tone was enthusiastic, nostalgic, and civic-minded.

memberPositions.evidence: Repeatedly praised the effort ('we're in for a big treat'), shared his own 1975-76 bicentennial memories, and urged businesses/residents and fellow board members to fund and take an active role.
Noted she and the beautification committee are developing red-white-and-blue plantings for gardens and public spaces to carry the celebration theme.

cases.name: Local Law Amending Chapter 60 (Officers & Employees) — Residency for Assistant Building/Fire Inspector Titles
cases.summary: The board opened, held, and closed a public hearing on a local law amending Chapter 60 to exempt the assistant building inspector and fire inspector titles from the state residency requirement for officers who take oaths of office, using the home-rule workaround that lets such employees live anywhere in New York State rather than in-town. Town Attorney Roland gave a brief overview; no one from the public or board raised objections and members called it 'pretty clear cut.' The board closed the hearing and adopted the local law by voice vote (motion, second, all in favor).
cases.publicComment: No public speakers.

memberPositions.evidence: Presided over the hearing and confirmed the item was clear cut with the clean version to be filed.

cases.name: Approval of Town Board Minutes — October 9 and October 17, 2024
cases.summary: The board approved the minutes of its October 9 and October 17, 2024 meetings with no questions raised. Adopted by voice vote (motion, second, all in favor).

cases.name: Receipt of Tentative Budget and Scheduling of Public Hearing (November 20)
cases.summary: The board formally received the town's tentative budget and scheduled the budget public hearing for November 20, 2024. Approved by voice vote (motion, second, all in favor). No substantive budget discussion occurred at this meeting.

cases.name: John A. Lombardi Park Water District Extension — Receipt of Map, Plan and Report
cases.summary: The board received the October 24 map, plan and report for the Lombardi Park water district extension, which was revised to run a larger main up School Street (rather than cutting through Byram Hills property) so it can serve seven additional residences and be expanded later. Discussion centered on the fact that those seven residents have not yet been consulted and will owe debt service whether or not they connect; the board decided against a separate work session and instead directed staff to send an informational notice/letter to the seven residents ahead of a required public hearing, with the draft to be circulated to all board members and counsel. The Town Attorney will prepare the order calling the public hearing (likely December or January), and plans have been submitted to the health department before bidding on main installation. Receipt approved by voice vote.

memberPositions.evidence: Pressed to confirm the plan changes were made and insisted the seven affected residents be properly noticed and the draft letter shared with all board members and counsel before proceeding.

cases.name: Town Pool Filter Media Replacement — Nuclear Swimming Pool Service LLC
cases.summary: At the recreation superintendent's request, the board approved purchase of pool filter media (sand and gravel) replacement for the town pool from Nuclear Swimming Pool Service LLC, together with a transfer of fund balance to cover it. Members noted the media in the below-grade vessels has never been changed, is breaking down, and is a Department of Health recommendation; doing it off-season avoids risking a delayed pool opening next season. Discussion added a condition that the town provide its own roll-off container on site and identify a proper disposal location for the roughly 20-30 yards of spent material. Adopted by voice vote (motion, second, all in favor).

memberPositions.evidence: Explained the filter media had never been changed and urged doing the work off-season to avoid delaying the pool opening, adding the disposal-container condition.

cases.name: Alcohol Permit — North Castle Public Library 'Paint and Sip' Program (Friends Gallery, Armonk)
cases.summary: The board approved an alcohol permit application from the North Castle Public Library for a 'paint and sip' library program in the Friends Gallery of the Armonk branch on December 17 and 19, 2024, and waived the permit fee. Approved by voice vote (motion, second, all in favor) with no questions.

cases.name: Eagle Ridge (North Castle Drive) — IBM/Mad Madonna Easement and Utility Agreements
cases.applicant: Mad Madonna Armonk LLC / International Business Machines Corporation (IBM)
cases.summary: The board approved, by separate votes, a series of agreements for the Eagle Ridge development on North Castle Drive: an easement dedication for Road A, a utility easement for water main installation and maintenance, an access and utility agreement, and receipt of a declaration of covenants and restrictions ensuring at least 60% of units have first-floor primary bedrooms (satisfying condition 10 of the master site plan resolution), all authorizing the Supervisor to sign. Supervisor Rende recused himself due to his IBM association, so the remaining members carried the motions. Extended discussion addressed coordinating snow plowing/ice treatment among the town highway department, IBM, and the future Eagle Ridge HOA (windrow and snow-storage concerns), confirmation that no CBA-triggering transfers had occurred, and a 2025 target for breaking ground.

memberPositions.evidence: Recused himself from the vote due to his association with IBM, but participated in discussion urging that highway/IBM/HOA snow-plowing logistics be coordinated to meet the highway department's approval.

cases.name: Summit Club Sewage Works Corporation and Sewer District Agreements
cases.summary: The board voted individually on four Summit Club sewer agreements (stock escrow; sewage works operation-and-maintenance and license; sewage works easement; public water system easement). A lengthy debate arose over the operation-and-maintenance agreement after Water/Sewer Superintendent Sal submitted a redline arguing the draft improperly obligates the town to initiate inspections, when regulatory agencies (DEC/health department/EPA via the SPDES permit) should be the trigger; the developer's counsel (Mark Weingarten) contends the language tracks the Transportation Corporations Law verbatim and cannot deviate. The board rescinded its initial approval of item two and re-approved it subject to Sal's comments (chiefly the Section 2B inspection lead-in) being made satisfactory to the Town Attorney, accepting that if developer's counsel will not agree the item returns to the board. Sal's proposed word changes conflicting with the statute (e.g., 'discontinuance' to 'default,' the 30-day figure) were not adopted. Items one, three, and four passed by voice vote.

memberPositions.evidence: Brokered the compromise to adopt the O&M agreement subject to Sal's Section 2B inspection edit being satisfactory to the town attorney, to avoid the item having to come back yet again.

cases.name: Personnel — Library Clerk Appointments, Highway Resignation, and Board Reappointments
cases.summary: The board made probationary appointments of Anna Dowing and Emma Goit as hourly clerks for the North Castle Public Library (effective October 24), received a letter of resignation from highway department mechanic Andrew Zakowinski (effective October 30), reappointed Aaron McCaffrey to the Conservation Board (two-year term to October 23, 2026), and reappointed Edward Loberman to the Board of Ethics (five-year term to October 23, 2029). All approved by voice vote. Members praised the reappointees and Rende explained the town re-interviews all willing volunteer board members regardless of tenure, thanking them for their service.

memberPositions.evidence: Said she was 'very happy that Ed is willing to serve another term,' calling him a great member.
Thanked the reappointed volunteers, describing them as two fine members and noting appreciation for their continued service; also wished departing mechanic Andrew Zakowinski good luck.

cases.name: Resident Concern — Removal of Political Lawn Signs
cases.summary: During closing remarks the Supervisor addressed numerous resident phone calls complaining that political signs had been removed from front yards, with some residents assuming town employees were responsible. Rende stated that after meeting with the town administrator and highway department, no signs were removed by any town staff, noting removals were reported overnight or during daytime Sundays. He urged residents to respect neighbors' right to display signs and to express disagreement at the ballot box instead. The discussion accompanied repeated get-out-the-vote encouragement from multiple members ahead of the November 5 election.
cases.publicComment: Residents had phoned the town upset about their political signs being removed; tone was frustrated.

memberPositions.evidence: Reported the sign-removal complaints, affirmed no town staff were responsible, and urged residents to respect each other's right to display candidate signs.
Corroborated that a lot of signs were removed in her neighborhood during the day on a Sunday, confirming it was not highway or building staff.

themes.note: The 250th Revolutionary War celebration work session dominated the meeting with broad enthusiasm.
Lombardi Park extension, Summit Club sewer agreements, and Eagle Ridge water main drove significant discussion.
Pool filter media purchase and multiple easement/utility agreements approved.
Inspector residency local law plus library, conservation board, and ethics board appointments/reappointments.
Repeated appeals for community and business sponsorship of the 250th celebration.
Tentative budget received and hearing set for November 20 with no substantive discussion.
Complaints over removed political lawn signs; town staff cleared of responsibility.
Public hearing, notice to affected residents, and get-out-the-vote reminders emphasized.

Water/Sewer Superintendent; advised on the Lombardi Park notice letter to seven residents and pushed a redline on the Summit Club O&M agreement so that regulatory agencies (not the town) trigger inspections, citing SPDES/DEC/EPA reporting experience.

Coordinated snow-plowing logistics with IBM and highway staff, and gave the administrator update on the School Street tree-removal closure (7am-3pm) and Water District 4 hydrant flushing on November 7.
Delivered community announcements on the November 5 election (early voting, absentee ballots, polling sites), the December 1 Frosty Parade, E-News/Nixle alerts, and notary/clerk services.
Developer's counsel/representative confirming preparation of Eagle Ridge recording documents (52-60, 17s and 4s) and CBA transfer status.

meetings.attributionNote: Raw ASR with no speaker labels; the presiding/supervisor voice was reliably identified as Joseph Rende, and Barbara DiGiacinto was identifiable as the sole woman (breast-cancer survivor remarks, sustainability/Furniture Sharehouse liaison update, Jim McLean Golf School new-business note, birthday wish to the clerk). Matt Milim was confirmed present ('Thank you, Matt. All set? Yep.') and Jose Berra appears (referenced looking for new golf clubs; gave 'no update' at liaison round) but neither took a clearly attributable substantive stance on a specific item, so they were not assigned member positions. Saleem Hussain was present but not separately distinguishable in the running text. Votes were near-unanimous voice votes ('all in favor / aye') with no roll calls or 'no' votes recorded, limiting per-member attribution. Note: the transcript's opening lines reference an 'October 23rd meeting' reconvening from executive session, an apparent ASR/label carryover; analyzed under the assigned file date 2024-11-13, and the internal references to the 'next meeting' being the 13th and 20th are consistent with an earlier-November session.

meetings.meetingSummary: The North Castle Town Board held a public hearing and adopted a local law adding an address-change notice to subdivision public-hearing notices, adopting the negative declaration and law after debate over whether the notice should be broader. The board handled a full agenda of contracts and resolutions: rescinding and re-awarding the Wampus Brook Northbridge replacement bid, awarding the Kent Place (former Verizon) parking-lot bid with ARPA funds, a Justice Court Assistance grant application, a 250th-anniversary bank account, Verity Electric and Spectra Serve service agreements, a PBA successor contract, and personnel items. The most contested matters were a 4-1 authorization of an Arconnex feasibility study toward relocating town offices to 333 Main Street (the 'Boys/Du Bois Schiller' building) with DiGiacinto opposed as premature, a received residents' petition to relocate two AFFH units at the Byram (referred to a future work session over Berra's objection), and receipt of the North Castle Fire District No. 1 budget amid concerns about its transparency. Public comment covered the Quarry Heights water project, and community items included a Historical Society Mount Misery sign, Frosty Day, and a girls tennis state championship.
meetings.durationNote: Quorum present throughout; all five members participated. Councilman Jose Berra joined via Zoom from Argentina (registered his remote location with the clerk) and asked to be excused late in the meeting after the 333 Main Street votes.

cases.name: Local Law amending Code Section 275-15.11 — subdivision public-hearing notice (potential address changes)
cases.summary: A public hearing was opened on a local law adding language to subdivision public-notice requirements advising that a subdivision may result in future address changes in the surrounding neighborhood, prompted by a resident upset over a forced renumbering (21/23 Whippoorwill Road). The Town Planner explained the added sentence; Councilman Berra argued the notice should be broader (more affected owners, more specificity about contiguous addresses, an informal police referral, and a move away from certificates of mailing to trackable certified mail). The planner and board explained a general notice at the start of the process can only say so much. The board closed the hearing, adopted the negative declaration, and adopted the local law, all by voice vote.
cases.publicComment: No residents spoke on this hearing item.

memberPositions.evidence: Called it a good addition residents will appreciate; explained it stemmed from a resident blindsided by an address change.
Supported the law but wanted more 'meat on it' — broader notification, specificity about contiguous addresses, and certified mail; voted yes saying he hopes he is 'wrong that it's not enough.'
Agreed with Berra's intention to make the language as clear as possible and asked the planner whether it could be made more specific.

cases.name: Approval of Town Board minutes — October 23, 2024
cases.summary: Under old business the board approved its minutes from the October 23, 2024 meeting. Motion made and seconded with no questions, adopted by voice vote.

cases.name: North Castle Historical Society — Mount Misery marker wording
cases.applicant: North Castle Historical Society (Tom Rice et al.)
cases.summary: The Historical Society presented proposed language for a new metal marker at Mount Misery (funding previously approved; sign to cost under $3,500 from an Ohio vendor). The text recounts two historical accounts of the name's origin, including one describing Huguenots slaughtering Native Americans. Councilman Hussain raised concern the killing language could feel 'assaulting' to Native American readers and suggested framing it as differing historical accounts rather than a 'disagreement'; Councilman Milim echoed the 'differing accounts' wording. The board voted to approve the wording with the suggested edits, to be redistributed to the board.
cases.publicComment: Historical Society members (Tom Rice, Ed Woodyard, Sharon Tombach on Zoom) presented and were receptive to the board's suggested edits; tone collegial and enthusiastic.

memberPositions.evidence: Praised the wording as driving curiosity and said history should not be softened; agreed the language depicts what may have happened.
Uncomfortable that the killing of Native American 'marauders' could feel traumatic/assaulting; urged 'different historical accounts' framing and considering readers.
Liked the language and agreed history can't be hidden, but suggested 'there are differing accounts' instead of 'disagreement.'
Offered the dictionary definition of 'marauder' and a light comment about comma usage; engaged but no strong stance.

cases.name: Byram (Armonk) unit-owner petition — possible relocation of AFFH units
cases.address: Byram, Route 128 / Old Mount Kisco Road, Armonk
cases.summary: The board formally received a petition from market-rate condo owners at the 16-unit Byram (2 AFFH units) asking the town to allow the two affordable units to be relocated off-site, triggered by a certificate-of-occupancy compliance issue and concern that planned HOA amenities would raise common charges. An extended policy debate followed on AFFH affordability rules, the risk of developer 'gaming,' one-off exceptions versus amending the local law to require a 1.5:1 or 2:1 replacement ratio, on-site embedding versus clustering, and small-complex divisiveness. The board received the petition (administrative) and, over Berra's objection, four members agreed to schedule a future work session; no substantive decision was made.
cases.publicComment: Petition submitted by 14 resident/homeowners; no residents spoke live on this item.

memberPositions.evidence: 'Vehemently concerned about this ongoing assault from developers'; felt a work session was not necessary and warned raising the ratio would just invite more exception-seeking.
Saw granting an exception as risking a precedent others would game; called it a deeper structural problem for a broader conversation, and warned against clustering AFFH units.
Disliked one-off exceptions and 'bailing out' developers who knew the terms when they bought, but was open to amending the law to a 1.5:1 or 2:1 replacement ratio for everyone.

Sympathetic to a work session; argued one-size-fits-all doesn't fit a small 16-unit complex and worried the arrangement creates stigma/divisiveness, while favoring extra units as a trade-off if relocation were allowed.
Recalled the Whippoorwill Hills MIU experience where no relief was available; said exceptions are tough to make but was agreeable to a work session.

cases.name: Order calling public hearing (Dec 11, 2024) — Water District No. 4 School Street extension
cases.summary: The board adopted an order calling a public hearing on December 11, 2024 to consider extending Water District No. 4, to be known as the School Street extension. Because it is an order requiring a district action, it was adopted by roll call, 5-0 (Berra, Milim, DiGiacinto, Hussain, Rende all aye).

cases.name: Wampus Brook Park Northbridge replacement — rescind Mega Painting award and award to JT Oranzio
cases.applicant: Town (Mega Painting & Contracting; JT Oranzio General Contracting)
cases.summary: The August 14, 2024 bid award to Mega Painting & Contracting was rescinded because the contractor could not meet the town's stringent insurance requirements. The board debated whether to draw on the 5% bid bond or impose a penalty; the Town Attorney explained the options, and members agreed the contractor appeared to have acted in good faith and had not sought to lower requirements, so the board rescinded without penalty. The board then awarded the bid to the second-lowest bidder, JT Oranzio General Contracting, and authorized the supervisor to sign. Both actions passed by voice vote.

memberPositions.evidence: Sympathetic to the small contractor; noted the town lost time but no money and favored not imposing an unnecessary penalty.
Raised the question of the 5% penalty/bond and potential net recovery after legal fees, then said 'I don't feel strongly on this, I was just hearing the issue.'

cases.name: Resolution — Justice Court Assistance Program grant application (up to $30,000)
cases.summary: The board adopted a resolution authorizing the Town Court to apply for a Justice Court Assistance Program grant in the 2024-2025 cycle for up to $30,000, primarily to scan and preserve criminal case files the court is required by law to retain (some dating to the 1800s). Rende praised the court staff for identifying the opportunity and asked the administrator to have the town's grant writer keep pursuing similar grants. Adopted by voice vote.

memberPositions.evidence: Called it 'a great project' and credited the judges and court clerk for finding the grant.

cases.name: Authorization to open bank account — North Castle 250th anniversary committee
cases.applicant: North Castle 250th steering committee / Finance Director
cases.summary: The board authorized the Director of Finance to open a dedicated JP Morgan Chase account for the North Castle Revolutionary War 250th anniversary committee to receive and record donations (to be named 'North Castle 250th'). The finance office will control the account and issue tax-deductible donation receipts; the committee anticipates donations and commemorative-item sales. A similar approach was used for the 1976 bicentennial. Adopted by voice vote.

cases.name: Eagle Ridge (3 North Castle Drive) — Declaration of Covenants and stormwater easement/maintenance agreement
cases.applicant: Zarin & Steinmetz LLP (on behalf of Eagle Ridge developer)
cases.summary: The board received a November 6, 2024 letter from Zarin & Steinmetz regarding Eagle Ridge and authorized the supervisor to sign the Declaration of Covenants and Restrictions and the Stormwater Control Facility Easement and Maintenance Agreement. Councilman Berra questioned whether the easement (town right to inspect and default obligation to perform maintenance) imposed liability on the town; the Town Attorney explained roughly 30 such DEC-designed agreements exist, the town is the default performer and charges back the HOA, with no undue liability. Rende reacted with mild impatience to the questions. Receipt and signature authorization both passed by voice vote (one board member recused).

memberPositions.evidence: Asked whether the inspection easement and default maintenance obligation exposed the town to liability and whether Exhibit B needed future flexibility; ultimately satisfied after the attorney's answers.
Defended the standard arrangement, noting the 88 homeowners are town residents the maintenance benefits, and pressed to move the vote along.

cases.name: Arconnex Architecture feasibility study — relocation of town offices to 333 Main Street
cases.summary: Supervisor Rende gave a lengthy explanation of exploring the purchase of 333 Main Street (the 'Boys/Du Bois Schiller' building) to consolidate town hall, police, court and staff under one roof, citing 2007 strategic-plan findings, ADA/code and egress deficiencies, sewage backups in the police locker room, and 30-year 'temporary' water/sewer trailers; the building owner proposed a 'friendly eminent domain' process, an appraisal and bond counsel are engaged. The board voted to authorize the supervisor to sign an Arconnex agreement for a test-fit/feasibility study, which staff said mainly pays for work already done. Town Historian Sharon Tombach objected the property sits in Landmarks Preservation District No. 1 and the two-page agreement read like an open-ended 'blank check'; the board pointed to its stated scope and hourly rates. It passed 4-1 by roll call (Milim, Berra, Hussain, Rende aye; DiGiacinto no, calling it premature). The board also adopted a companion bond-counsel resolution allowing all professional fees from that date forward to be captured into any future financing.
cases.publicComment: Town Historian Sharon Tombach (staff/co-historian) raised historic-preservation and 'blank check' concerns; no other residents spoke, though the supervisor invited public input and tours.

memberPositions.evidence: Championed it as a 'golden opportunity' the town won't see again; voted 'yes with great enthusiasm.'
Voted no on roll call, calling the agreement premature and asking to postpone until the appraisal is known and viable; noted taxpayer-cost questions.
Called it an exciting, proactive long-term move that would surface immediate needs; supported going through the process.
Said 'it's a feasibility study, you need to do the feasibility work,' warned of past opportunity costs, and pushed to go to a roll-call vote.
Voted aye, saying the right people are in place to study it, though he flagged wanting the appraisal information.

cases.name: Kent Place parking lot (former Verizon property) improvements — bid award to Tony Casale Inc.
cases.address: Kent Place / Kent Street, Armonk (former Verizon property)
cases.summary: The board awarded the Kent Place parking-lot (former Verizon property) improvement bid to Tony Casale Inc. and authorized the supervisor to sign. Members discussed dedicating a portion of roughly $1.2 million in ARPA funds (which must be committed by year-end) to this project plus equipment purchases such as a senior bus and a plow/dump truck, with a separate ARPA-allocation resolution to be prepared before the next meeting. Councilwoman DiGiacinto recused herself due to her family's ownership of commercial property on the west side of Main Street. Adopted by voice vote.

memberPositions.evidence: Called it 'a long time coming' and 'great news' and a tremendous improvement for merchants and daily users of the back parking lot.

cases.name: 2025 agreement with Verity Electric — traffic signal and flashing beacon maintenance
cases.address: Bedford Road & Maple Avenue; four flashing beacons on Route 22
cases.summary: The board authorized the supervisor to sign the 2025 agreement with Verity Electric for maintenance of the Bedford Road/Maple Avenue traffic signal and four Route 22 flashing beacon assemblies. The administrator noted Verity has done this work for the town for about 20 years and there are few providers. Supervisor Rende disclosed, for the record, that the Verity principal donated to his election campaign, and later praised Verity for donating labor and materials after the town's eagle statue was vandalized. Adopted by voice vote.

memberPositions.evidence: Disclosed the campaign donation for transparency and commended Verity's generosity after the eagle vandalism.

cases.name: Sewer District No. 2 sludge-hauling agreement extension — Spectra Serve Inc. (2025)
cases.summary: The board approved extending the Sewer District No. 2 sludge-hauling agreement with Spectra Serve Inc. for the 2025 fiscal year. Treated as self-explanatory; adopted by voice vote with no discussion.

cases.name: PBA successor contract — stipulation agreement (Jan 1, 2024 – Dec 31, 2027)
cases.summary: The board authorized the supervisor to sign a stipulation agreement between the North Castle PBA and the town for a successor contract covering January 1, 2024 through December 31, 2027. Adopted by voice vote without discussion.

cases.name: Personnel items — Ficaris appointment, Libertari vacation carryover, Stevens resignation
cases.applicant: Town departments (Building Maintenance, Highway, Water & Sewer)
cases.summary: The board approved the probationary appointment of Austin Ficaris to maintenance mechanic in the Building Maintenance Department effective November 14, 2024; approved a request by Rocco Libertari (Highway Department) to carry over 2024 vacation days; and received the letter of resignation of Anthony Stevens (Water and Sewer Department) effective October 15, 2024. All handled by voice vote.

cases.name: Receipt of North Castle Fire District No. 1 (North White Plains) 2025 budget
cases.applicant: North Castle Fire District No. 1 (North White Plains)
cases.summary: Pulled from the consent agenda (item C), the board received the North Castle Fire District No. 1 adopted 2025 budget (~$700,000+). Supervisor Rende detailed his concerns: the district first sent a two-page 'summary,' a zero fund-balance line despite past unremitted hydrant fees, a certification referencing 'estimates,' and a response that the full budget must be FOILed. He contrasted it with Armonk's detailed submission and cited the state comptroller's accounting manual. Milim shared the concern that being told to FOIL implied a withheld document; the Town Attorney said any worksheets are FOIL-exempt and recommended asking the state comptroller to review sufficiency. DiGiacinto was uncomfortable airing it publicly and defended the volunteer firefighters. The board received the budget 'as presented' (a mandatory administrative appendage to the town budget) by voice vote, with further discussion to follow.

memberPositions.evidence: Troubled by the 'summary' document, zero fund balance, 'estimates' certification, and the 'if he wants it, FOIL it' response; stressed fiduciary/transparency duty while making no accusation of wrongdoing.
'Does that imply there's a different document they're just not giving us? ... that doesn't feel right to me.'
'Very saddened by the discussion'; felt grievances should have been aired privately and defended the volunteer firefighters, while still moving to receive the budget.

cases.name: Quarry Heights water project — resident public comment
cases.applicant: Resident (Rob Kanana) / Westchester Joint Water Works
cases.summary: During public comment, resident Rob Kanana (69 James Street) said the town board had not responded to his email about the Quarry Heights water-line project and voiced community anxiety over contamination, drought, temporary above-ground hookups freezing, and whether homes will be connected before the $1.1 million (DOJ consent-order-funded, Westchester Joint Water Works) money runs out in the rocky terrain. Supervisor Rende explained the process is unusually 'backwards' (no map-plan-report because the work is capped by available funds), apologized for missing his email, said the town knows little more than residents, and committed to a community meeting once next steps and cost-sharing are known. No vote; discussion only.
cases.publicComment: Resident Rob Kanana was frustrated and anxious about lack of response and the project's uncertainty; tone respectful but worried.

memberPositions.evidence: Empathetic and candid — apologized, explained the consent-order constraints, and promised a community meeting, while cautioning residents not to expect the town or outside money to cover future costs.

themes.note: 333 Main Street town-hall relocation study, Kent Place parking lot, water district and bridge projects dominated.
Fire district budget transparency, subdivision notice, and 'blank check' contract concerns recurred.
Byram AFFH-relocation petition drove a lengthy, contested affordable-housing policy debate.
Multiple bids/agreements: bridge (Oranzio), Kent Place (Casale), Verity, Spectra Serve, Arconnex, PBA.
Quarry Heights project public comment, Water District 4 hearing order, sludge hauling.
Fire District No. 1 budget receipt and ARPA fund dedication before year-end.
Mount Misery marker wording, 250th anniversary account, Frosty Day, girls tennis state champions.
Police space needs driving the relocation, PBA contract, fire district, Route 22 accidents.
Sidewalk advocacy along Route 128 and Route 22 and traffic-signal maintenance.
Ficaris appointment, Libertari vacation carryover, Stevens resignation, PBA stipulation.

staffInput.summary: Gave the town clerk report (election thanks, Thanksgiving office closures, E-News/Nixle reminders); noted required documents for the subdivision public hearing; and conveyed the fire district's responses, including that the supervisor would need to FOIL the full budget.

Advised throughout: stormwater easement is a standard DEC-designed agreement with the town as default performer and no undue liability; explained bid-bond/penalty options and receipt-versus-acceptance for budgets; addressed AFFH affordability and litigation-risk of a negative vote; described the FOIL-exempt status of worksheets and the state-comptroller-review remedy; and flagged the bond-counsel fee-capture resolution.

Explained Mega Painting could not meet insurance requirements (necessitating the bridge re-award); gave Verity Electric background; discussed ARPA fund dedication and equipment; and agreed to look into sidewalks/bid-packet inclusion for the water-line project.

Town Planner; drafted the subdivision address-change notice language and explained why a general start-of-process notice can only say so much; explained the Byram certificate-of-occupancy/affordable-marketing compliance issue and AFFH mechanics.

Town co-historian; raised historic-preservation concerns that 333 Main relocation could affect Landmarks Preservation District No. 1 buildings and warned the Arconnex agreement read like an open-ended 'blank check' lacking scope, cap, and timeframe.

meetings.attributionNote: No speaker labels; speakers inferred from role, content, and two roll-call votes (Water District 4 order 5-0; 333 Main feasibility 4-1 with DiGiacinto the recorded 'no'). The presiding/supervisor voice was attributed to Joseph Rende (ASR rendered him 'Rende/Rendez/Endy' and sometimes 'Jose'), and the polled councilman 'Jose/Bera/Barra' to Jose Berra, who participated by Zoom from Argentina and was excused before adjournment. ASR manglings resolved: DiGiacinto ('Dicacento/Digacinto'), Hussain ('Hussein'), Milim ('Milam/Melham'). Note: the transcript's spoken opening references 'November 13, 2024,' but this file is dated 2024-11-20 per the source; date field follows the filename. Berra vs. Rende ('Jose') disambiguation and a few unlabeled 'I'll second/aye' lines lower confidence on some routine attributions; the Eagle Ridge item includes an unnamed member recusal.

meetings.meetingSummary: The Town Board held two substantive public hearings and worked through a full old/new-business agenda. It adopted the Gavi Restaurant special use permit for a mixed-use building on Old Route 22, opened (and kept open until its December meeting) the public hearing on the 2025 Town and Special District preliminary budget of about $42.6M featuring a fourth consecutive 0% tax increase, and adopted a local law adding dog park rules to the town code after extended debate over enforcement and permitting. It also handled a Highlands Conservation Act grant resolution, several contracts (WSP dam safety, Clove Road baseball field survey, Aquest pre-demolition inspection), committee resignations/reappointments, and routine liaison and administrator reports.
meetings.durationNote: Meeting reconvened from executive session (personnel and board/committee interviews) at 5:30 PM; full board present (Rende, DiGiacinto, Hussain, Milim, Berra); Town Attorney Roland attended via Zoom. No board absences noted.

cases.name: Special Use Permit — Gavi Restaurant Mixed-Use Building
cases.applicant: Joseph R. Crocco / Gavi Restaurant (Croco & Croco Architecture)
cases.summary: Public hearing on a special use permit for a new 5,000 sq ft mixed-use building with two ground-floor retail spaces and four apartments (two 1-bedroom on the first floor, two 2-bedroom on the second), with basement garages for tenants. County and Planning Board correspondence and the SEQRA short form were received; Town Planner Adam Kaufman confirmed no unusual county comments and that site-plan details return to the Planning Board. No residents spoke. The board closed the hearing, adopted a negative declaration, and adopted the resolution granting the permit (all by voice vote). Board members suggested (non-binding) bike racks and more permeable parking surfaces.
cases.publicComment: Applicant's architect Chris Croco presented; no members of the public spoke. Tone favorable throughout.

memberPositions.evidence: Called it a big aesthetic improvement to an old eyesore and 'perfect' for that end of Old 22; guided hearing to adoption.
Suggested (non-binding) bike racks and more permeable/pervious parking surfaces given the sensitive stormwater area.

cases.name: 2025 Town and Special District Preliminary Budgets
cases.summary: Finance Director Abbas Sura presented a roughly $42.6M total 2025 budget (3.2% higher than 2024), with the general fund about 65% and highway about 21%, funded partly by ~$4M of fund balance and a total tax levy near $24.2M. The budget delivers a 0% tax increase — the fourth consecutive year — and stays about $158K under the NYS tax cap. The board opened the public hearing but deliberately kept it open, adjourning to its December meeting for adoption. Extensive board discussion covered budgeting 'to actual,' a smooth 'glide path' toward moderate future increases, the ~$25M fund balance, AAA bond rating, ARPA funds (~$1.1-1.2M), and upcoming capital projects (turf fields, pool, 333 Main, library).
cases.publicComment: No members of the public spoke on the budget.

memberPositions.evidence: Thanked the board/staff for full engagement; stressed budgeting 'more to actual,' a smooth path avoiding artificial one-year spikes, and preserving the AAA bond rating for future capital borrowing.

As library liaison secured funding to extend library hours (a library-clerk-to-librarian-assistant title change); explained fund balance as the town's ~$25M 'bank account' and that town taxes are ~15% of a resident's bill.
Praised for 'excellent analysis'; coined the 'glide path' framing for moderate, predictable increases.

Reflected that prior budgets were 'unduly conservative' and added to fund balance; said he was 'grappling' with whether a small increase now would make for a smoother path; explained ARPA funds as quasi-fund-balance.
Asked for amended library budget pages to be added to members' binders and for a separate sheet of anticipated 2025 capital improvement expenses (library, turf field, pool).

cases.name: Local Law — Amend Chapter 146 (Dogs) to Add Dog Park Rules and Regulations
cases.address: Community Park (near town floodplain), North Castle
cases.applicant: Town of North Castle (Recreation & Parks; drafted with resident Molly Meyer)
cases.summary: Public hearing and adoption of a local law codifying North Castle dog park rules and regulations (Chapter 146). Residents Molly and Juliet Meyer presented supportive research; the board added a wording change to the hold-harmless/indemnification agreement (narrowing the gross-negligence carve-out) at Councilman Berra's suggestion. Debate centered on Councilwoman DiGiacinto's requests — a permit/application form capturing dog-license numbers, initially restricting use to North Castle residents, and clearer enforcement/contact info — which the majority viewed as unnecessarily burdensome versus a practical honor-system approach plus a posted contact number. The board closed the hearing, adopted the negative declaration, and adopted the local law by voice vote; the Town Attorney confirmed no roll call was required. DiGiacinto voted yes despite her stated reservations.
cases.publicComment: Residents Molly and Juliet Meyer (with family/friends) spoke strongly in favor, citing survey support (dog park in the town's top-five desired projects) and researched safety/rules; tone enthusiastic and appreciative.

memberPositions.evidence: A self-described dog lover who supported the park but repeatedly pressed for a permit form with dog-license numbers, resident-only start, and explicit enforcement/contact, citing insurance agent RJ; voted yes 'despite such reservations.'
Pushed to proceed, warned against 'over-legislating' to anticipate problems that don't yet exist, and said rules can be adjusted later if issues arise.
As the board's lawyer, worked with Attorney Roland on the hold-harmless/indemnification wording change and flagged a broader release-vs-indemnification issue to revisit with the insurance carrier.

Argued the requested extra form is impractical ('still honor system... adds administrative burden') and that the board should set the law and delegate operational details to Rec Superintendent Matt Traynor rather than micromanage.

cases.name: Approval of Town Board Minutes — November 13, 2024
cases.summary: Routine old-business approval of the November 13, 2024 town board minutes. Motion made and seconded, approved by voice vote with no discussion.

cases.name: Map Clarification — New Town Roadways and Names, Airport Campus Subdivision
cases.address: Airport Campus Subdivision (Weber Farm / Fieldstone Knoll / Cove View), North Castle
cases.summary: The board adopted a corrected configuration of new roadways in the airport campus subdivision. The road names recommended by the Road Naming Committee were unchanged; only the road configuration was clarified so the entrance road to the 50-unit senior housing has a proper address consistent with 911/emergency addressing, verified with the builder and police department. On the Town Attorney's advice the board voted to adopt the sketch map.

cases.name: Resolution — Inclusion in Federal Highlands Boundary for Conservation Act Grant Program
cases.summary: The board adopted a resolution requesting North Castle be officially included in the federal Highlands boundary (U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service) to qualify for Highlands Conservation Act grant funding and technical assistance. Members raised concerns about whether joining could bind the town to federal environmental regulations, but Attorney Roland and materials from Kerry Kasak clarified that merely joining imposes no obligation and only enables the town to apply for grants (with any accepted grant to be reviewed closely for conditions). Adopted by voice vote.

memberPositions.evidence: Raised the concern that federal involvement can 'bind you to do other things'; vetted it with Kevin, Roland and Kerry Kasak and concluded it's 'a free option' with no binding obligation.
