Pressed whether adopting the resolution could subject the town to stricter environmental regulation or loss of control; satisfied after confirmation it only allows applying for a grant.

cases.name: Release of Guarantee Bond — Santucci Construction, 25 Orchard Drive
cases.summary: The board received a recommendation from KSCJ Consulting Engineers and released a guarantee bond from Santucci Construction for 25 Orchard Drive. Motion made and seconded, no questions, adopted by voice vote.

cases.name: Alcohol Permit — Michelle Falkenstein Art Exhibit Reception, North Castle Public Library
cases.summary: The board approved an alcohol permit application from Michelle Falkenstein for an opening reception for an art exhibit at the North Castle Public Library on December 7, 2024. Approved by voice vote with no discussion.

cases.name: 2025 NYS Association of Towns Membership and Voting Delegate Designation
cases.summary: The board approved 2025 membership in the New York State Association of Towns and designated the Supervisor as the town's voting delegate at the February annual meeting. Members asked the Supervisor to report back informally on the votes; staff and members were encouraged to attend sessions of interest. Adopted by voice vote.

cases.name: Engineering Services Agreement — WSP USA, Long Pond Dam Safety Certification
cases.summary: The board authorized the Supervisor to execute a professional engineering services agreement with WSP USA for coordination of P&G forms for the dam safety annual certification and review/update of the emergency action plan for Long Pond Dam, as required by NYS DEC. Councilman Jose Berra recused himself (a party had spoken to him in his prior capacity as a lawyer before he joined the board). Adopted by voice vote.

memberPositions.evidence: Recused himself from the WSP/Long Pond Dam agreement, noting a party had consulted him as a lawyer before he was on the board (not ethically required, but out of caution).

cases.name: Agreements — Clove Road Park Baseball Fields (Survey and Engineering)
cases.applicant: TC Merits Land Surveyors; KSCJ / Kellard Consulting
cases.summary: Two related items for Clove Road Park baseball field renovation. The board authorized the Supervisor to sign the TC Merits topographic survey agreement (adopted). The second item — a ~$62,200 Kellard/KSCJ engineering agreement — was tabled after the Parks & Rec Advisory Board and Councilman Milim objected that its scope covered a potential seven-figure drainage project the board is unlikely to pursue; the board will get the survey first, then scale back Kellard's scope for a biddable field-releveling project (est. ~$100K-300K). Rec Superintendent Matt Traynor and Kensico Little League volunteer Bob provided background; drainage/flooding at the low-lying field was debated.
cases.publicComment: Bob, a longtime Kensico Little League volunteer (27+ years), described the field's drainage, prior fixes, and the contractor's ~$140-150K field-leveling scope; supportive and cooperative tone.

memberPositions.evidence: Opposed spending on Kellard's broad drainage scope ('scar tissue' from the ~$4.5M Lombardi drainage estimate); favored the survey and a tangible field project, saying he'd rather spend $60K on something physical than on engineering.
Backed doing the survey now and tabling the Kellard agreement to negotiate a scaled-back, biddable scope; called it a good approach that won't slow the project.
Argued the field's drainage/flooding is a real issue that may 'regrettably' need to be addressed, given the low-lying location near the river.

cases.name: Proposal with Aquest — Pre-Demolition Inspection, Old Recreation Building at Lombardi Park
cases.summary: The board authorized the Supervisor to sign a proposal with Aquest to conduct a pre-demolition inspection of the old recreation building at Lombardi Park. Motion made and seconded, adopted by voice vote with no discussion.

cases.name: Resignation — Mitzy Weissman, Beautification Committee
cases.summary: The board accepted the resignation of Mitzy Weissman from the Beautification Committee, effective January 13. Councilwoman DiGiacinto praised her contributions as a master gardener and environmentalist and her family's long town history. Accepted by voice vote with appreciation for her service.

memberPositions.evidence: Warmly thanked Weissman, a master gardener and environmentalist, for her service and contributions to the committee.

cases.name: Reappointment — Diane Borgia, Library Board
cases.summary: The board reappointed Diane Borgia to the Library Board for a five-year term expiring December 31, 2029. Motion made and seconded, adopted by voice vote.

cases.name: Term Adjustment — Angelina Colombo, Assessment Review Board
cases.summary: The board corrected the five-year term date of Angelina Colombo on the Assessment Review Board to now expire September 30, 2026, fixing prior incorrect information (confirmed with the Town Attorney and Town Clerk). Adopted by voice vote.

cases.name: Consensus Agenda
cases.summary: The board adopted the consensus agenda by motion, second, and voice vote with no separate discussion.

themes.note: Central item: ~$42.6M 2025 budget, 4th straight 0% tax increase, 'glide path' to moderate future increases.
Dog park local law, Clove Road baseball fields, Lombardi pre-demolition, and capital plans for pool/turf.
Gavi mixed-use special use permit and airport campus roadway map clarification.
WSP dam safety, Aquest inspection, Clove Road survey adopted; Kellard engineering scope tabled.
Weissman resignation, Borgia reappointment, Colombo term correction.
Highlands Conservation Act inclusion resolution and ARPA fund designation discussion.
Rising thefts, key-fob PSA, and 911 addressing behind the roadway map clarification.
Drought warning conservation reminder and Quarry Heights well hookups.
Girls tennis state-championship parade, Frosty Day, and an unclaimed-funds PSA.

staffInput.summary: Gave community announcements (Thanksgiving closures, interfaith service, e-news/Nixle), recited the documents to be received for the Gavi and dog park hearings, and tracked motions/votes procedurally.

Presented the 2025 budget: ~$42.6M total, 0% tax increase (4th consecutive), under the tax cap by ~$158K; explained fund balance use, revenue sources, and the shift to budgeting 'to actual'; agreed to circulate amended binder pages.

Advised on ARPA fund designation, dog park enforcement/complaint routing (to his office rather than police), Clove Road maintenance equipment, and gave the administrator's report (winter parking ban, rec lottery, theft/key-fob PSA).

Recreation & Parks Superintendent: explained the dog park rules were drafted with resident Molly Meyer and are enforceable once codified, and that a contact number can go on signage; on Clove Road recommended proceeding with the survey and scaling back Kellard's engineering scope.
Town Planner: confirmed the county's Gavi letter had only typical comments and that site-plan details return to the Planning Board; noted he did not draft the dog park code (Traynor did).

Attended via Zoom; agreed to the hold-harmless wording change, advised the roadway map should be voted on as a board adoption, confirmed the Highlands resolution imposes no binding obligation, and confirmed no roll call was required for the dog park local law.

meetings.attributionNote: Raw ASR with no speaker labels; the presiding/Supervisor voice (Joseph Rende) and Councilwoman DiGiacinto (only woman; distinctive dog-park positions) were identifiable with high confidence. Saleem Hussain was pinned via his library-liaison role; Jose Berra via his lawyer role (hold-harmless drafting, WSP recusal) and verbose reflective budget commentary; Matt Milim via the 'glide path' credit and turf/drainage 'scar tissue' analysis — several of these are medium confidence. NOTE: the transcript's own header identifies this as the November 20th (2024) meeting whose budget hearing was adjourned to December 11; it is analyzed here under the assigned output date 2024-12-11. ASR mangled several names (e.g., 'Jose' used for both Rende and Berra, 'Digacinto', 'Hussein'), normalized to the roster. Full board present; no absences.

meetings.meetingSummary: The first Town Board meeting of 2025 opened after an executive session and began with a lengthy work session on Board of Ethics recommendations to amend the Code of Ethics, followed by the annual reorganization/organizational agenda (depositories, policies, appointments, and 2025 professional-services contracts). The board then handled its regular agenda: scheduling a public hearing on the Greenwich Realty zoning text amendment at 23 Bedford Banksville Road, calling a public hearing to establish Water District No. 9, adopting a resolution urging the state to pause centralized arraignment, adopting a resolution supporting a Hudson River Valley Greenway trail grant for Wampus Brook Park, and approving several appointments, consulting agreements, and merit-based salary increases. A final payment to the North White Plains Community Center contractor was tabled pending punch-list verification.
meetings.durationNote: Full board present (roll call: Councilman Berra, Councilman Milim, Councilwoman DiGiacinto, Councilman Hussain, Supervisor Rende, all aye). Meeting opened at 5:30 PM and immediately recessed into executive session (personnel and real estate), then reconvened. DiGiacinto recused herself from the Greenwich Realty/23 Bedford Banksville Road zoning item; Berra recused himself from the Long Pond Park District agreement.

cases.name: Board of Ethics 2024 Recommendations to Amend the Code of Ethics
cases.summary: Board of Ethics Chair Brett Summers presented five reform recommendations: barring town board members, department heads and consultants from holding office/voting positions in political parties; requiring recusal (not just disclosure) when aggregate campaign contributions exceed $500; making failure to file campaign-finance disclosures a code violation; a new mirror disclosure obligation on applicants; and barring members of land-use boards from appearing on behalf of third parties before town boards. The board broadly supported the package but debated the constitutionality of the political-party-membership ban, whether the applicant-disclosure rule should also cover town contractors, how applicants would be educated, and the effective date. No vote was taken; the board directed liaison Berra to work with the Ethics Board, receive a revised law at the Feb 12 meeting, and schedule a public hearing.
cases.publicComment: Former Judge 'Sue' (a resident/former justice) spoke on interpretation of 'appear on behalf of' and on the constitutionality of the political-party provision, citing the Hatch Act; resident Ed Loberman asked for clarity on the board's recusal position.

memberPositions.evidence: Framed the reforms as vital for building public trust in the board ('so, so important for us to do... build more and more trust in us'); raised only an operational concern about the board being unable to reach quorum on recusals.
In favor of nearly all proposals but urged that recusal rules take effect only for the next election cycle so candidates/donors who acted under the old rules aren't disqualified.
As Ethics Board liaison said he is 'heavily in support of a lot of these... just about all of them,' with some constructive drafting comments; agreed to liaise on revisions.
Supportive; pushed to extend the applicant-disclosure requirement to parties holding contracts/agreements with the town and asked how applicants would be educated about the new obligation.

Generally supportive but skeptical of the ban on political-party voting membership (constitutionality/fairness) and argued disclosure largely suffices; conditioned support on legal confirmation and a fair effective date.

cases.name: 2025 Organizational/Reorganization Agenda — Designations, Policies, Appointments
cases.summary: The board adopted its annual reorganization items by voice vote: designating depositories (adding new bank PPAC/PCSB alongside JP Morgan Chase and others), payment/ACH authorizations, appointment of Jose Berra as Deputy Supervisor, liaison and committee appointments, legal-notice policy (Journal News and Examiner), the second-and-fourth-Wednesday 7:30 PM meeting schedule, 70-cents-per-mile reimbursement, the 2025 master fee schedule, and various financial and workplace policies. All passed unanimously; a clerical date error (January 12, 2023) on several pages was noted for correction. DiGiacinto voted for the workplace-violence and sexual-harassment policies while stating they have flaws that Administrator Kevin is drafting improvements for.

memberPositions.evidence: Voted to continue the workplace-violence and sexual-harassment policies because it is important to have them in effect, while flagging flaws and noting a draft improvement is coming.
Presided over and moved the reorganization items; noted several other policies are being updated for a joint work session and adoption.

cases.name: 2025 Legal Services Agreement with Abrams Fensterman LLP
cases.summary: The board authorized the Supervisor to sign the 2025 legal-services agreement with Abrams Fensterman LLP, the firm to which Town Attorney Roland moved in 2024. Supervisor Rende disclosed, for public knowledge, that several members of the firm made campaign contributions to his 2023 campaign. The board praised the move as beneficial (retaining Roland's expertise plus a full firm behind him) and adopted the agreement, along with separate 2025 agreements for justice-court counsel (Patrick Bliss), labor counsel (Bond Schoeneck & King), engineering/stormwater services (KSCJ Consulting), ambulance and fire-protection districts, and financial advisory services (Capital Markets Advisors).

memberPositions.evidence: Called the move to Abrams Fensterman 'a great move,' citing continuity of Roland's expertise plus a full supporting staff; proactively disclosed firm members' campaign contributions to his campaign.

cases.name: Greenwich Realty Group Zoning Text Amendment — 23 Bedford Banksville Road
cases.applicant: Greenwich Realty Group LLC (attorney Tony/Anthony Veneziano; owner Mark Masiello)
cases.summary: Attorney for Greenwich Realty asked the board to reset a public hearing to legalize two interior industrial uses (wood processing and iron/aluminum assemblage) at a split-zoned CBB/GB property. Councilman Milim strongly objected that rezoning the whole parcel to GB (as originally proposed) would expand the potential for a warehouse/self-storage use that neighbors had opposed. After a brief executive session for counsel's advice, the board directed that instead the entire parcel be zoned CBB with the two uses added by special-use permit, and voted to schedule the public hearing for February 12, 2025, pending a re-referral to the county. DiGiacinto recused herself (her husband owns 25% of Band Monk Realty, which holds a mortgage on the property).
cases.publicComment: Applicant's attorney and owner appeared; no adverse resident comment (hearing not yet held). Applicant noted outreach to a Conyers Farm HOA representative.

memberPositions.evidence: Repeatedly objected that rezoning the whole property to GB would 'give extra rights for a warehouse'/self-storage on part of the property; pushed the alternative of adding the uses to the CBB zone instead.
Commended the owner for cleaning up and improving the site and favored legalizing the interior uses while protecting the neighborhood via the appropriate rezoning approach.
Asked whether adding the uses to the CBB zone would create new risk for other CBB properties townwide and asked Planner Kaufman to check which properties could qualify.

cases.name: Establishment of Water District No. 9
cases.summary: The board received the WASP Engineering Group report and environmental assessment form for proposed Water District No. 9 and adopted an order calling a public hearing for February 12, 2025 (roll call 5-0). Counsel Roland and Water/Sewer Superintendent Sal explained that the district cannot be finalized until Westchester Joint Water Works confirms served parcels and WASP prepares an amended as-built report (fewer hydrants and uncompleted meter chambers than originally reported, because the funded work ran out of money). Superintendent Sal flagged the need to verify that installed hydrants are active for fire protection and that a New York City water agreement is in progress.

cases.name: Resolution Urging the State to Pause the Central Arraignment Plan
cases.summary: The board adopted a resolution urging the New York State court system to pause a centralized (White Plains) arraignment plan, subject to minor text corrections to be sent by Milim. Supervisor Rende argued the plan imposes heavy costs and manpower burdens (two officers per prisoner transfer), pulling police off the road, and criticized it as another erosion of local authority. Former Justice 'Sue' spoke against it on justice-administration grounds (loss of one-on-one interaction with defendants). The resolution passed by voice vote.
cases.publicComment: Former Town Justice 'Sue' spoke in support of pausing the plan, citing loss of individualized defendant attention; tone: supportive and expert.

memberPositions.evidence: Detailed the manpower/overtime burden and safety impact of prisoner transfers and said if the state wants this it should supply the vehicles and officers; noted the police chief called it costly and chaotic.
Backed the resolution, framing it as another instance of the state taking power and accountability away from locally elected officials.

cases.name: Final Payment (Requisition #8) — North White Plains Community Center Renovation
cases.summary: The board considered final payment (requisition #8) and release of the guarantee bond to AFL General Construction for the North White Plains Community Center renovation. Councilman Berra objected that library-board concerns (a shower door lacking a proper sweep and a kitchen-cabinet ADA layout) were never resolved, and Supervisor Rende raised a broader concern that the architect (Sullivan Architecture) failed to properly oversee the work. Administrator Kevin said both the architect's and engineer's punch lists were fully completed. The board agreed to defer the payment to the next meeting to reconcile the punch list and check back with the library board.
cases.publicComment: Library-board members (Kim Longo, Diane, Stephanie Paul) had previously raised the shower-door and kitchen concerns that prompted the objection.

memberPositions.evidence: Said it would be a disservice to approve final payment because agreed fixes (shower-door sweep, kitchen layout) were never properly done despite his repeated follow-ups; wanted the punch list resolved first.
Proposed the fair test: verify the punch list — if everything was done, pay and release the bond; if not, they shouldn't be paid; wanted more information before voting.

Emphasized the need for proper project oversight — the architect who designed the change orders should have ensured the work was correct, not library-board volunteers — as the town prepares for larger projects.
As library-board liaison wanted the same library-board members who flagged the issues to review and sign off before the board approves payment.

cases.name: Resolution Supporting Hudson River Valley Greenway Trail Grant — Wampus Brook Park Greenway Trail
cases.address: Wampus Brook Park / 128 Main Street, Armonk
cases.applicant: Town of North Castle (Town Planner Adam Kaufman)
cases.summary: The board adopted a resolution supporting a 50% Hudson River Valley Greenway trail grant to build an 8-foot multi-use path (with boardwalk over wetlands) from Wampus Brook Park toward the pool and ultimately the Sands Mill development, reviving a 2007/2008 Kellard-designed plan. Planner Kaufman explained the grant is due at month's end and adoption is non-binding but needed to proceed; cost estimates are pending. Members were enthusiastic, framing it as safer connectivity for children and a highly rated park-and-rec priority, though DiGiacinto reiterated her call for a townwide capital-improvement plan. The resolution passed by voice vote.

memberPositions.evidence: Called it 'an absolute home run' for keeping kids safe off Route 128 and a very cool project; argued against creating a capital plan, calling these judgment calls for elected officials, not an appointed budget committee.
Enthusiastically backed applying for the grant and asked about the timeline/path forward for residents.
Championed pursuing the grant and additional county/state/federal funding to defray cost, praising staff for catching the opportunity.
Supported the idea but urged fiscal caution and reiterated her wish for a capital-improvement/capital-project plan given multiple multimillion-dollar projects underway.

cases.name: Salary Increases for Department-Head / Non-Union Employees (Merit-Based)
cases.summary: The board approved merit-based salary increases for department-head and non-union employees. The item passed, but Councilwoman DiGiacinto — while voting for the raises — objected to the methodology, arguing there was no matrix and employees were never told the expectations, and urged a better process next year. Supervisor Rende and Councilmen Milim and Hussain defended the merit approach as fairer and more productive than across-the-board increases, crediting Administrator Kevin's input; Berra assured staff the decisions were fully considered.

memberPositions.evidence: Voted for the raises but objected to how they were calculated — no matrix, no midpoint feedback, employees not told the new merit approach in advance; called the prior comparative method thoughtful, not haphazard.
Strongly defended merit/performance-based increases as positive for both the workforce and taxpayers, calling automatic comparisons to similar towns 'ludicrous.'
Said he liked how it was done — fair, rewarding those who went above and beyond with bigger raises — using the town administrator's objective feedback.
Said factoring performance into compensation clearly makes for a better-run town; separated the sound compensation decision from the room to improve day-to-day employee feedback.
Assured department heads the decisions were 'fully considered,' with strong debate and input from Kevin, and that the board recognizes the importance of people's paychecks.

cases.name: Acceptance of Retirement/Resignation — Angel Morales, Police Department (Animal Control Officer)
cases.summary: The board accepted, with regrets, the retirement/resignation of longtime animal control officer Angel Morales, effective January 24, 2025. Supervisor Rende and Councilwoman DiGiacinto offered warm tributes to his care for animals and long service, and noted his gracious six-week advance notice. Accepted by voice vote.

memberPositions.evidence: Praised Morales as a special man and asset to the police department who cared deeply about animals; moved acceptance 'with regrets.'

cases.name: Reappointment of John Krupa to the Conservation Board
cases.summary: The board reappointed John Krupa to the Conservation Board for a two-year term ending December 31, 2026, by voice vote. A member praised him as a great community member.

cases.name: Probationary Appointment — Jose Sala, Highway Department Mechanic
cases.summary: The board approved the probationary appointment of Jose Sala as a mechanic in the Highway Department, effective January 9, 2025, by voice vote.

cases.name: 2025 Agreements with Bundio & Co. LLP — GASB 87/96 and Town/Justice Court Audits
cases.summary: The board authorized the Supervisor to sign 2025 agreements with Bundio & Co. LLP for GASB 87 and 96 professional consulting services and for the Town of North Castle and Justice Court audits. Adopted by voice vote.

cases.name: 2025 Renewal Agreement with WeatherWorks (Weather Consulting Services)
cases.summary: The board accepted the 2025 renewal agreement with WeatherWorks for weather consulting services by voice vote.

cases.name: Extension of Special Use Permit — St. Nersess Armenian Seminary, 486 Bedford Road
cases.applicant: Robert Architect PC (for St. Nersess Armenian Seminary)
cases.summary: The board received a letter and adopted a resolution granting a one-year extension of a special use permit for building modifications at the St. Nersess Armenian Seminary, giving the applicant additional time to address conditions of approval. No applicant appeared (a routine extension); passed by voice vote.

cases.name: Town Board Liaison Updates and Procedural Exchange
cases.summary: During liaison updates the board noted a Suburban recycling-schedule mix-up (two consecutive glass/plastic weeks) to be corrected, praised Open Space Committee member Doug Manson's award for invasive-vine cleanup, and flagged bumps in the new Route 128 paving to raise with NYSDOT at an upcoming meeting. A pointed exchange occurred when DiGiacinto expressed disappointment at not being reappointed liaison to the building/planning departments; Milim criticized her for raising it during updates rather than in advance, calling it an attempt to create drama, and she called his characterization inappropriate.

memberPositions.evidence: Expressed disappointment that the Supervisor again did not appoint her liaison/co-liaison to the building and planning departments.
Told DiGiacinto raising the liaison grievance during updates rather than in advance was inappropriate and 'trying to create drama' to make a colleague look bad.

cases.name: Public Comment — Anti-Income-Tax Remarks (Tony Voutier)
cases.summary: Resident Tony Voutier (89) used the public comment period to describe his 25-year effort challenging the federal income tax and his correspondence with Donald Trump, unrelated to town business. The board took no action; Supervisor Rende thanked him, and Town Attorney Roland cautioned the public not to rely on tax advice given in the room without consulting a tax professional.
cases.publicComment: Tony Voutier delivered a lengthy off-topic statement opposing the federal income tax; tone: passionate advocacy, no town-business ask.

themes.note: Dominated by the ethics-code work session, plus disclosures, contract oversight, and a liaison-appointment dispute.
Reorganization appointments, merit-based salary increases (with DiGiacinto dissenting on method), and a retirement/reappointment.
Many 2025 professional-services agreements adopted; contractor final payment tabled over oversight/punch-list concerns.
Greenwich Realty zoning text amendment debated and set for hearing; a routine seminary permit extension.
Enthusiastic support for the Wampus Brook greenway trail grant application.
Resolution opposing central arraignment; fire/ambulance agreements; hydrant activation for Water District 9.
Water District No. 9 order and public-hearing scheduling with as-built report caveats.
Fee schedule, financial policies, and DiGiacinto's call for a capital-improvement plan.
Central arraignment pushback and IMAs with Bedford and fire/ambulance districts.
Recycling schedule, invasive-vine cleanup, Conservation Board reappointment.

staffInput.summary: Advised on ethics-code drafting and effective dates; gave executive-session counsel on the Greenwich Realty rezoning approach (recommend zoning entire parcel CBB with the two uses by special permit); explained Water District No. 9 cannot close until Westchester Joint Water Works confirms parcels and WASP amends the report; noted the special-permit referral requirement; cautioned public against relying on informal tax advice.

Administered motions and notices; advised on the process/timing to receive the revised ethics law and schedule the public hearing; wished residents happy new year and reminded of a library blood drive and January 31 school-tax deadline; will distribute the Ethics Board statement.

Reported the architect's and engineer's punch lists for the community center were fully completed and explained the shower-door partition and ADA kitchen changes; provided input on merit-based salary determinations; to notify businesses of Verizon parking-lot construction.

Town Planner; recommended structuring the Greenwich Realty rezoning and checking which other CBB properties could qualify; presented the Wampus Brook greenway trail grant opportunity (8-ft multi-use path, 50% grant, due month's end) and next steps.

Water/Sewer Superintendent; explained the as-built differences for Water District No. 9 (fewer hydrants, uncompleted meter chambers due to funding), the need to verify hydrant activation for fire protection, and pending New York City water agreements.

meetings.attributionNote: Roll call confirmed all five members present (Councilman Berra/Bera, Councilman Milim/Millam, Councilwoman DiGiacinto/Digacinto, Councilman Hussain, Supervisor Rende — ASR renders his name as 'Endy'). The presiding/supervisor voice was mapped to Joseph Rende; polled 'Councilman Bera' to Jose Berra (2025, still on the board). Some quotes in the wide-ranging ethics discussion and community-center debate were hard to assign precisely and were attributed only where speaker role was clear. Non-members quoted include Brett Summers (Ethics Board chair), former Justice 'Sue,' residents Ed Loberman and Tony Voutier, and applicant attorney 'Tony'/Anthony Veneziano — all kept out of memberPositions.

meetings.meetingSummary: The Town Board reconvened from an executive session (board interviews, personnel, real estate) to a full public agenda. Headline items were the adoption of a special-use permit and negative declaration for Breezemont Day Camp, a lengthy debate over authorizing an appraisal of surplus town property at 535 Main Street for Awesome Landscaping, and adoption of an order setting a February 12 public hearing on the friendly eminent-domain acquisition of 333 Main Street (the Du Bois building) to consolidate town offices and the police department. The board also awarded a water-district well treatment-building bid (rejecting/rebidding the site-work portion), acted on several wetland mitigation bonds, an asbestos-remediation proposal, routine agreements, and personnel matters. Liaison and staff updates covered a new water main activation, library board committees, and a $494,700 salt-dome grant.
meetings.durationNote: Meeting opened at 5:30 PM and immediately adjourned to executive session (board/committee interviews, personnel, advice of counsel on real estate), then reconvened in public. Full five-member board present; no absences noted. Special counsel Bob Spolzino sat in for Town Attorney Roland Barone. Board recessed to a second executive session at the end for an additional personnel matter with no further public votes.

cases.name: Approval of Town Board Minutes — January 8, 2025
cases.summary: Routine approval of the prior meeting's minutes. Motion made and seconded, carried on a voice vote. No discussion.

cases.name: Special Permit — HZBR LLC / Breezemont Day Camp, 60 Cox Avenue
cases.summary: The board adopted a negative declaration (SEQR) and a resolution granting a special-use permit to Breezemont Day Camp, formerly a legal non-conforming use, after the town amended the zoning code to allow day camps by special permit and the applicant resolved outstanding site-plan issues with the Planning Board. Town Planner Adam Kaufman explained the permit conditions and the two restrictions (15-acre minimum, interstate-highway frontage) that limit day camps to very few parcels. Members praised the applicant's cooperation, the resolution of neighbor concerns (noise, PA system, parking), and the camp's voluntary landmarking of the building facade. As a fail-safe the board first moved to close the hearing 'to the extent it had not previously been closed,' then adopted the negative declaration and resolution by voice vote.
cases.publicComment: No public speakers on this item; applicant declined to add remarks.

memberPositions.evidence: Called the resolution 'more than satisfactory,' said it responded to neighbors' concerns on the PA system and parking, and praised the applicant and Planning Board.
Praised the applicant's handling of resident concerns as 'best in class' while still running a business; noted his kids attended and joked about the tie-dye shirt.
Disclosed a grandchild attends the camp; called Breezemont 'a tremendous asset to the town' and moved to adopt the negative declaration and resolution.

cases.name: Acquisition Request / Appraisal — Awesome Landscaping Corp., 535 Main Street
cases.applicant: Awesome Landscaping Corp. (via Geist Schwartz & Jelnick PLLC)
cases.summary: Attorney Jerry Geist, representing Awesome Landscaping, asked the board to accept a letter and authorize Assessor Georgeanne Richardson to obtain a USPAP appraisal of a small surplus town parcel (a former oil terminal the town acquired and remediated) so the client could pursue buying it for an office, garage, and truck parking to augment his adjacent business. A roughly hour-long debate followed over process (appraise-before-offer vs. offer-before-appraise), the parcel's tight CB-zoning constraints, aesthetics of trucks in a highly visible downtown location, and whether the board would retain zoning/decision control versus deferring to other boards. The board ultimately voted to receive the letter and to instruct the assessor to seek an appraisal (client-funded, under ~$1,000), with several members reserving judgment on any eventual sale and requesting concept drawings once an appraisal is in hand. Supervisor Rende disclosed the firm does landscaping at his significant other's home.
cases.publicComment: Resident Tony Fiuti sought to comment but was reminded it was not a public hearing; he later noted he'd like the property back on the tax roll and praised former officials.

memberPositions.evidence: Argued the process was backwards ('putting things in the wrong order') — preferred a real offer and understanding of intended use before spending on an appraisal, and pressed the attorney and planner on what would actually go on the parcel.

Detailed the tough CB constraints (setbacks, ~90% coverage, ZBA relief needed) but was okay proceeding for the nominal appraisal cost; raised the fairness point that the board should keep its long-standing practice for this applicant and only change the policy prospectively.

Called it a 'very, very visible space in the heart of our town' and was concerned about the detrimental look of high-density truck parking; wanted the board to make the zoning/use decision carefully and not relegate it to other boards.
Willing to proceed but asked that, once an appraisal is obtained, the applicant provide a sketch/drawing of the proposed structure and parking so the board has 'something to talk about.'

Disclosed his significant other uses the landscaper; expressed faith in the ZBA, Planning, and Architectural Review boards to shape the outcome and supported starting the process to get the parcel back on the tax rolls.

cases.name: Order Calling Public Hearing — Eminent Domain Acquisition of 333 Main Street (Du Bois Building)
cases.summary: The board received a SEQR short-form EAF Part 1 and the appraisal (BS F&F LLC / Mike Ferrari, dated Nov. 18, 2024) and adopted an order calling a public hearing on February 12, 2025 for the friendly eminent-domain acquisition of 333 Main Street to house all town offices, the police department, and the water/sewer staff currently in 30-year-old trailers. Supervisor Rende laid out the deficiencies (cited since a 2007 study) — flooding police locker rooms, inadequate holding cells, ADA non-compliance, an unsafe farmhouse annex — and urged an outright referendum from the start rather than the minimum permissive referendum. Members broadly supported pursuing the opportunity but urged cost scrutiny, at least two public hearings, a parallel study of the existing town-hall campus, and aggressive public outreach. Special counsel Bob Spolzino explained why condemnation benefits the town (it brackets/forces the negotiation and forecloses competing buyers).
cases.publicComment: Resident Tony Fiuti spoke skeptically, questioning why eminent domain was being used, whether the town has a 5-/10-year facilities plan, and criticizing past town construction oversight; he requested the EAF and appraisal before the hearing.

memberPositions.evidence: Championed the acquisition as a prudent, fact-based response to long-cited deficiencies and pushed for a full referendum from the outset rather than a minimum permissive referendum.

Called it a 'once in a lifetime, no-brainer opportunity,' detailing police flooding and cramped space, and argued buying an existing building is far cheaper and lower-risk than building from scratch under prevailing-wage costs.

Supported consideration but stressed scrutinizing the economics, confirming space needs, weighing alternatives, holding at least two (possibly three) public hearings, and pursuing the highway garage on a parallel track; welcomed the 'friendly' condemnation.

Wanted to proceed 'but with caution' — a parallel study of the existing town-hall campus, distinguishing needs vs. wants, noting many unknowns on retrofit cost and warning that President's Week could suppress public input.
Agreed Matt 'said it really well,' called it an extreme need, and urged pursuing it aggressively with appropriate due diligence to 'solve the problem' for staff.

cases.name: Bids — Water District No. 4 New Well Supply (on Sewer District No. 2 Property)
cases.summary: On the recommendation of Water/Sewer Superintendent 'Sal,' the board awarded the bid for the prefabricated turnkey treatment building (pumps, UV/chlorination, controls) to Enginuity Fluid Inc. and authorized the Supervisor to sign. For the separate site-work portion, the board rejected all bids and authorized a rebid after Sal flagged confusing, inflated line-item numbers (e.g., ductile iron) that didn't match other projects; the ~10-month building lead time leaves ample schedule to rebid. Both actions passed by voice vote, with the board praising Sal's due diligence for avoiding overpayment.

memberPositions.evidence: Said he'd spoken with Sal the day before; noted his only concern (that rebidding the site work might delay the building) was addressed since there's plenty of schedule slack.

cases.name: Street Naming & Addressing — Airport Campus, 113 King Street (E-911 Referral)
cases.summary: The board received a January 13, 2025 memo from KSCJ Consulting on the assignment of new street names and addresses for the Airport Campus and referred it to the Town E-911 Coordinator. The naming committee had to revisit the plan because it had not accounted for the amenities building (senior/older housing) remaining on site. Received by voice vote.

cases.name: Wetland Mitigation Bonds — 34 Kremer Road
cases.summary: On the town engineer's recommendation, the board established a wetland mitigation bond for 34 Kramer LLC and released the original mitigation-plantings bond to the prior property owner. Both motions carried by voice vote.

cases.name: Wetland Mitigation Bond — 2 Tripp Lane
cases.summary: The board established a wetland mitigation bond for mitigation plantings at 2 Tripp Lane, followed by a five-year monitoring and maintenance bond, on the town engineer's recommendation. Passed by voice vote. A member noted the Conservation Board has been working with staff to better enforce and monitor such mitigation requirements.

memberPositions.evidence: Noted the Conservation Board, working with the town administrator, has been getting more on top of enforcing and monitoring mitigation requirements — 'a good thing for the town' given the importance of wetlands and buffers.

cases.name: Payment Requisition No. 8 — Final Payment (Tabled)
cases.summary: The board tabled approval of Payment Requisition No. 8 (final payment) to February, needing to look into a couple more items. Tied to broader concern that a project done two years earlier may not have been managed correctly and is now in dispute.

cases.name: Proposal — Asbestos Remediation Bid/Spec & Management Services, Old Recreation Building, 85 Cox Avenue
cases.applicant: Quality Environmental Solutions and Technologies Inc.
cases.summary: The board approved a proposal from Quality Environmental Solutions and Technologies Inc. to provide bids, specifications, and management services for asbestos remediation at the old recreation building. A member questioned whether the open-ended management-services scope was needed given licensed remediators, asking staff to keep a close eye on cost; the board concluded that professional oversight/air monitoring is money well spent for accountability, especially in light of a separate project just tabled over disputed prior management. Passed by voice vote.

memberPositions.evidence: Argued a professional should manage taxpayer-funded projects for accountability if something goes awry — 'that's money well spent,' referencing the requisition just tabled over disputed management.
Questioned whether the open-ended management-services scope was necessary given licensed remediators and asked staff to keep a close eye on the cost.

cases.name: 2025 Renewal Agreement — ESI Group Employee Assistance Program
cases.summary: The board authorized the Supervisor to sign the 2025 renewal agreement with ESI Group for the Employee Assistance Program. Motion made, seconded, and carried by voice vote with no discussion.

cases.name: MOA with CSEA Unit No. 2 — Salary Schedule Modification (Lead Maintenance Mechanic)
cases.summary: The board authorized the Supervisor to sign a memorandum of agreement with CSEA Unit No. 2 modifying the salary schedule for the lead maintenance mechanic position. Passed by voice vote with no discussion.

cases.name: Provisional Appointment — Dane Fender, Water & Sewer Maintenance Worker Grade 2
cases.summary: The board approved the provisional appointment of Dane Fender as water and sewer maintenance worker, grade 2, effective February 10, 2025, welcoming him to North Castle. Passed by voice vote.

cases.name: Receipt of Resignation — Jane Rothschild, North Castle Public Library
cases.summary: The board received the resignation of Jane Rothschild from the North Castle Public Library, effective January 16, 2025, and wished her well. Accepted by voice vote.

cases.name: Town Board Liaison & Administrator Updates
cases.summary: Liaison and administrator updates included cleanup of the Erico/Children's Preserve on Byram Lake (path clearing and invasive-vine removal), the Library Board's formation of focused committees (bylaws/policies, strategic planning, facilities, marketing, executive) to advance its long-term plan, progress on the Verizon-portion parking-lot improvements behind Main Street and plans for a downtown parking district, and a $494,700 salt-dome grant (75% reimbursement on a 25% share) reported by the Town Administrator. The Supervisor stressed a renewed emphasis on building maintenance.

memberPositions.evidence: Reported the ecologically important Erico/Children's Preserve on Byram Lake will get path cleanup and invasive-vine removal so residents can enjoy and hike it.
As Library Board liaison, reported the board's new focused committees (bylaws/policies, strategic planning, facilities, marketing, executive) as a strong step toward executing its long-term strategy.

themes.note: Dominated by the 333 Main Street office/police consolidation and the water-well treatment building; strong board appetite tempered by cost caution.
Recurring debate over process (referendum choice, appraise-before-offer, retaining board decision authority) and heavy emphasis on public input.
Breezemont special permit (positive) and the contested Awesome Landscaping surplus-parcel appraisal (mixed, aesthetics and zoning concerns).
Deteriorated, flood-prone police facility and inadequate holding cells were a central justification for the 333 Main acquisition.
Well-supply bids, a new water-main activation for fire protection, and a personnel appointment; strong appreciation for the superintendent's diligence.
Cost scrutiny threaded through the 333 Main acquisition, tabled requisition, and asbestos management scope; school-tax deadline announced.
Well bid award/rebid, asbestos proposal, EAP renewal, and CSEA MOA; recurring theme of professional oversight for accountability.
Provisional water/sewer appointment, library resignation, CSEA salary MOA, plus two executive sessions on personnel.
Wetland mitigation bonds and strengthened Conservation Board monitoring; Byram Lake preserve cleanup.

staffInput.summary: Delivered community announcements: second-half school taxes due Jan. 31, the Feb. 11 special election for county executive with early voting Feb. 1-9, and the relocation of polling for districts 6/7/11 into the Armonk firehouse community room; reminded residents to sign up for E-News/Nixle. Later checked the record on whether the Breezemont hearing had been closed.

Town Planner: recapped the Breezemont zoning-amendment/special-permit history and the 15-acre and interstate-frontage limits on day camps; explained that vehicle storage for the landscaping parcel is only permissible as accessory to a permitted office use and recounted the prior 1,000 sq ft office/apartment marketing plan for the surplus parcel.

Special counsel (Abrams Fensterman), sitting in for Roland Barone. Advised that the board may set property-disposition terms at its discretion without amending the code, and explained why condemnation benefits the town on 333 Main Street: it brackets/forces the negotiation to an end and forecloses competing buyers.

Water/Sewer Superintendent: recommended awarding the prefab well treatment-building bid to Enginuity Fluid Inc. and rejecting/rebidding the site-work bid due to inflated, confusing line items; reported Health Department verbal approval activating 853 ft of new Westchester Joint Waterworks water main (three new hydrants) for fire protection on Quarry/William/James streets; previewed next steps and grant pursuit for district formation and a $2.9M wastewater award.

Reported the $494,700 salt-dome grant (75% reimbursement on the town's 25% share) with the large dome wrapping up and the small dome rehabbed, and is coordinating on maintenance priorities and grant applications.

meetings.attributionNote: Raw ASR with no speaker labels; the presiding/supervisor voice was mapped to Joseph Rende throughout. Council members were inferred from context and forms of address: Barbara DiGiacinto identified via 'Councilwoman' and the sketch/parallel-study remarks; Jose Berra via references to 'Councilman Barra/Barrow' and 'the point that Jose made,' the appraise-before-offer/friendly-condemnation and Byram Lake comments (Berra is valid for 2025); Matt Milim via 'what Matt explained/said' (fairness point, CB-zoning 'nerd' detail, 'once in a lifetime no-brainer'); Saleem Hussain ('Sween'/'Celine' ASR manglings) via the library-liaison update and the visibility/aesthetics concerns. Some overlapping compliments (Breezemont) and the asbestos management-services exchange could not be pinned to a single member with high confidence, so those carry lower confidence. Sonny Vitaj not attributed (2026 only). No absences noted; full five-member board present. Name manglings normalized: 'engineer Fluid' = Enginuity Fluid Inc., 'Bob Roberts Spino' = Bob Spolzino, 'George Ann Richardson' = Georgeanne Richardson.

meetings.meetingSummary: The Town Board held a heavily-attended regular meeting dominated by three public hearings. It opened and closed the hearing on establishing Water District No. 9 to bring municipal water to PFAS-contaminated Quarry Heights wells, then adopted two enabling resolutions 5-0 (subject to permissive referendum). It held and closed a hearing on a zoning text amendment/local law to rezone 23 Bedford Banksville Road to permit two specific light-industrial uses, adopting the local law with a negative declaration (Councilwoman DiGiacinto recused). The board then opened a public hearing on acquiring 333 Main Street, Armonk by eminent domain to consolidate town offices, police and court; that hearing drew extensive, largely skeptical public comment and was left open and continued to February 26. The board also cleared a routine consent/administrative agenda.
meetings.durationNote: Full board present: Rende, DiGiacinto, Hussain, Milim, Berra (all five roll-called aye on Water District 9). DiGiacinto recused herself from the 23 Bedford Banksville Road hearing due to a family financial interest in the mortgage holder.

cases.name: Establishment of North Castle Water District No. 9 — Quarry Heights
cases.address: Quarry Heights (Starkey Rd / McClure Pl / William St / Old Orchard), West Harrison
cases.applicant: Town of North Castle Water & Sewer Department
cases.summary: First step in creating a municipal water district to serve Quarry Heights homes whose private wells are contaminated with PFAS and running dry. The board opened and closed the public hearing, then adopted two resolutions: one making certain determinations and one approving establishment of Water District No. 9 subject to a permissive referendum, each passing 5-0 by roll call. Superintendent 'Sal' explained that a $1.1-1.2M Westchester Joint Water settlement funded only part of the main, and the town intends to extend the district (~30 more homes toward Rocky Ledge/Old Orchard) using grants via DEC/EFC. Residents pressed the board to commit to including all affected homes at no undue cost; Supervisor Rende committed on the record that the district's purpose is to eventually cover all homes.
cases.publicComment: Several Quarry Heights residents (Lisa Alvarez, Nico Marino, Martha Rosen, Erminio Maresa) spoke, appreciative of progress but frustrated and urgent about ~5 years of PFAS exposure, dry wells, missing fire hydrants, cost burden, and unequal hookups; a few exchanges with the Supervisor grew heated. Tone: supportive of the district but critical of the slow pace.

memberPositions.evidence: Committed on the record that the district's whole purpose is to eventually take in all homes and continue seeking funds; said the board is now 'very focused' on Quarry Heights.
Noted she and the Supervisor had received Quarry Heights residents' concerns and moved the hearing up in the agenda; voted aye.
Roll-call aye on both establishment resolutions.
Roll-call aye on both establishment resolutions.
Roll-call aye on both establishment resolutions.

cases.name: Zoning Text Amendment / Local Law — 23 Bedford Banksville Road light-industrial special use (CB-B)
cases.applicant: Greenwich Realty Group LLC (Anthony Veneziano, Veneziano & Associates)
cases.summary: A local law/zoning text amendment to create a narrowly-tailored light-industrial special use (wood processing and pre-cut metal/aluminum assemblage) applicable essentially only to this one 10.8-acre, 15,500 sq ft pre-1990 building, legalizing existing tenant operations while dropping a previously proposed self-storage use. Framed by the board as a compromise (worked out with planner Adam Kaufman and in executive session) to protect the Banksville hamlet from larger uses. The board opened and closed the public hearing, adopted a SEQRA negative declaration, and adopted the local law. Councilman Berra secured amendments requiring indoor storage, ventilation of fumes/odors, a 'not subsequently expanded' building limit, and town-board review/approval of the operation plan; a formal special-permit application will follow at a later meeting. DiGiacinto recused herself.
cases.publicComment: Two residents signed up; Peter Noira said he supported the board's position and did not need to speak further if it held. Resident Sonny Vitage (of Bedford Road, a member of the public, NOT a board member in 2025) asked whether the CB-B zone could later allow storing electric batteries; counsel clarified the special permit is limited to woodworking and metalworking only.

memberPositions.evidence: Called it 'an important change,' stressed restricting uses bad for wetlands/buffers, and proposed detailed language edits (indoor storage, proper ventilation of fumes/odors, town-board approval of the operation plan, building not to be expanded).
Gave context that zoning stays with the property and this approach avoids allowing self-storage or other unwanted uses; said 'I'm very supportive of it.'
Described the outcome as a good compromise that protects Banksville while letting the owner legalize and realize revenue; credited the applicant's cleanup efforts.

cases.name: Acquisition of 333 Main Street via Eminent Domain — proposed consolidated Town Hall
cases.applicant: Town of North Castle (owner: partnership incl. Mike Ferrari; law firm tenant Boies Schiller)
cases.summary: The board opened a public hearing on acquiring the ~45,000 sq ft, 18-year-old 333 Main Street building by eminent domain (EDPL) to consolidate police, court, and all town offices, presenting a $7M appraisal, special counsel Bob Spolzino's overview of the condemnation process, and architect Gary Gianfrancesco's/CGR's detailed report documenting severe deficiencies in the current court and police facilities at 15 Bedford Road. Supervisor Rende gave a lengthy case for the move and stressed the board voluntarily committed to a mandatory (not merely permissive) referendum. Public comment was extensive and largely skeptical, focused on the fate of the historic 15 Bedford Road site, renovation/total cost uncertainty, eminent-domain risk of a court-set price above $7M, traffic, and taxes; a minority (adjacent owner, Neil Schwartz, Stefan Martinovic) were supportive. No vote taken; the hearing was left open and continued to February 26, 2025.
cases.publicComment: Heavy turnout and many speakers, in person and on Zoom. Most (former Judge Sue Shimer, Ed Woodyard, Tim Radice for the Historical Society, Keith Rosenthal, Neil Bauman, Antoinette Rocco, Ed Loberman, Fred Cohen, and others) were skeptical or opposed, urging preservation of the Bedford Road historic district, a firm plan for 15 Bedford Road, a white-paper/FAQ, and warning of renovation costs, eminent-domain price risk, and traffic; several supported renovating/rebuilding on the current site instead. A minority (adjacent owner K. Alzida, Neil Schwartz, Stefan Martinovic) endorsed the acquisition as a once-in-a-generation opportunity. Tone: engaged, detailed, cost-conscious, and in places distrustful.

memberPositions.evidence: Passionately argued the current facilities are unsafe and factually inadequate, called 333 a 'golden opportunity that will never come around again,' and emphasized the voluntary mandatory referendum and transparency.

Gave a detailed financial case that the depressed post-COVID office market means 333 can be bought below replacement cost, whereas a new municipal build would run $600-800/sq ft (~$30M); stressed the vote is only whether to send it to referendum. (Supervisor attributed the office-market point to 'Matt.')

Agreed something must be done but said his 'biggest concern' is the uncertain ultimate price via eminent domain; urged negotiating the price and, as a former tax lawyer, noted the seller's 1033 exchange benefits could be leveraged; questioned whether the building is bigger than needed.

Said she is 'very conservative' with taxpayer money and 'very apprehensive' about buying 333 given unknown purchase/retrofit costs and the uncertain future of 15 Bedford Road; wished the town were doing a parallel study of the current site and considering the Legion property.

Called the resident comments valuable (even critical ones) for building the FAQ, encouraged continued written input, and fully supported the Supervisor's push to move forward and solve the problem quickly.

memberPositions.evidence: On the AFL final payment, noted a $10K adjustment obtained through close review and cited it as a lesson in vigilance on town projects.
Added that town projects go well when the right professionals oversee them, praising the Kent Place parking-lot work.

themes.note: The 333 Main Street acquisition and facility-consolidation question dominated the meeting.
Water District 9 created to address PFAS contamination and failing wells at Quarry Heights.
Recurring public and member concern over cost, debt service, and tax impact of a $7M+ acquisition.
Banksville rezoning compromise plus concern over the future zoning/use of the historic 15 Bedford Road site.

Board emphasized transparency, a mandatory referendum, a public white paper/FAQ, and continuing the hearing.
PFAS 'forever chemicals,' floodplain/high groundwater at 15 Bedford, and wetland-buffer protection in Banksville.
Eminent-domain (EDPL) process and the risk that a court sets a price above the $7M appraisal.
Historic-district charm, traffic, and equitable water access were central resident themes.

staffInput.summary: Read in correspondence and affidavits for each public hearing, monitored the 3-minute speaker time limit, and proposed creating a dedicated landing page on the town website for the 333 Main Street project materials.

Explained the Water District 9 process, the Westchester Joint Water consent-order settlement (~$1.1-1.2M) that funded only part of the main, the plan to extend to ~30 more homes, and pursuit of DEC/EFC grants; will bill District 9 as a Westchester Joint customer.

Special counsel who gave an overview of the eminent-domain/condemnation process: public-use standard (a town hall clearly qualifies), the $7M just-compensation offer, filing in state Supreme Court, and the risk of a battle-of-appraisers determination.
Sitting Town Attorney (Abrams Fensterman); assisted the Supervisor in explaining the permissive-referendum threshold (5% of last gubernatorial vote) versus the mandatory referendum the board chose.

Architect/consultant who presented the Center for Government Research facility report detailing safety, accessibility, size, security-circulation, and code deficiencies of the current court and police facilities, concluding the town should invest in a new facility elsewhere.
Town Planner; worked with the applicant and building department on the 23 Bedford Banksville special-use criteria and was referenced on the R-10 zoning yield of 15 Bedford Road.
Arranged for department heads to attend, surfaced the recurring police-station sewage backup, and worked with staff on grants/EFC for the water-district extension.

cases.name: Acquisition of 333 Main Street by Eminent Domain — New Town Facilities (continued public hearing)
cases.summary: Continued public hearing on whether to acquire 333 Main Street via eminent domain procedure law to relocate town hall, police and court from the deficient 15 Bedford Road campus. About two dozen residents spoke, nearly all opposed or urging a pause: they objected to an open-ended 'blank check,' warned the ~$7M appraisal would balloon in court (owner's counsel already disputes it), demanded a full cost comparison with renovating/expanding 15 Bedford Road, and voiced fears the historic 10-acre town hall site would be sold for development. The board received a batch of letters/emails into the record and Supervisor Rende announced an ad hoc concept study committee and a commitment to a public referendum. No vote to close was taken; the hearing was adjourned and continued to the March 12 meeting.
cases.publicComment: Very heavy public participation (in-person and Zoom), overwhelmingly opposed or cautionary. Residents (Keith Rosenthal, Betty Sancharico, Nora Manueli, Sue Scheimer, Neil Bauman, Tom Rice, Carl Henricks, Sharon Tombeck, Carolyn Hoffman and others) pressed for full cost data, alternatives analysis, historic preservation, direct mail notice, and a commitment not to sell 15 Bedford Road without a referendum; one resident (Steven Martinovic) supported the move with a detailed financing/revenue plan.

memberPositions.evidence: Believes 333 will prove the most cost-effective and least impactful option ('buying a building at below replacement cost'), but insists no vote until all facts/costs are gathered, pledges alternatives study, a concept committee and a public referendum; also flatly opposed outsourcing police to Westchester County.

Argued 333 is likely substantially cheaper than building at 15 Bedford (municipal builds run ~$800/sf), defended spending money to study alternatives, and framed the referendum as a chosen community decision rather than a board mandate.

Not in favor of getting rid of the existing town hall; warned the eminent-domain price would exceed $7M (likely $8-9M+) with court risk, and urged direct negotiation with the owner's LLC rather than leaving price to a judge.

Serious reservations about the eminent-domain route and 'not 100% committed' to buying 333; fiscally conservative, wants equal study effort put into preserving/expanding 15 Bedford, the finance committee engaged on total multi-year tax impact, and direct-mail notice to every resident.

Process-focused: laid out the open questions (location/facility need, all physical options including current site, historic preservation, traffic/safety, timeline, referendum, future planning) to be answered clearly in a public FAQ; stressed residents need to see the current location evaluated as a real option.

cases.name: 10 & 20 Round Hill Way — Lot Line Realignment; Access & Utility Agreement
cases.address: 10 & 20 Round Hill Way, North Castle, NY

cases.summary: Request tied to a planning-board-approved lot line realignment of two lots (a family compound plus guest house) from the old Rolling Hills subdivision, requiring the supervisor to sign an amended declaration of access and utility agreement (removing the fire-department-declined water cistern requirement, keeping second-floor sprinklers). Motion carried.

memberPositions.evidence: Had legal questions on construction/cost-sharing and indemnity terms and 'trouble seeing why things like this should be coming to the town board,' worried about locking in terms for future owners; agreed to vote subject to the attorney's satisfaction.
Comfortable voting the same night, seeing no jeopardy to the town, and proposed approving subject to the Town Attorney's reasonable satisfaction to meet the plat deadline.

cases.name: IBM Community Park Turf Field Improvements — SEQRA Lead Agency & Bid Receipt (~$4.07M)
cases.address: IBM Community Park, North Castle, NY
cases.applicant: Town of North Castle (Recreation & Parks / Kellard Engineering)
cases.summary: The board declared its intent to act as SEQRA lead agency and circulated to interested and involved agencies (notably NYSDEC, up to 30 days), and received the environmental assessment form, negative declaration, and the ~$4,074,831 SourceWell cooperative proposal for artificial turf at IBM fields 1 and 2. Members enthusiastically discussed the project's playability gains, maintenance savings and long life; the funding/award vote was deferred pending SEQRA. A side debate on the notification list clarified the Conservation Board would not be circulated as an involved agency, prompting Supervisor Rende to criticize liaisons over-involving themselves in other boards. Lead-agency and receipt motions carried.
cases.publicComment: Resident concern (relayed) that fields might exclude non-Armonk hamlet residents; board clarified they are North Castle-wide fields.

memberPositions.evidence: Champion of the project since 2021; recounted the resident petition, town-wide survey (turf ranked #1 by a wide margin), the superior new field layout enabling two rectangular fields plus baseball, existing lights, and tens of thousands in annual maintenance savings.

Praised the cooperative (SourceWell/Shaw/DeRosa) procurement approach for the cost savings and due diligence, and noted it opened a path to cheaper Clove Road field improvements for North White Plains.

Framed recreation as a post-COVID mental-health/quality-of-life issue and walked through a 15/30/45-year cost extrapolation (site work is ~$3M of the $4M and doesn't wear out) to argue the economics are compelling.

Supportive but stressed drainage is critical and repeatedly urged that this be weighed alongside the town's other big capital costs (town hall, pool, highway garage) with the full multi-year tax picture on the table.

cases.name: Former MBIA Headquarters — Authorization to Negotiate PILOT (age-restricted apartments)
cases.address: Former MBIA headquarters / Airport campus site, Armonk, NY
cases.applicant: Town of North Castle (via Town Attorney)
cases.summary: The board adopted a resolution under General Municipal Law §923A authorizing negotiation of a payment-in-lieu-of-taxes (PILOT) agreement tied to repurposing part of the former MBIA headquarters into an age-restricted multi-family apartment building. Special counsel Roland explained this fulfills the last milestone of a tax-certiorari stipulation of discontinuance (~$5.5M in refunds) the court now wants filed; because the building's interior will be gutted, its assessment must drop anyway, so a PILOT gives the town a 15-year non-challengeable assessment. Members probed how assessment works after 15 years and litigation exposure; satisfied, they adopted it. Motion carried.

memberPositions.evidence: Recalled the negotiation history (fee-simple townhomes, no condo taxation) and signaled he's fine so long as the PILOT's tax impact roughly matches what condo taxation would have produced.
Wanted to understand how the property is assessed once the 15-year PILOT ends (income/expense basis) and, once explained and with Milim comfortable, said he'd be okay with it.

cases.name: Adoption of Electronic Records Policy (digital copies as official records)
cases.summary: The board adopted an electronic records policy allowing digitized copies (e.g., in Laserfiche, TIFF/PDF-A formats) to serve as the town's official records, bringing the town into compliance with the records-retention schedule (LGS-1) it adopted in 2020. Councilman Milim raised data-security concerns and objected to language requiring paper 'convenience copies' to be disposed of when no longer needed; the board amended it to 'may be disposed of.' Councilwoman DiGiacinto also flagged cybersecurity/hacking concerns and the value of the technology committee. Adopted as amended.

memberPositions.evidence: Supportive of digitization but worried about security and premature disposal of paper; secured the change from 'and disposed of' to 'may be disposed of' so paper copies can be retained.
Raised hacking/cybersecurity concerns about digital-only storage and asked how well the town's processes and vendors were vetted, referencing the technology task force.
Asked clarifying questions about why the policy must restate the retention-law adherence and confirmed the explicit reference to the adopted schedule made sense.

cases.name: Acquisition of 333 Main Street, Armonk via Eminent Domain (Town Hall relocation)
cases.summary: The board reconvened the continued public hearing on acquiring 333 Main Street by eminent domain procedure law to relocate Town Hall, citing deteriorated, non-ADA-compliant, and unsafe conditions in the current facilities (police basement flooding, mold, undersized space per a 2007 study). Dozens of residents spoke or submitted letters; a clear majority opposed or expressed concern about eminent domain, traffic, historic-district loss, potential development of the current town parcel, and lack of cost information, while some developers argued the purchase is financially sound. The board repeatedly stressed no decision would be made without full cost studies of multiple options and a town-wide referendum, and committed to an FAQ, a process one-pager, and possible mailings. The board received several resident letters into the record and voted to recess/adjourn the hearing to April 23, 2025 (with the option to postpone further by public notice). No acquisition decision was taken.
cases.publicComment: Very heavy public participation, in person and on Zoom. A clear majority (Alisa Brickell of Whippoorwill Hills, Ed Loberman, Keith Rosenthal, Tom Rice, and letters from Jerry Mariano, John Junker, Mark Wolfson) opposed or was concerned about eminent domain, cost uncertainty, traffic, and loss of the historic parcel; several (developer Vito Erico, Stefan Martinovic) argued the town is financially able and 333 is a smart move. Recurring demand: independent study of all options and full costs before any referendum. Tone at times contentious; the Supervisor cut off accusatory remarks about the current owner.

memberPositions.evidence: Called 333 'a valuable option' that would let the town do other things on the current site; passionate about ADA access and unsafe employee conditions and urgency, but insisted on an open process and a full public referendum.

Wants 15 Bedford Road (current parcel) studied as intensively as 333, ideally by a different, objective architect; warned the fund balance can only cover a few more years of zero tax increases, and raised historic-district, traffic, school, and water-capacity concerns.

Believes 333 will come in cheaper than building new; shared a Facebook view favoring relocating and developing only the highway-yard portion while preserving the town parcel; warned against 'paralysis by analysis' and fear of making a mistake.

Said he is considering all practical alternatives and has not dismissed the Boies building, but is concerned about a court-determined condemnation price and the amount of space deemed necessary; wants to preserve the town parcel and favored getting it on the November referendum.

Focused on process and transparency: encouraged critical (not personal) public input, Zoom participation and rotating speaking order, offered to draft an FAQ of ~15-20 resident questions, and supported one well-timed mailing.

cases.name: Local Law and Master Fee Schedule for Water District No. 8 and Water District No. 9
cases.address: New King Street (District 8) and Quarry Heights, North White Plains (District 9)
cases.applicant: Town of North Castle (Water & Sewer Operations)
cases.summary: The board opened a public hearing to establish the operating local law (district rules/regulations) and water rates for newly formed Water District No. 8 (five New King Street properties transitioning from private wells) and Water District No. 9 (Quarry Heights, where DEC is remediating PFOA/PFAS contamination and hooking homes to public water). The Supervisor read a letter he sent to Senator Schumer seeking grant funding to extend service to ~30 additional Quarry Heights residents facing dried-up or contaminated wells. After Water/Sewer Superintendent Sal explained the districts and next steps (including a needed water-taking agreement with Westchester Joint Water Works for District 9), the board received the superintendent's memo, the EAF and negative declaration, adopted the negative declaration, closed the hearing, adopted the local law, and updated the master fee schedule. All actions passed by voice vote.
cases.publicComment: No resident opposition; the Supervisor placed his Schumer funding-request letter into the record on behalf of Quarry Heights residents.

memberPositions.evidence: Called the vote 'the first step in creating the district,' pledged continued effort to secure grants and remedy the Quarry Heights water problems, and read his Senator Schumer letter into the record.
When polled by the Supervisor for questions, said 'I'm good. I'm on top of this, too,' indicating he was engaged and comfortable moving the districts forward.

cases.name: $4.1M Construction/Drainage and Turf Field Contract at IBM/Community Park
cases.applicant: Recreation & Parks Department (Matt Traynor); contractor pending
cases.summary: A $4.1 million contract for drainage work and installation of turf fields was tabled because the 30-day DEC lead-agency period had not yet expired; the Supervisor had called Senator Shelley Mayer's office to try to obtain written DEC clearance and speed the process. The board hoped to break ground in mid-June to minimize disruption to youth sports. Barbara DiGiacinto pressed to see the eight-year manufacturer warranty (Shaw) in writing and urged a proactive soil test given resident concerns about arsenic contamination on adjacent Eagle Ridge; Kevin (Town Administrator) agreed to arrange the soil test, noting state records show no contamination on the field site and that excavated soil will be tested before off-site disposal. The item was tabled by voice vote, with the Administrator and Supervisor to handle the DEC and testing steps.
cases.publicComment: Resident Mike Ferrari (via Zoom) raised environmental/arsenic concerns, argued the highway garage and town hall are higher priorities, questioned the shrinking developer donation ($1M reduced to $250K), and requested a super-majority vote; the Supervisor noted the item was being tabled.

memberPositions.evidence: Pushed to keep the project on track for a mid-June groundbreaking to minimize disruption to youth sports, and asked whether board members had outstanding documentation questions to resolve before the vote.
Asked for the eight-year warranty in writing and urged doing a soil test proactively during the holding pattern in case arsenic contamination adds cost to the $4.1M project.

cases.name: Residential Contract of Sale to Oliver and Samantha Baranovic (0.334 acres)
cases.address: Town-owned parcel contiguous to 101 Old Hickory Way, Bedford (Crossroad)
cases.summary: The board approved a residential contract of sale of a 0.334-acre town-owned parcel contiguous to 101 Old Hickory Way for a private, non-gated driveway, authorizing the Supervisor to sign. The buyers had spent since 2022 obtaining RPRC, Conservation Board, wetland, and culvert-mitigation approvals, and the contract includes a covenant surviving closing that keeps the passageway open for town emergency-vehicle access. The price was reviewed by the assessor and is stated in the contract. The board first received a related letter from an interested neighbor into the file, then approved the sale, which is subject to permissive referendum by statute. Passed by voice vote.
cases.publicComment: Engineer Peter Catazone and the Baranovics spoke in support; no opposition.

cases.name: 535 Main Street Vacant Land — Appraisal Received and Withdrawn from Sale
cases.summary: The board received an RDM Valuations real estate appraisal dated February 4, 2025 for the vacant town-owned land at 535 Main Street, then, on Barbara DiGiacinto's motion, voted to take the parcel off the market and not offer it as surplus for sale at this time. Members agreed unanimously. Passed by voice vote.

memberPositions.evidence: Moved to take 535 Main Street off the market and not declare it surplus 'at this time'; other members concurred.

cases.name: Authorization to Seek Proposals for 2025 Pool Concession Services
cases.summary: The board approved Superintendent Matt Traynor's request to seek proposals for 2025 pool concession services. The Supervisor asked to review the RFP scope with the Town Administrator, noting past difficulty securing quality vendors (a prior year the concessionaire backed out) and resident feedback about quality. Passed by voice vote.

cases.name: Road-Use Request — Columbia University Irving Cancer Center 'Velocity Ride to End Cancer'
cases.summary: The board approved a request for use of roads for the Velocity Ride to End Cancer on Sunday, October 5, 2025, confirming the Police Department had reviewed and given its blessing. Passed by voice vote.

cases.name: Troy's Nursery Gardens Design LLC Special Event Permit and Public Hearing Scheduling
cases.summary: The board received a special event permit application from Troy's Nursery Gardens Design, LLC for an Easter event on April 13, 2025 and fall festivals on October 5 and 12 at 97 Bedford Banksville Road, and scheduled the associated public hearing for March 26, 2025. Passed by voice vote.

cases.name: Resolution Authorizing Appeal in Connecticut Superior Court re Greenwich American Center Development
cases.address: Greenwich American Center property (Connecticut, adjacent to North Castle)
cases.summary: As an add-on resolution, the board authorized attorney John P. Tessie of Gilbride Tessie to file an appeal in Connecticut Superior Court challenging approvals granted by the planning and zoning commission for the proposed development at the Greenwich American Center property, with no legal fees as agreed by Tessie. Passed by voice vote.

cases.name: Provisional Appointments — Parks Groundsmen (Guillmet, Ross, Crawley)
cases.summary: The board made three provisional appointments to Parks Groundsman in the Parks and Recreation Department, all effective March 17, 2025: David Guillmet, Brian Ross, and Leroy Crawley Jr. Each passed by voice vote.

cases.name: North Castle Public Library Hourly Staff Salary Increases
cases.summary: The board approved hourly staff salary increases for library employees Diana Cunningham (hourly librarian), Karen Prophet (hourly librarian), Susan Medico (hourly clerk), and Nicholas Shallcross (hourly clerk), effective January 10, 2025. Passed by voice vote.

cases.name: Conference Travel Approvals — Deputy Town Clerk and Town Administrators
cases.summary: The board approved Deputy Town Clerk Maria Scharf to attend the 2025 New York State Town Clerks Association conference in Syracuse (April 27-29, 2025), and approved the Town Administrator and Assistant Town Administrator to attend the New York State Conference of Administrators in Cooperstown (April 30-May 2, 2025). Passed by voice vote.

cases.name: Appointment of Alex Henderson to the Board of Assessment Review
cases.summary: The board appointed Alex Henderson to the Board of Assessment Review for a five-year term ending September 30, 2030, and also approved the consensus agenda. Passed by voice vote.

cases.name: Board Liaison Updates, Announcements, and Approval of Minutes
cases.summary: The board approved prior town board minutes and heard announcements and liaison updates. The Supervisor announced Police Chief Simonson (35 years of service) and the business Beescake as this year's Chamber of Commerce honorees. Liaison reports covered the Sustainability Committee's food-scrap composting kits, a proposed town-wide cleanup day (April 26), a resident-led volunteer effort to clear invasive vines (with liability releases required), the Library Board's four new subcommittees and completed hallway renovation, new self-watering planters, highway-crew cleanup work along Wampus Brook and Hart's Gravel Circle, the upcoming north bridge repair, and the Supervisor's outreach to the District Attorney on rising criminal activity. The meeting closed with a tribute to longtime resident Ray Pooter (died at 101) and a nod to Women's History Month.

memberPositions.evidence: Reported enthusiastically on the Sustainability Committee's composting kits, town-wide cleanup day, and the volunteer invasive-vine clearing effort, thanking participating residents and urging more volunteers.
Shared the Library Board's newly formed subcommittees (bylaws/policies, buildings/grounds, marketing/technology, strategic planning) and praised the maintenance team's hallway renovation.

Debate over the town's fund balance, debt capacity, and cost uncertainty of Town Hall options.
Concern about potential development/units on the current town parcel and historic-district preservation.

Water Districts 8 and 9 established; PFOA/PFAS remediation and future capacity discussed.
Turf-field contract (tabled), pool concession RFP, and groundsmen appointments.
