All five members present; no absences noted.

meetings.meetingSummary: The North Castle Town Board opened with an extended work session with the Conservation Board on strengthening the town's tree-removal code (clarifying clearing vs. thinning, permit triggers, fines, and homeowner/contractor responsibility), ultimately authorizing the town planner to keep refining the draft rather than adopting anything. Two public hearings followed: an amendment to a 1992 equestrian special use permit at the Casson property (40 Cowdery Park Drive / 50 Round Hill Road), which drew contentious neighbor objections over alleged commercial use and was adjourned to a date uncertain; and a landmark designation for the Armonk 'Eagle,' which the board adopted for the sculpture alone (declining the streetscape land on legal advice). The board also approved the annual Armonk Art Show 'Armonk has a Heart' installation, cancelled the July 9 meeting, declined to adopt a nonprofit fee-waiver policy, scheduled a June 11 parking-law hearing, and approved a slate of contracts, water/fire-district agreements, payments, and personnel appointments.
meetings.durationNote: Full board present — Supervisor Rende plus Council Members DiGiacinto, Hussain, Milim, and Berra; no absences noted. Meeting opened 5:30 PM, adjourned to executive session (contracts / real-estate counsel), then reconvened for the public session.

cases.name: Tree Code Amendment — Conservation Board Work Session
cases.applicant: Conservation Board (John Krupa, Adam Barnett, co-chairs)
cases.summary: The Conservation Board presented proposed amendments to the town's tree code: clarifying the definitions of 'clearing' versus 'thinning,' tightening permit triggers (down to three trees or 25% of a parcel), simplifying regulated-setback language, making compliance explicitly the homeowner's responsibility, and raising the maximum fine from $1,000 to $2,000 (double for significant/wetland trees). Debate centered on whether higher fines would deter violations (Building Inspector Melillo argued judges rarely impose meaningful tree fines and the town sees few complaints), whether contractors could be held liable, and how to better detect unpermitted cutting. The board reached no decision but authorized Town Planner Adam Kaufman to keep refining the local-law language, with strong consensus that a public education campaign (mailers, video, outreach to realtors and contractors) is the most important component. Roland (Town Attorney) noted the fine must be worded 'up to' to preserve judicial discretion, so the flat-$2,000 draft was not viable as written.
cases.publicComment: Conservation Board members (John Krupa, Adam Barnett, Vince Jodan, George Strappel) and residents spoke supportively about preserving the town's tree canopy; residents recounted large 'significant' trees being clear-cut on weekends without permits and urged weekend police checks and easier reporting.

memberPositions.evidence: Committed 'in front of God and country' to keep the tree code on the front burner and pushed hardest for an educational piece (YouTube video, seasonal mailers) over exorbitant fines.

Argued a $1,000 fine doesn't deter when removing a big tree costs several thousand, and pressed repeatedly to make contractors liable — 'which is why I feel so strongly about going to the contractors.'
Contended the real problem is too few violations being observed, not fines being too low; proposed granular canopy/tree audits (~$6-8k) to detect changes over time rather than simply raising fines.
Drove the clearing-vs-thinning distinction, worried about a neighbor clear-cutting a parcel and its effect on adjacent property values and street character.
Struggled with the $2,000 fine falling on well-meaning first-time homeowners and championed an eye-catching educational mailer like the annual trash-collection calendar.

cases.name: Speeding and Stop-Sign Concerns on Nethermont Avenue, North White Plains
cases.summary: During public comment a North White Plains resident raised dangerous speeding and stop-sign running on Nethermont Avenue, asking for speed bumps or cameras. Supervisor Rende reported the police chief will reinstall a speed sign and is recommending reducing the town-road speed limit in North White Plains from 30 to 25 mph, and agreed to ask for extra patrols. The board asked the chief and traffic sergeant to evaluate options; members noted speed humps/tables versus bumps and rumble strips, and that state law and bus routes limit where bumps are allowed.
cases.publicComment: Resident Sue Pola spoke with frustration and alarm about near-misses while walking her dog and children biking around a blind corner; a second resident cautioned that speed bumps/humps were previously researched on Wampus Avenue and are prohibited in some bus-route locations.

memberPositions.evidence: Relayed the chief's plan to lower the limit to 25 mph and committed to ask Administrator Foley and the chief for extra patrols and traffic-calming options.
Asked that the police look into speed humps, speed tables and rumble strips, distinguishing them from prohibited speed bumps.
Noted prior research with Chief Simonson found speed humps/bumps prohibited in some places, especially bus routes, and cited state law.

cases.name: Casson Equestrian Special Use Permit Amendment (1992 SUP)
cases.address: 40 Cowdery Park Drive and 50 Round Hill Road (Conyers Farm)
cases.applicant: Marianne Casson (James G. Dabini & Associates, attorneys)
cases.summary: The applicant sought to amend a 1992 private-stable special use permit (up to 41 horses) to formally recognize continued equestrian use alongside the principal dwelling built in 2006 — a conversion that was never made when the house was constructed, voiding the 1992 SUP under its condition 22. The building inspector's May 13 letter flagged multiple property deficiencies and the planning board had not yet issued its recommendation, so the board could only condition any SUP on compliance. Neighbors (Lauren Pincus, Fred Cohen) and members raised sharp concerns that the property is being used commercially (renting stalls, up to 30 horses under lease, riders on the roads, manure/setback issues), which the town code and 1992 permit appear to prohibit; counsel disputed the meaning of the 'no commercial leasing' clause. Because recognizing the residence-plus-equestrian use would require a use variance from the Zoning Board, the board adjourned the public hearing to a date uncertain to let the applicant address planning-board items, pursue the variance, and cure the building deficiencies (roughly two months).
cases.publicComment: Contentious. Conyers Farm neighbors (Lauren Pincus of 5 Cowdery Park Drive, Fred C. Cohen of 57 Round Hill Road) alleged ongoing commercial equestrian use, unaddressed HOA complaints, manure/setback violations, an apparently vacant caretaker cottage at 50 Round Hill with workers congregating, and questioned granting a permit given the property's history; tone was skeptical and opposed.

memberPositions.evidence: Said leasing stalls for ~30 outside horses 'sounds like pretty black and white commercial to me' and that the town should not, as policy, allow commercial equestrian use on a residential lot.
Pressed how the board can get comfortable that violations won't recur and what to do when an applicant has a history of not following the rules — answer: 'you take it into account.'
Pointed to advertised Conyers Farm polo matches and questioned the private-vs-commercial distinction, seeking to interject during the hearing.
Doubted the 1992 resolution permitted any commercial use, insisted on town-initiated periodic inspections as a condition, and steered the matter to fact-finding and adjournment to a date uncertain.

cases.name: Landmark Designation of the North Castle Eagle
cases.address: Corner of Route 128 and Route 22, Armonk
cases.summary: The Landmark Preservation Committee asked the board to landmark the restored Armonk 'Eagle,' requesting the surrounding streetscape (fence-to-Eagle) as it had done conceptually for the gazebo. On the advice of counsel, citing unresolved legal issues over the underlying land, the board chose to landmark the Eagle sculpture itself — as it had with the gazebo and barber pole — without the land. The public hearing was held and closed, and the board unanimously adopted the designation of the Eagle alone, leaving possible streetscape/land questions for future investigation.
cases.publicComment: LPC co-chair Linda Fernberg presented drawings and photos and advocated (respectfully, while accepting the board's decision) for landmarking the fuller streetscape to preserve the view, as with the gazebo.

memberPositions.evidence: 'The eagle is us... it ain't going anywhere,' fully comfortable landmarking the Eagle itself but deferred to counsel's legal concerns in declining to include the land now.
Recounted her work getting the barber pole set in galvanized poles and concrete and supported the landmark, engaging on the streetscape-protection rationale.
Serves as the board's liaison to the Landmark Preservation Committee and was thanked for that role on the item.

cases.name: Approval of Town Board Minutes — April 23, 2025
cases.summary: The board approved the minutes of its April 23, 2025 meeting by unanimous voice vote as a routine old-business item.

cases.name: Armonk has a Heart — Art Show Signs & Sculptures (Sept/Oct)
cases.applicant: Friends of the North Castle Public Library / Armonk Outdoor Art Show (Nancy Rosner)
cases.summary: The board approved a request from the Friends of the Library and the Armonk Outdoor Art Show to place 12 decorated fiberglass heart sculptures and temporary signage around town for September (and possibly October) leading up to the Sept. 27-28 art show. Sculptures will be sponsored by local businesses, painted by local artists, and auctioned to benefit the North Castle Public Library. Members were enthusiastic, noting the effort drives visitors into downtown businesses; the board approved the temporary installation unanimously.
cases.publicComment: Managing director Nancy Rosner presented the concept enthusiastically; positive, celebratory tone with thanks to Chamber, town staff (Allison Simon, Anthony Ruvo) and idea originator Robbie Morris.

memberPositions.evidence: Praised the initiative for drawing art-show visitors into downtown and possibly to move to Armonk; 'I love the enthusiasm.'
Called it 'such an awesome idea' and asked how businesses could sponsor a heart and when they would go up.

cases.name: Cancellation of the July 9, 2025 Town Board Meeting
cases.summary: The board voted unanimously to cancel the July 9, 2025 meeting, moving to a single July meeting mirroring its longstanding single-August-meeting practice, on the recommendation of the Town Clerk's office.

cases.name: Policy — Waiver of Application Fees for Not-for-Profit Organizations
cases.summary: Staff drafted a broad policy allowing not-for-profit organizations to seek waivers of town application fees, prompted by a recent request. The board declined to adopt it, voting on a motion to not approve. Members felt the town has never needed such a policy (only occasional tent/alcohol-permit waivers), that a $300 planning-board fee is not a genuine hardship for an organization building an addition, and that a broad policy would invite a flood of waiver requests; some were open only to a much narrower policy limited to demonstrated financial hardship. A related tabled fee-waiver request was left tabled rather than acted on.

memberPositions.evidence: 'I'm really not in favor of this,' citing that nonprofits like the seminary and Whippoorwill Club have paid planning/ZBA fees and the town needs the revenue.
'I don't see a need for it... it's kind of late in the game to start a policy like this,' noting it only arose once in his time on the board.
Called it 'far fetched' that an organization funding a building addition couldn't afford a $300 fee.
Opposed the broad draft but said he'd be open to a much narrower policy limited to nonprofits demonstrating serious financial hardship.
'I thought this was a good case for doing it... but I understand wanting a policy'; acknowledged the difficulty of defining appropriate situations and agreed not to adopt.

cases.name: Local Law — No Parking on Old Mount Kisco Road (Ch. 325); Public Hearing Scheduled
cases.summary: The board received a memo from Police Chief Simonson recommending an amendment to Chapter 325 (Vehicles and Traffic), Section 325-55, Schedule 13, to establish no-parking-anytime restrictions on portions of Old Mount Kisco Road, and scheduled a public hearing on the local law for June 11, 2025.

cases.name: IBM Community Park Artificial Turf Field — DEC Letter & Soil Fill Characterization
cases.summary: The board received a May 2, 2025 letter from the NYS DEC and a May 12, 2025 preliminary soil fill materials characterization from Hydro Environmental Solutions for the IBM Community Park artificial turf field improvements. The Supervisor noted the excavated material was confirmed clean and stable and can be reused at other town sites (Clove Field, Quarry Heights park), saving carting and fill costs by using town staff and equipment.

memberPositions.evidence: Highlighted reusing the confirmed-clean fill at Clove Field and Quarry Heights to lower project cost by avoiding carting and purchased fill.
Asked whether the fill could also be sold to others and carted away, exploring cost recovery.

cases.name: New Street Address Assignment — 100 Business Park Drive Condominium Units
cases.summary: The board received a KSCJ Consulting memo on assigning new street addresses to base-space commercial condominium units, changing 100 Business Park Drive to 100, 112, 114 and 116 Business Park Drive, and referred the matter to the town E-911 coordinator by unanimous voice vote.

cases.name: Kent Place Parking Lot (Former Verizon Property) — Payment Req. #3 & Change Orders
cases.address: Kent Place parking lot (former Verizon property), Armonk
cases.summary: The board approved Payment Requisition No. 3 to Tony Casale Incorporated for the Kent Place parking lot / former Verizon property improvements (on the revised requisition with sales tax removed), and separately approved change orders 1-3 and 6-9 per a KSCJ Consulting letter, authorizing the Supervisor to sign. Members noted the finished library-area work looks excellent, and discussed advancing a parking-district concept and interim pothole patching for the adjacent business-owned lot.

memberPositions.evidence: Pushed to expedite the parking-district meeting/invites now that the work is complete and explained repaving the adjacent lot needs the private property owners' involvement.

cases.name: Water District / Board of Fire Commissioners Agreements (Districts 1, 2, 4, 5, 8, 9)
cases.applicant: Town Water Districts / North Castle & Armonk Fire Districts
cases.summary: The board approved, by unanimous voice votes, a series of agreements between town Water Districts (Nos. 1, 2, 4, 5, 8 and 9) and the respective Boards of Fire Commissioners (North Castle Fire District No. 1 and Armonk Fire District No. 2), authorizing the Supervisor to sign each. It also approved a license agreement for parking on a portion of roadway at 111 Lafayette Avenue, North White Plains.

cases.name: Award of Bid — Water District No. 4 New Well Site Work
cases.summary: The board awarded the bid to Papatito Construction Co. Incorporated for the Water District No. 4 new well site work and authorized the Supervisor to sign the agreement, by unanimous voice vote (water/sewer superintendent 'Sal' present and satisfied).

cases.name: North Castle Pool and Tennis Club — Engineering Services Proposals
cases.address: North Castle Pool and Tennis Club, Armonk
cases.applicant: KSCJ Consulting and Engineering Services; Grossfeld Macri Consulting Engineers PC
cases.summary: The board approved two professional-services proposals for the North Castle Pool and Tennis Club — one with KSCJ Consulting and Engineering Services and one with Grossfeld Macri Consulting Engineers PC for structural engineering services — and authorized the Supervisor to sign the agreements.

cases.name: Renewal Agreement — J. O'Connell Associates Grant Writing Services
cases.summary: The board approved a renewal agreement with J. O'Connell & Associates for grant-writing services and authorized the Supervisor to sign. Administrator Kevin Foley reported the firm secured an approximately $450,000 Assault Dome grant, is aggressive, and is worth continuing despite some unsuccessful applications; members asked for follow-up on why some grants weren't awarded.

memberPositions.evidence: Asked whether the firm had been useful and affirmed the value of continuing given the grant secured.

cases.name: Personnel — Appointment of Alfonso D'Abruzio and Reappointment of Adam Barnett
cases.summary: The board unanimously appointed Alfonso D'Abruzio as a seasonal road maintainer in the Highway Department, effective May 19, 2025, and reappointed Adam Barnett to the Conservation Board for a two-year term expiring May 14, 2027, thanking him for his service. The consensus agenda was also approved.

memberPositions.evidence: Made the motion to reappoint Adam Barnett and thanked him for his service to the Conservation Board.

themes.note: Tree-code overhaul work session and contentious Casson equestrian SUP dominated the meeting.
Tree preservation code, clean turf-field fill reuse, and town-wide cleanup day (62 bags).
Eagle landmark designation and 'Armonk has a Heart' art installation drew strong enthusiasm.
Numerous approvals: Casale payment/change orders, Papatito well bid, pool/tennis and grant-writing agreements.
Water District No. 4 well bid and a slate of water-district/fire-commissioner agreements.
Nethermont Ave speeding, Old Mount Kisco Rd no-parking hearing, fire-district agreements, chief's award.
Meeting cancellation, minutes, and the rejected nonprofit fee-waiver policy.
Central to the tree-code fine/permit debate and the equestrian SUP compliance issues.
Turf field, Kent Place parking lot, pool/tennis club, and well site work.
Seasonal highway hire and Conservation Board reappointment.

staffInput.summary: Advised that tree-code fines must be worded 'up to' to preserve judicial discretion (making the flat-$2,000 draft unviable), and to look into whether contractors can lawfully be fined; on the Casson SUP, explained the residence-plus-equestrian use requires a use variance from the Zoning Board, guided the planning-board referral sequence, parsed the disputed 'no commercial leasing' clause, and recommended town-initiated periodic inspections as a condition; cited legal concerns over the land underlying the Eagle as the basis to landmark only the sculpture.

Building Inspector: reported the town sees few tree-cutting complaints and that judges rarely impose meaningful tree fines, questioned the practicality of chasing contractors and increased fines given his department's workload, and issued the May 13 letter listing deficiencies at the Casson property; recalled the 1992 permit's likely prohibition on commercial use.

Town Planner: translated the Conservation Board's proposed tree-code changes into local-law form and was authorized to keep refining them; explained the planning board's review role and the outstanding items the Casson applicant must address before a recommendation.

Reported on reusing clean turf-field fill at town sites to cut costs, the value of the O'Connell grant-writing contract (~$450k Assault Dome grant), and advancing the parking-district and pothole-patching for the Kent Place area; to coordinate library quarterly reports and speak with the police chief on speeding.

Read the public-hearing documents for the Casson SUP (notices, affidavits, county planning recommendation, staff reports), delivered community announcements (EMS Week/Staying Alive event, 914 Cares fundraiser), coordinated the art-show heart installation, and recommended consolidating July to a single meeting.

meetings.attributionNote: This is an unlabeled ASR transcript with no roll-call votes; all board votes were unanimous voice votes ('all in favor / aye'), so no split or 'no' votes were named. Individual council members were identified by role and by first-name address in discussion — Supervisor Joseph Rende (presiding voice, sometimes 'Jose'/'Supervisor'), Councilman Jose Berra ('Jose', disambiguated from Rende by role), Councilwoman Barbara DiGiacinto ('Barbara'), Councilman Saleem Hussain ('Saleem', notably on tree-detection and fee-waiver narrowing), and Councilman Matt Milim ('Matt', on contractor fines and the equestrian commercial-use objection). Full board present, no absences. Attribution is most confident on the tree-code work session, the fee-waiver policy, and the Casson SUP where members spoke at length; lower on routine consent items where speakers making motions were not distinguishable. Staff names were garbled in places (e.g., Dabini/Dabari counsel, 'Rendezvous' for Rende).

meetings.meetingSummary: The Town Board reopened after executive session and handled a light agenda of routine approvals, water district financing, and one contested land-use extension. Major items included creating a new capital project fund with a fund-balance transfer for the EDR contract, an internal general-fund loan to Water District 4 for a new well building, and a well-rehabilitation bid award. The most substantive debate concerned extending special use permits for the Park Place parking structure and, more contentiously, the NCD Acquisitions/Mariani Gardens Gateway redevelopment, where the board granted only a short extension to July 23, 2025 pending property cleanup and tax payment. The meeting also covered summer camp agreements, a liquor license notice, a police training request, and community announcements about Folderol.
meetings.durationNote: Full board present (Rende, DiGiacinto, Hussain, Milim, Berra); roll-call vote on the Gateway extension recorded all five members.

cases.name: Approval of Town Board Minutes — May 14, 2025
cases.summary: The board approved the minutes of its May 14, 2025 meeting. A motion was made and seconded and passed on a voice vote with no discussion. Routine procedural matter under old business.

cases.name: New Capital Project Fund and Seward District Fund-Balance Transfer for EDR Contract
cases.summary: On a memo from the Finance Director, the board voted to create a new capital project fund and to approve use of Seward District's fund balance of $161,300 to fund the amendment to EDR's contract (previously approved). After some procedural confusion over whether to receive and approve separately, the board consolidated it into a single amended motion that passed on a voice vote. Supervisor Rende urged developing an actual three- to five-year capital improvement plan to prioritize future spending.

memberPositions.evidence: Called it a move in the right direction and pushed for a formal three- to five-year capital improvement plan to designate priorities.
Responded 'Absolutely' endorsing the capital improvement planning endeavor.

cases.name: General Fund Loan to Water District 4 for New Well Building and Site Work
cases.summary: The board received a memo and approved an internal loan from the town's general fund to Water District 4 to finance a prefab turnkey well building and site work, repaid with interest at the town's earning rate rather than issuing an outside bond, saving an estimated $55,000. The plan is to eventually roll this short-term loan into a larger long-term bond tied to the Airport Campus/Water District 8 interconnection to Westchester Joint Water Works. Motions to receive and approve both passed; the approval motion included a caveat that the loan remains callable if the town needs the funds, though counsel confirmed the town retains that right regardless. Members debated liquidity risk given the project could take 1.5 to 5+ years due to Health Department delays.

memberPositions.evidence: Supported the savings but pressed counsel on liquidity risk — whether the town could 'call' the loan and force the district to bond if funds are locked up for years; satisfied once counsel confirmed it could.
Framed it as a wise, cost-saving bridge loan benefiting all town residents through the pass-through interest rate; optimistic the project would proceed.
Raised concern that the district would normally lock in a fixed rate whereas this floats, but concluded it was not a huge risk and liked the idea; asked where the building would be sited.

cases.name: Bid Award — Water District 4 Well Rehabilitation Project (Weston & Sampson)
cases.applicant: Weston & Sampson CMR Inc. (DBA SB Church)
cases.summary: The board awarded a bid to Weston & Sampson for rehabilitation of an overburden (gravel-pack) well in Water District 4 and authorized the Supervisor to sign the agreement, at a cost of roughly $67,787. The superintendent explained the roughly 10-year maintenance cycle needed to restore the well's declining yield (down from 350 to 230 gallons per minute). Motion made and seconded, passed on a voice vote.

cases.name: Fourth Two-Year Extension of Special Use Permit — Park Place Long-Term Parking Structure
cases.applicant: Park Place, 11 New King Street, LLC (Neil Alexander, Cuddy & Feder)
cases.summary: The board received a letter and adopted a resolution granting a fourth two-year extension (to July 2027) of the special use permit for a mechanized long-term parking structure. The applicant explained the delay was due to water-service issues with Westchester County that are now largely resolved, with the county bringing public water along New King Street. Counsel noted public water (not a well) is required partly because nearby wells were contaminated and for fire prevention. Motion passed on a voice vote.

memberPositions.evidence: Asked why public water was needed rather than a well; explained for the public that nearby contaminated wells and fire service made public water necessary.
Clarified the prior water and legal issues with the county and confirmed the project is moving forward, not stalled.

cases.name: Special Use Permit Extension — Gateway Residential Redevelopment (former Mariani Gardens)
cases.applicant: NCD Acquisitions (Jeffrey Buss, Smith Buss & Jacobs LLP)
cases.summary: The applicant requested a second one-year extension of the special use permit for the Gateway multi-family redevelopment at the former Mariani Gardens site. Instead of a full year, the board granted only a short extension to July 23, 2025, conditioned on the applicant paying delinquent taxes (a $49,016.82 payment including penalties was made the day of the meeting) and bringing the eyesore vacant property into compliance with the town's property-maintenance code (Chapter 241) — including removing stored rock/equipment, filling the excavation, and mowing. Supervisor Rende disclosed campaign donations from LLC members but affirmed impartiality. The motion, framed by special counsel Spolzino and moved by DiGiacinto, passed 4-1 on a roll-call vote with Councilman Berra opposed.
cases.publicComment: Residents had raised concerns on social media about the property's poor maintenance, which several board members cited as motivating the shortened, conditioned extension.

memberPositions.evidence: Flagged the unpaid school/town taxes and cited Chapter 241 property-maintenance code; proposed extending only to July 23, 2025 and requiring cleanup; disclosed campaign donations but affirmed fairness.
Criticized the piled rock, big excavation pit and unmowed lawn, calling the gateway property's condition unacceptable; moved the shortened conditioned extension.

Backed the short extension and suggested that if not maintained the building inspector could issue a violation and the town could hire a contractor and lien the cost onto the tax bill; seconded the motion.

Spoke strongly that the property 'looks terrible' and is inappropriate for the town, said he personally would not vote to extend, and cited a meaningful change in circumstances; voted 'No' on the roll call.
Concurred with the majority position and voted aye on the shortened conditioned extension.

cases.name: Liquor License Notice and Waiver of 30-Day Notice — Cuckoo Armonk Inc.
cases.summary: The board received notice of a new liquor license application for Cuckoo Armonk Inc. and waived the 30-day notice requirement. Counsel confirmed no further action was required beyond the notification. Motion passed on a voice vote.

cases.name: Subdivision Construction Performance Bond and Inspection Fees — Rolling Hill Subdivision
cases.applicant: 111 Round Hill Road Realty, LLC (per KSCJ Consulting recommendation)
cases.summary: On a recommendation from KSCJ Consulting, the board approved establishing a subdivision construction performance bond for a common driveway and subdivision inspection fees for the Rolling Hill Subdivision. Motion made and seconded, passed on a voice vote with no discussion.

cases.name: Summer Camp Bus Lease Agreement — Byram Hills Central School District
cases.summary: The board authorized the Supervisor to sign a summer camp bus lease agreement with the school district effective June 30 through August 8, 2025. Motion made and seconded, passed on a voice vote.

cases.name: Summer Camp Facilities Agreement — Chittenden Middle School and Wampus Elementary
cases.summary: The board authorized the Supervisor to sign an agreement with the Byram Hills Central School District for use of H.C. Chittenden Middle School and Wampus Elementary School for the town summer camp from late June through the first week of August 2025. Supervisor Rende and DiGiacinto thanked the district as great partners, noting the camp would be impossible without the buildings. Motion passed on a voice vote.

memberPositions.evidence: Thanked the Byram Hills School District as great partners, noting summer camp would be impossible without the use of the school buildings.

cases.name: Police Training Approval — Detective Steven Vitolo, Homicide Seminar
cases.summary: As a late addition brought in that morning by the chief, the board approved Detective Steven Vitolo attending the Colonel Henry F. Williams Homicide Seminar in Albany, September 21-26, 2025. Members noted the town has sent detectives to this training before. Milim briefly questioned not having seen the email but voted in favor. Motion passed on a voice vote.

memberPositions.evidence: Asked when the late-addition item came in (noting he hadn't seen the email) but voiced no objection and said he would vote in favor, praising the chief as conscientious.

cases.name: Consensus Agenda
cases.summary: The board adopted the consensus agenda on a single combined motion, made and seconded, passing on a voice vote with no separate discussion.

cases.name: Town Board Liaison Updates and Closing in Memory
cases.summary: Board members gave liaison updates: DiGiacinto praised the Beautification Committee's new Hergenhan Center sign and Main Street plantings; Berra promoted the Sustainability Committee's food-scrap composting table at Folderol; Hussain urged residents not to leave keys in cars amid a rise in vehicle thefts. Supervisor Rende reported the approved home-rule occupancy (hotel) tax extender, upcoming budget/appropriations updates from Senator Mayer and Assemblyman Burdick, DOT funding progress, near-completion of the Main Street parking lot, library pressure-washing, and the dog park start after Folderol, plus the pool's Memorial Day opening. The meeting closed in memory of North White Plains resident John Ryan.

memberPositions.evidence: Praised the Beautification Committee's new Hergenhan Center sign, hanging baskets and plantings; also lauded the town clerk's condolence letters when closing in memory.
Promoted the Sustainability Committee's food-scrap composting table and kits at Folderol and thanked Milim for organizing the event.
Urged residents to remove keys from cars, citing a wave of vehicle thefts making the town an easy target.

Reported the approved home-rule hotel occupancy tax, optimism on DOT/state funding via Senator Mayer and Assemblyman Burdick, and progress on the Main Street parking lot, library cleanup and dog park.

cases.name: Community Announcements — Folderol and Revolutionary War 250 Committee
cases.summary: Councilman Milim announced the Lions Club Folderol festival (June 5-8), detailing hours, the crafts fair, opening ceremony on Hunter Field, a duck-adoption charity fundraiser and a call for volunteers. During public comment, Ed Witt updated the board on the North Castle Revolutionary War 250 steering committee: a June 19 time-capsule disinterment at the Cornell Birdsall House, town banners, a Folderol merchandise booth, and a proposed donation fund to restore Sands Mills as a historic public park. The board expressed enthusiasm and suggested involving staff (Kevin Foley, Doug) on the Sands Mills tree/vine cleanup.
cases.publicComment: Resident Ed Witt spoke at length and enthusiastically about the Revolutionary War 250 committee's events, banners and Sands Mills restoration; the board thanked him warmly for his volunteer efforts.

memberPositions.evidence: Enthusiastically promoted the Lions Club Folderol festival, its charity fundraising and volunteer needs, and coordinated details with residents.
Thanked Ed Witt and the 250 committee for their enthusiasm and support, and suggested getting staff out to assess the Sands Mills cleanup sooner.

themes.note: Two special-use-permit extensions dominated; the Gateway/Mariani item was sharply contested over property maintenance.
Water District 4 financing, well building and rehabilitation, plus the Airport Campus/District 8 interconnection framed much of the meeting.
Board frustration over the neglected 45 Bedford Road gateway property and a rise in vehicle thefts.
New capital project fund, internal loan financing, delinquent-tax enforcement, and a call for a multi-year capital plan.
Folderol festival and the Revolutionary War 250 committee's events drew warm, enthusiastic support.
Summer camp agreements, pool opening, and dog park progress.
Well rehab bid award and subdivision performance bond.
Detective training approval and a vehicle-theft prevention appeal.

staffInput.summary: Water & Sewer Superintendent explained the internal general-fund loan financing structure and savings, the prefab turnkey well building components required by the Health Department, the Airport Campus/Water District 8 interconnection to Westchester Joint Water Works, and the overburden-well rehabilitation process and its ~10-year maintenance cycle.

Special counsel confirmed the town may call the Water District 4 loan at any time, advised deferring a sensitive question about revoking the Gateway special use permit to executive session, and framed the legal standard and motion for the shortened, condition-based Gateway extension tied to property-maintenance code enforcement.
Sitting Town Attorney handled correspondence on the Gateway applicant's delinquent taxes, relaying that payment would be made before the meeting.
Town Clerk reported no community announcements, took roll-call votes and motions, and was noted for sending personalized condolence letters to families when the board closes meetings in memory.

Town Administrator was referenced as involved in coordinating the Water District financing discussions with Sal, the parking lot/library improvements, and dispatching staff (Kevin Foley) for the Sands Mills cleanup.
Town Planner clarified that the crushed rock on the Mariani/Gateway site was intended to be reused on-site to raise the grade for the site plan.

meetings.attributionNote: The presiding supervisor voice was clearly Joseph Rende. The Gateway item's roll call explicitly named all five members (Digacento=DiGiacinto aye, Milam=Milim aye, Hussein=Hussain aye, Vera=Berra no, Rende yes), enabling confident attribution including the 4-1 split. ASR manglings normalized: Digacento/Digacinto to DiGiacinto, Milam/Millam to Milim, Hussein to Hussain, Vera/Behr to Berra. Full board present; no absences noted. Berra attributed as a member (2025 meeting); Vitaj not present per roster. Voice votes on routine items lacked named attribution, so those cases carry few or no member positions.

meetings.meetingSummary: The Town Board held a public hearing and adopted a local law adding no-parking restrictions on Old Mount Kisco Road after a police traffic-safety presentation and extensive resident testimony. It received the 2024 Annual Comprehensive Financial Report (clean/unmodified audit) from the Bonadio Group, approved several agreements (WSP water-well engineering, a Byram Hills SRO agreement, Long Pond dam inspection), a wetland-bond release, a Kent Place parking-lot payment, open-space dedication of a town parcel, and personnel appointments. The most contentious item was the proposed revised workplace-violence and sexual-harassment policies, which the board voted 4-1 to table for executive-session review with Labor Council over the Supervisor's objection.
meetings.durationNote: Meeting opened 5:30 PM into executive session (personnel, boards/committees, real estate advice of counsel), then reconvened in public. Full board of five present (Rende, DiGiacinto, Hussain, Milim, Berra); no absences noted.

cases.name: Local Law amending Chapter 325 (Vehicles & Traffic), Section 325-55, Schedule 13 — No Parking Anytime on Old Mount Kisco Road
cases.address: Old Mount Kisco Road, Armonk (near Main Street / Wago Avenue)
cases.applicant: North Castle Police Department (Lt. Tom McCormick)
cases.summary: Amends the town code to prohibit parking on portions of Old Mount Kisco Road (east side from Main Street north to Crossroad; west side from Main Street to Wago Avenue) in response to years of resident complaints about hazardous parking by commercial employees on a narrow, curving residential road with heavy pedestrian use. Lt. McCormick presented photos and a safety analysis, noting NYSDOT had also agreed to add a stop sign at the Main Street intersection. A public hearing was opened, several residents spoke, and it was closed; the board adopted the local law (motion by Jose Berra, seconded by Barbara DiGiacinto), to be filed with the Secretary of State. Board members flagged a possible 'whack-a-mole' displacement of parked cars to be revisited if it arises.
cases.publicComment: Several residents spoke in strong support of the restrictions (Mel Orolana, Ken Kicaro, Jack DiPietro, Michael Akavan), citing pedestrian safety, a prior hit-and-run injury, and complaints about the deteriorated/unmaintained rear of the adjacent Garson/commercial shopping center. One business owner, Austin 'Awesome' Riza (567 Main St), objected, saying a no-parking rule would be an extreme hardship after 30+ years of parking off the blacktop and suggesting gravel instead.

memberPositions.evidence: Said he'd received calls since his first week in office and that photos of a school bus and sanitation truck squeezing past parked cars showed a very severe, dangerous condition; directed staff to also address commercial property-maintenance and site-plan conditions.
Called it 'obviously a safety issue' and 'a quality of life' matter, saw no reason not to post the no-parking signs, and seconded the motion to adopt the local law.
Raised the 'whack-a-mole' displacement concern (cars moving to Wago Ave) but backed the measure as the real safety fix and made the motion to adopt the local law.

Walked the road with Lt. McCormick, supported the restriction but worried it may just push parking into residential streets ('whack-a-mole'); disclosed that Awesome Landscaping maintains his home. Suggested revisiting the town-owned parcel/parking idea.
Called it 'a good step forward,' said other problems can be addressed as they arise, and stated 'I totally support it.'

cases.name: Receipt of 2024 Annual Comprehensive Financial Report (ACFR) — Bonadio Group
cases.applicant: Bonadio Group (Michael Connolly, manager); Comptroller Abbas
cases.summary: Auditor Michael Connolly presented the ACFR and required communication letter for the year ended December 31, 2024, giving an unmodified (clean) opinion consistent with prior years. He explained the government-wide net-position deficit is driven by a $77M OPEB liability and that fund-level balance is a positive $33.6M, and noted implementation of GASB 101 (compensated absences). No difficulties or disagreements with management were reported. The board voted to accept the audit and thanked Comptroller Abbas and his team; staff noted continued GFOA recognition.

memberPositions.evidence: Thanked the auditor, asked whether the financials were clean and if there was anything the public should be aware of; satisfied with the responses.
Praised the detailed report and credited Comptroller Abbas with keeping the town on a good financial path.

cases.name: Agenda Item B — Tabled pending report of law-enforcement activity
cases.summary: The Supervisor asked to table an unspecified agenda item (Item B) because law enforcement had been involved at the location the previous night and no clear report was yet available. He said it was in the community's best interest to take no action. The board voted to table it.

memberPositions.evidence: Moved to table Item B, saying a recent law-enforcement incident at the location meant it was best not to act.

cases.name: KSCJ Consulting recommendation — Eisenberg Residence, 47 Windmill Road: release wetland mitigation bond and extend monitoring/maintenance bond to 2030
cases.summary: On the recommendation of the town's consultant KSCJ, the board acted on the Eisenberg Residence project to release the wetland mitigation bond and extend the five-year monitoring and maintenance bond through May 2030. Approved without substantive discussion.

cases.name: Adoption of revised Workplace Violence and Sexual Harassment Policies
cases.applicant: Town Administrator Kevin / Labor Counsel (Bond Schoeneck)
cases.summary: The board considered two Labor-Counsel-drafted policy rewrites (workplace violence and sexual harassment) that update long-outdated existing policies. A sharp dispute erupted over process and substance: Councilman Berra had submitted track-changes comments only that day and wanted an executive session with Labor Counsel before adopting, and Councilman Milim wanted to 'get it right' rather than adopt and re-issue. The Supervisor and Councilmembers Hussain and DiGiacinto argued to adopt now and amend later, deferring to the experts, with Rende frustrated by repeated last-minute edits. The board voted 4-1 to TABLE both policies (Milim, Berra, DiGiacinto, Hussain aye; Rende no), to revisit in executive session with Labor Counsel at the next meeting and vote at the following meeting, with all changes to be circulated in advance under privilege.

memberPositions.evidence: Pushed to adopt the expert-drafted policies immediately given how outdated the current ones are, objected repeatedly to last-minute comments, and cast the lone NO vote against tabling.

Wanted Labor Counsel in executive session before adopting; flagged vague definitions ('any act of aggressive behavior' as workplace violence; a 'hug' as sexual harassment) as too loose; submitted track-changes comments and voted to table.

Made the amended motion to table; said members can change their view up to the vote, favored an executive session for board alignment, and preferred to 'wait a month and get it done right' rather than adopt and re-issue.
Argued strongly to adopt now and defer to Labor Counsel, criticizing recurring last-minute edits ('not the way to govern'), yet voted aye to table for board consensus.
Agreed with the Supervisor to adopt the expert recommendation and revisit if needed, expressed frustration that edits weren't shared with the whole board in time, but voted aye to table.

cases.name: Resolution designating town-owned parcel 122.16-2 (5 General Heath, North White Plains) as dedicated open space
cases.summary: Championed by Councilwoman DiGiacinto, the resolution dedicates a small (0.37-acre) town-owned steep-slope parcel contiguous to the historically significant Miller Hill/Miller Park as protected open space, to help guard against erosion and development impacts near the historic site. She noted the negligible tax impact. The board expressed unanimous support and adopted it.

memberPositions.evidence: Led the item, arguing the town has a responsibility to preserve property contiguous to the historic Miller Hill and that this is 'our one chance to do the right thing.'
Said he'd examined the site, warned it could become 'Miller Flats instead of Miller Hill' if not preserved, and fully supported it.

cases.name: Payment Requisition No. 4 — Tony Casale Inc., Kent Place parking lot (former Verizon property) improvements
cases.summary: The board approved payment requisition No. 4 to Tony Casale Inc. for the completed Kent Place parking-lot improvements, already cleared by the town's engineer. Members praised the finished lot (now open and in use) and discussed remaining holdback, extra fence work, and fall overseeding, plus plans to encourage Main Street business owners/employees to use the new lot and to advance a future parking-district effort.

memberPositions.evidence: Praised the completed lot, raised holdback/overseeding follow-ups, and said the town is close to identifying property owners to launch a parking-district discussion.

cases.name: Amendment to agreement with WSP USA Inc. (Jan 13, 2021) — construction engineering for Water District No. 4 new well
cases.summary: The board authorized the Supervisor to sign an amendment to the 2021 WSP USA agreement for construction engineering on the Water District No. 4 new-well project, paid from the water district No. 4 operating budget. Water/sewer superintendent Sal noted the long-running project (permitting began years before 2021) is now in its 'home stretch.' Approved.

memberPositions.evidence: Said it 'would make me very happy to make this motion,' noting the long project is nearing the finish line.

cases.name: MOU with Byram Hills School District — School Resource (Police) Officer services, 2025-2026 school year
cases.applicant: Town of North Castle / Byram Hills School District
cases.summary: The board authorized the Supervisor to sign a memorandum of understanding with the Byram Hills School District for the town to provide School Resource Officer (SRO) police services for the 2025-2026 school year. Approved without substantive debate.

cases.name: Proposal from WSP USA Inc. — engineering services for Long Pond dam safety inspection
cases.summary: The board approved a WSP USA proposal for engineering services for the Long Pond dam safety inspection, an obligation because DEC requires Class B dams to be inspected every four years. Supervisor Rende recused himself (a person had once consulted him about the matter in his capacity as a lawyer). Approved.

memberPositions.evidence: Recused himself because someone had spoken to him about the matter in his capacity as a lawyer while on the board.

cases.name: Personnel appointments — Irwin Hernandez (Water & Sewer maintenance worker) and Luke Wynn Land (seasonal road maintainer, Highway)
cases.summary: The board approved the probationary/provisional appointment of Irwin Hernandez as a Water and Sewer maintenance worker and the appointment of Luke Wynn Land as a seasonal road maintainer in the Highway Department, both effective June 16, 2025. Members welcomed the additions while noting the water/sewer department still needs more staff.

cases.name: Town Board liaison updates and Administrator report (discussion)
cases.summary: Liaison and administrator updates covered: beautification committee planters at the Route 22/Cox Avenue triangle and a 'welcome home' new-resident postcard directing residents to the town website (DiGiacinto); a forthcoming library website RFP to be a decision item June 25 (Hussain); a donated senior-center piano and the ethics-code review to be scheduled for executive session/public hearing (Berra); sidewalk grant applications and priorities including North White Plains, aggressive Route 128 trail tree-cutting done without a still-pending NYSDOT permit, and a proposed pollinator garden at Wampus Brook Park South (Milim); plus the successful Folderol community festival and 'Coffee with a Cop' on June 14 (Rende/Kevin). Two residents (Thomas Zimmerman, Frederick Ozdoba) were remembered.

memberPositions.evidence: Reported beautification planters and the new-resident welcome postcard, and pressed that North White Plains sidewalks not be forgotten relative to Route 22.
As library liaison, briefed the board on the upcoming library website RFP and confirmed alignment to keep it a June 25 decision item.
Relayed the Park & Rec board's push on sidewalks and proposed a pollinator garden at Wampus Brook Park South to preserve future flexibility.
Reported the donated senior-center piano resolution and, as ethics-board liaison, asked for certainty on scheduling the ethics-code review.
Thanked the police, parks staff, and Lions Club for the successful Folderol festival and praised the town's volunteer-driven community events.

Water District No. 4 well engineering nearing completion; new maintenance worker hired.
Folderol praise, welcome-resident postcard, in-memoriam closings.
Byram Hills SRO MOU; NYSDOT stop sign and pending trail permit.

Police Lieutenant; presented the traffic-safety analysis, photos, and recommendation for no-parking restrictions on Old Mount Kisco Road and reported NYSDOT agreement to install a stop sign at the Main Street intersection.

meetings.meetingSummary: The Town Board reconvened from executive session and, in a light legislative session ahead of its reduced summer schedule, appointed and swore in a new police officer, Michael Calderola, bringing the department to its budgeted staffing level. State legislators Senator Shelly Mayer and Assemblyman Chris Burdick presented major good news, including $26.5 million in DOT funding to repave Routes 120 and 22, plus state budget wins on EMS, education aid, and environment. The board also heard from the Revolutionary War 250th committee about a town-wide art contest, and handled a routine consent-style agenda of resolutions, permits, and personnel appointments.
meetings.durationNote: Meeting opened 5:30 PM into executive session (board/committee interviews, advice of counsel on personnel and real estate) then reconvened; late start acknowledged. Full board appears present (Rende, DiGiacinto, Hussain, Milim, Berra). No absences noted.

cases.name: Appointment of Michael Calderola as Police Officer
cases.summary: The Chief formally recommended Michael Calderola, a licensed master social worker and Coast Guard Auxiliary member, for appointment to the budgeted position of police officer effective June 28, 2025, following a thorough background investigation. The board voted by voice ('all in favor, aye') to approve the appointment, after which the Supervisor administered the oath of office. Rende noted the appointment finally brings the department to its long-budgeted staffing level after years stuck around 28 officers. Calderola will attend the Westchester County Police Academy beginning July 7.
cases.publicComment: Family members were introduced and congratulated; celebratory tone.

memberPositions.evidence: Said swearing in new officers is 'the part I enjoy the most' and touted reaching budgeted staffing levels through the board's and chief's work.

cases.name: State Legislative Update — DOT Road Funding & End-of-Session Report (Sen. Mayer, Asm. Burdick)
cases.applicant: Sen. Shelly Mayer; Asm. Chris Burdick
cases.summary: State Senator Shelly Mayer and Assemblyman Chris Burdick reported securing $26.5 million in additional DOT funding to rebuild Route 120 ($11M) and repave Route 22 from Kensico Dam to Route 120 ($15.5M), moved up into the current five-year capital plan after years of the town pressing the state. They also reviewed budget wins on EMS (a county-led planning process and EMS costs excluded from the tax cap), education aid (updated Westchester regional cost index, foundation aid, universal school meals, cell-phone ban), environment funding, and the Con Edison rate-case intervention. This was an informational presentation, not a board vote. Rende publicly apologized for being 'heated' in prior DOT meetings and thanked the legislators and the police chief for driving the results.

memberPositions.evidence: Apologized for being 'a little bit heated' fighting for road results, thanked legislators and asked them to extend gratitude to the Senate Majority Leader; praised the chief's road-safety focus.

Called the funding 'an incredible achievement' but pressed repeatedly on quality control, insisting the earlier Route 128 repaving 'wasn't done right' with 'little bumps all along' and asking what the acceptance process is to ensure quality.
Thanked Sen. Mayer warmly, praising that she comes through on 'little things and big things' and lauding her stature in Albany.

cases.name: Revolutionary War 250th Committee — Art Contest & Events Update
cases.applicant: North Castle Revolutionary War 250 Steering Committee (Ed Woodyard, Marion Hamilton)
cases.summary: Committee members Ed Woodyard and Marion Hamilton updated the board during public comment on 250th-anniversary programming, thanking the town and Highway Department for retrieving a time capsule. They launched a town-wide original art contest (submissions July 4 through January 15, 2026, juried with prizes and a 2026 exhibit) and a companion library history exhibit. No board action was required. Milim asked whether AI-generated or digitally manipulated art must be disclosed; the committee confirmed disclosure is required per the contest specifications.
cases.publicComment: Ed Woodyard and Marion Hamilton presented enthusiastically; celebratory, community-oriented tone. Discussed possible permanent installation of winning artwork.

memberPositions.evidence: Praised the effort as 'absolutely wonderful' and 'crucial' for the town, asked who designed the flyer, and raised whether AI art would need to be disclosed.
Expressed fascination with the committee's enthusiasm, described plans to reseal time-capsule letters marked for 2076, and looked forward to 'a full year of a lot of great celebration.'

cases.name: Approval of Town Board Minutes — June 11, 2025
cases.summary: The board approved the minutes of its June 11, 2025 meeting by voice vote on motion and second. Routine procedural item with no discussion.

cases.name: Resolution Authorizing Health Dept Permit Application — Commercial Wading Pool Pump Modification
cases.summary: The board ratified/adopted a resolution authorizing a permit application to the Westchester County Department of Health for modification of the existing commercial wading (kiddie) pool, specifically for the pool pump change. Approved by voice vote with no discussion.

cases.name: Payment Requisition #1 — Engineered Fluid Inc., Water District #4 New Well Building
cases.summary: The board approved Payment Requisition No. 1 to Engineered Fluid Incorporated for work on the Water District #4 new well building. Water/Sewer superintendent 'Sal' was present to answer questions; none were raised. Rende reflected that the roughly 350-gallon-per-minute well project has taken years but is an important move, and approved it by voice vote.

memberPositions.evidence: Noted the new 350-gpm well 'takes so long' but is 'all good' and 'a very important move,' and made the motion.

cases.name: Receipt of Email Rescinding Owner Consent — Be Yourself Spa Special Use Permit (99 Lafayette Ave)
cases.summary: The board accepted receipt of an email from the 99 Lafayette Avenue property owner (May 99 Holdings, LLC) rescinding the owner's consent for the Be Yourself Spa special use permit application. Handled by motion and voice vote as a receipt item, with no substantive discussion.

cases.name: Alcohol Permit Application — Armonk Outdoor Art Show Closing Reception
cases.summary: The board approved an alcohol permit application for the Armonk Outdoor Art Show 'Armonk Has a Heart' closing reception at the North Castle Public Library on October 9, 2025. Approved by voice vote with no discussion.

cases.name: Kellart Sessions Recommendation — Wetland Mitigation & Maintenance Bond, Nassau Massar Residence
cases.address: 8 Cole Drive and 24 Davis Drive, Armonk
cases.summary: The board received a recommendation from Kellart Sessions Consulting regarding a new wetland mitigation bond, to be followed by a maintenance plan bond, for the Nassau Massar residence project at 8 Cole Drive and 24 Davis Drive. Handled as a receipt item by motion and voice vote with no discussion.

cases.name: Film Permit — YDEO Productions Inc., Cranberry Lake Preserve
cases.summary: The board approved a film permit application for YDEO Productions Incorporated to film a feature film at Cranberry Lake Preserve from July 16 to July 18, 2025. Approved by voice vote; Rende joked he had no idea what the acronym stood for.

cases.name: Appointment of Stephanie Paul — Hourly Librarian, North Castle Public Library
cases.summary: The board approved the appointment of Stephanie Paul as an hourly librarian at the North Castle Public Library, effective July 10, 2025. Approved by voice vote with no discussion.

cases.name: Resignation of Charles Hornbeck III — Highway Department
cases.summary: The board accepted the letter of resignation of Charles Hornbeck III from the Highway Department, effective June 28, 2025, by voice vote. Rende asked Town Administrator Kevin how long the employee had served and pressed to ensure an exit interview is conducted, saying exit interviews should be a standing policy.

memberPositions.evidence: Wished the departing employee good luck and urged that an exit interview be completed, calling it 'a worthwhile endeavor' that 'should be a policy.'

cases.name: Conference Attendance — Kevin Neely, Assistant Assessment Clerk (NYS Assessors Cornell Conference)
cases.summary: The board approved Assistant Assessment Clerk Kevin Neely's attendance at the New York State Assessors Association Cornell Conference on July 14 and 15, 2025. Rende highlighted that Neely received a scholarship of up to $1,200, making the roughly $700 conference cost effectively no cost to the town, and noted its focus on artificial intelligence. Approved by voice vote with congratulations.

memberPositions.evidence: Praised the scholarship covering the cost to the town, calling the AI-focused conference 'very worthwhile.'
Seconded the motion and 'the congratulations to him,' calling it 'great.'

cases.name: Appointment of Shruthi Franklin — Records Digitization Intern, Town Clerk's Office
cases.summary: The board appointed Shruthi Franklin to a records digitization intern position in the Town Clerk's office, effective June 30, 2025. Approved by voice vote. Rende asked that the position's goals and accomplishments be documented so the board can evaluate the value of such temporary/intern roles in future.

memberPositions.evidence: Asked that goals and outcomes for the intern position be documented so the board can judge whether such roles are 'a worthwhile endeavor' going forward.

cases.name: Consensus Agenda
cases.summary: The board adopted the consensus agenda by motion and voice vote with no separate discussion.

cases.name: Liaison Updates & Supervisor Announcements
cases.summary: Board members gave liaison reports: Hussain reported strong library summer programming (summer reading launch with ~345 participants, magic show, crafts) and an RFP that can proceed without a new board vote; DiGiacinto noted Armonk businesses featured in Best of Westchester 2025. Rende praised the new in-house maintenance department for cost-saving work at the library, promoted the newly improved west-side Main Street/library parking lot and a phase-two meeting with property owners targeted for July 15-17, and encouraged residents to use the town as a cooling shelter during extreme heat. He also recounted police quickly rescuing a dog left in a hot parked car, and Berra reported nothing to add. The meeting closed with a memorial for lifelong resident Muriel Hubfeld.

memberPositions.evidence: Reported enthusiastically on library summer programming turnout, calling it 'really awesome to see so much activation with the town.'

Proud that many Armonk businesses were cited in Best of Westchester 2025 and urged residents to keep supporting local independent businesses; also urged neighbors to check on elderly residents during the heat.
Praised the in-house maintenance department as a money-saver, pushed the parking-lot phase two forward, and offered town buildings as cooling shelters during extreme heat.
When asked for a liaison update, said he had 'nothing at all,' joking he could come up with something.

State and county partnerships (Mayer, Burdick, Kunzeho) delivered road, EMS, education and agricultural-district wins.
Swearing-in of a new officer reaching budgeted staffing; EMS tax-cap exclusion; dog rescue from a hot car.
Multiple appointments (officer, librarian, records intern) and a highway resignation with an exit-interview policy push.
Revolutionary War 250th art contest and history exhibits launched by the steering committee.
Library summer programming, film permit, and wading-pool permit.
Water District #4 well building, parking lot improvements, road capital plan.
Alcohol, film, and health-department pool permits; a rescinded spa consent.
Payment requisition for the new Water District #4 well building.
State budget report on tax relief, aid, and looming federal Medicaid/SNAP cuts.

staffInput.summary: Gave community announcements about the Armonk Summer Music Series concerts; confirmed at-home public-comment sign-ups; supported the records digitization intern posting and library RFP process.

Answered questions on the departing highway employee's tenure and exit interview, coordinated the library RFP so it can proceed without a new board vote, and is arranging the parking-lot phase-two property-owner meeting.
Water/Sewer superintendent present to answer questions on the Water District #4 new well building payment requisition; no questions were raised before approval.

meetings.meetingSummary: The Town Board held its July monthly meeting, opening with a presentation from Westchester County Executive Ken Jenkins on storm/flooding response, a projected $25M county budget shortfall, and the county's intervention in the ConEd delivery-rate case. The bulk of the meeting was consumed by a contested vote to release a Request for Expression of Interest (RFEI) for the Town Hall/police/court project, which passed 4-1 over Councilwoman DiGiacinto's objection that the public had no chance to review it. The board also granted a contested one-year extension of the Gateway (former Mariani Gardens) special-use permit with maintenance/tax conditions (3 aye, DiGiacinto no, Berra abstaining), scheduled a public hearing for the Mianus River Gorge special-use permit, received a resident letter on a problem short-term rental at 31 Washington Avenue, and approved a range of routine items (road naming, historic-site clearing, a wetland bond change, a donation, a festival permit, contracts, and personnel resignations).
meetings.durationNote: Full board present; roll-call votes named Milim, Hussain, DiGiacinto, Berra, and Supervisor Rende. Hussain recused himself from the Eagle Ridge road-naming item (IBM employment, adjacent property). Long meeting running past midnight.

cases.name: County Executive Update & ConEd Rate-Hike Intervention
cases.summary: County Executive Ken Jenkins addressed the board on the July storms and Route 22/I-287 flooding, an emergency-operations debrief with the town, a projected ~$25M shortfall in the county's $2.5B budget, the Banksville Road bid, the airport main-terminal modernization RFP, and the county's intervention in the ConEd (and forthcoming NYSEG) delivery-rate cases. Barbara DiGiacinto thanked him for the county's seat at the table on the 'jaw-dropping' proposed 2026 delivery-rate hikes and urged residents/ratepayers to file comments before the November deadline. No vote; this was an informational presentation and advocacy discussion.
cases.publicComment: No formal resident comment on this item; county executive presented and answered board questions.

memberPositions.evidence: Thanked Jenkins for reaching out during the storm, praised the town's relationships with state and county partners and said he has the county executive 'on speed dial.'
Called the proposed 2026 ConEd delivery-rate hikes 'absolutely jaw dropping' and stressed the importance of the county having a seat at the table to negotiate them down.
Added that Assemblyman Burdick advises residents to submit rate-case comments by end of August; 'the more information the better' to influence the rates.

cases.name: Public Comment — Tributes to Tony Futia
cases.summary: During public comment several residents (Mike Shaliro of 14 Orchard Drive and a longtime resident/judge) offered tributes to the late Tony Futia, a passionate civic gadfly and former water superintendent who died in April, recalling his ward-vote petition, his primary runs, and his dedication to the town despite frequent disagreements. Supervisor Rende and Councilwoman DiGiacinto responded warmly with their own recollections. No action taken.
cases.publicComment: Residents Mike Shaliro and others spoke fondly and respectfully in memory of Tony Futia.

memberPositions.evidence: Said he admired Futia's courage of conviction and willingness to respectfully address the board, and keeps a 'Tony Futia file' of materials Futia dropped off.
Shared that Futia had emailed her about running for supervisor to force a debate, and praised that 'he cared' and used legal means like the ward vote.

cases.name: Approval of Town Board Minutes (June 25 & July 15, 2025)
cases.summary: Under old business the board approved the town board minutes of June 25, 2025 and July 15, 2025 by voice vote. Routine procedural item passed on a motion and second, all in favor.

cases.name: Receipt of Resident Letter on Short-Term Rental at 31 Washington Avenue
cases.applicant: Neighboring property owners (Tan Nguyen and others)
cases.summary: The board voted to receive a letter and petition from neighbors of 31 Washington Avenue documenting years of quality-of-life problems (all-night parties, noise, reckless driving, blocked hydrant and shared driveway, harassment) from an out-of-state owner's Airbnb operation with up to 40+ guests. Because North Castle has no short-term-rental regulation, the board noted Town Planner Adam Kaufman and counsel are beginning to draft an STR law, and a public hearing will be held before any law is adopted. The letter was received by voice vote; the underlying legislation was not yet discussed on its merits.
cases.publicComment: Resident Tan Nguyen (33 Washington Ave, next door) detailed the disturbances and said the Florida-based owner told him 'the money's too good' to stop; residents were sympathetic and appreciative of the board.

memberPositions.evidence: Said the neighbors' hardship 'really reflects' serious quality-of-life issues and that 'we really do need to regulate Airbnbs in North Castle,' hoping the regulations are 'simple and enforceable.'
Called the situation 'unforgivable, inexcusable,' promised the board will pay attention and draft legislation to control irresponsible rentals while not infringing responsible owners.

cases.name: Mianus River Gorge — Special Use Permit Public Hearing Scheduled
cases.summary: The board received a request from Mianus River Gorge Inc. for a special use permit for a scientific research center in a residential zone and scheduled the public hearing for August 13, 2025 (moved up from a proposed September 10). Executive Director Rod Christie explained the preserve has operated at the site since the 1950s and only recently learned a special use permit was needed in connection with a building project; it has already been through zoning and planning with no objections. Approved by voice vote to set the hearing.
cases.publicComment: Rod Christie, executive director of Mianus River Gorge, spoke; no opposition expressed.

memberPositions.evidence: Thanked the preserve 'for all the good work that you do' and expressed no anticipated issue with the permit.

cases.name: Gateway (former Mariani Gardens) — Third One-Year Special Use Permit Extension
cases.address: Former Mariani Gardens site, RMFDA district, Armonk
cases.summary: The board considered a third one-year extension of the special use permit for the Gateway attached/multifamily development on the former Mariani Gardens site. After extended debate over the property's eyesore condition, rocks allegedly stored in a floodplain, past tax delinquency, and how long the extension should be, the board went into executive session for advice of counsel. It returned and conditioned the one-year renewal on the applicant's written commitments to maintain the property in current condition, keep secure/locked access, and pay taxes timely. On a roll-call vote the extension carried with Milim, Hussain and Supervisor Rende in favor, DiGiacinto opposed, and Berra abstaining. Rende disclosed that principals of the ownership had contributed to his campaign but said it did not preclude a fair vote.
cases.publicComment: No resident comment; the applicant's attorney argued the applicant was legally entitled to the one-year extension.

memberPositions.evidence: Voted 'No'; pressed the applicant on rocks stored in the floodplain 'since 2022,' the property being an eyesore, and past tax delinquency.
Said he was 'unlikely to support this' and suggested a three-month extension over concerns about maintenance and delinquent taxes, but ultimately voted 'Aye' after conditions were added.
Pushed the applicant on 'what guarantees' the town has that the property will be maintained, then voted 'Aye' once the maintenance/tax commitments were secured.
Questioned the design/bid timeline and whether a full year was required, then abstained, saying he could not in good conscience support it.
Defended granting the extension, comparing it to the long-vacant lumberyard project, and voted in favor after disclosing campaign contributions from the principals.

cases.name: Eagle Ridge Subdivision — New Road Names
cases.summary: The board approved the road naming committee's recommendation to name the new Eagle Ridge subdivision roads 'Kesper Crossing' and 'Parkview Road,' with notification to the town's E-911 coordinator. Councilman Hussain recused himself because he works for IBM, which is adjacent to the property, then returned. Passed by voice vote as a routine item.

memberPositions.evidence: Recused himself 'to be conservative' as an IBM employee (adjacent property), citing the ethics code, and stepped out for the vote.

cases.name: Sands Mill Historic Site — Vegetation Clearing Contract
cases.applicant: North Castle Historical Society / Demo Landscape LLC
cases.summary: The board approved a request from the North Castle Historical Society to have Demo Landscape LLC clear dead trees and invasive vines from the Major Andre / Sands Mill historic site at no cost to the town, with the contractor providing insurance naming the town as additional insured and indemnity. This is phase one, done by hand with no heavy machinery and staying within the stone-wall boundaries to protect any wetland buffer, with a phase-two review by the Conservation Board to follow. Approved by voice vote; the board praised the volunteer effort.
cases.publicComment: A representative of the Historical Society / North Castle 250 group was present and thanked.

memberPositions.evidence: Described walking the site, praised Steve Dempsey and the Historic Society, and called it a great example of volunteers getting things done at no cost to the town.

cases.name: Wetland Mitigation Bond Change — Rogel Project, 18 Caroline Place
cases.summary: The board accepted an amended recommendation from KSCJ Consulting regarding the five-year wetland mitigation, monitoring and maintenance bond for the Rogel residential project at 18 Caroline Place. Town Planner Adam Kaufman clarified that going forward the planting/completion bond will only be required in specific circumstances (e.g., off-season plantings or illegal wetland disturbance not tied to a certificate of occupancy) rather than across the board, since the CO itself motivates completion. Approved by voice vote.

memberPositions.evidence: Asked clarifying questions to understand that the bond would no longer be required across the board and only in circumstances without a CO to compel completion.

cases.name: Accept $1,000 Donation from Byram Hills Preschool Association
cases.applicant: Byram Hills Preschool Association / Superintendent of Recreation and Parks
cases.summary: The board approved a request from the Superintendent of Recreation and Parks to accept a $1,000 donation from the Byram Hills Preschool Association. Approved by voice vote with thanks for the donation.

cases.name: Armonk Cider and Donut Festival / BHPA Carnival Permit
cases.applicant: Armonk Chamber of Commerce and Byram Hills Preschool Association
cases.summary: The board approved a request from the Armonk Chamber of Commerce and the Byram Hills Preschool Association to hold the Armonk Cider and Donut Festival, featuring Jamie's 5K Run for Love and the BHPA Carnival, on Sunday, September 14, 2025. Approved by voice vote.

cases.name: Town Hall Project — Release of Request for Expression of Interest (RFEI)
cases.applicant: Town of North Castle (memo from special counsel Robert Spolzino)
cases.summary: The centerpiece and most contested item: the board voted to release an RFEI inviting responders to propose options for consolidating town offices, a new police station, and an OCA-compliant court (potentially including public-private-partnership and mixed-use concepts) on the town-owned campus or another hamlet site. Supervisor Rende framed it as a no-cost, non-binding fact-finding exercise following the earlier 333 Main Street condemnation hearings, and stressed any real decision would go to a public referendum. Numerous residents (Keith Rosenthal, Andrew Lester, Mike Shaliro, Marilyn Huck, Sue Shimer, Sharon Tombach, others) objected to the process, the summer timing, non-disclosure of the document, traffic/density concerns, and preservation of the historic district. On separate motions the board received counsel's memo, added the item to the agenda, and voted by roll call to send the RFEI out July 24; it carried 4-1 with DiGiacinto opposed. The privileged counsel memo was read aloud after the board waived privilege.
cases.publicComment: Heavy resident opposition/skepticism: speakers argued the RFEI was rushed, released without public input, invited developer self-interest, would increase traffic/density, and could threaten the Bedford Road historic district; several demanded the process be more transparent.

memberPositions.evidence: Championed the RFEI as a broad, no-cost, non-binding request for ideas that doesn't lock the town in, defended keeping it confidential on advice of counsel to avoid giving anyone a head start, and rejected the 'sky is falling' criticism.

Voted 'No,' stating it was because the public had no input and calling summer timing 'inappropriate'; wanted it held until September and objected to Rende speaking to the press about a confidential matter.
Urged the board to 'stay focused on the issue' rather than finger-pointing, warned that 'doing nothing is a choice and it's a bad outcome,' and voted Aye.

Said he is 'a bit skeptical' about how productive the RFEI will be and wished there had been public input, and voiced strong concern about density/character and excessive square footage, but voted Aye to move things forward.
Framed the phase as 'expanding the aperture' for all ideas, said he had no conversations with developers, supported going forward with full transparency, and voted Aye.

cases.name: Peak Power Systems — Emergency Generator Service Extension (Water & Sewer)
cases.summary: The board approved a proposal from Peak Power Systems Inc. to extend annual emergency generator service for the 15 associated units in the Water and Sewer Department from August 1, 2025 through August 15, 2026. Approved by voice vote.

cases.name: D&B Engineers — Water District 8 to District 4 Interconnect Proposal
cases.summary: The board conceptually approved a proposal from D&B Engineers and Architects for engineering services to interconnect Water District No. 8 (the airport-campus water main extension) into Water District No. 4, subject to the town attorney's review of the forthcoming contract before the supervisor signs. Approved by voice vote to keep the project moving as the developer's side of the water-main work is already underway.

cases.name: Personnel — Resignations and Court Clerk Conference Approval
cases.summary: The board received the resignation of Irwin Hernandez from the Water and Sewer Department (effective June 18, 2025) and of Michael Calderola from the Police Department (effective July 1, 2025), and approved court office personnel attending the 2025 NYS Association of Magistrates Court Clerks annual conference in Albany (Sept 28-Oct 1, 2025). All approved by voice vote as routine personnel items.

cases.name: Ethics Code Amendment — Legal Review and Public Hearing Status
cases.summary: Raised under liaison updates, the board discussed the stalled ethics-code amendment proposed by the Ethics Board, on which special counsel had opined a portion was legally invalid/overreaching. Because a substantive change requires re-drafting and a new public hearing (with the existing hearing to be closed), the board set a deadline for members to submit comments to counsel by the August 13 meeting and agreed to take it up in executive session then. DiGiacinto objected that airing the matter under a liaison update, tied to an executive-session request not on the agenda, was 'not fair.' No vote taken; direction only.

memberPositions.evidence: Said she still wanted to comment and found it 'very offensive' that the topic was brought up as a liaison update rather than a proper agenda item; agreed to submit comments by Tuesday/Wednesday.
As liaison pressed to move the ethics-code review forward, asked to resume or close the public hearing at the next meeting, and questioned the added procedural steps.
Said several members felt some Ethics Board recommendations were 'overreaching' and wanted counsel's legal opinion on whether they were challengeable before proceeding.

themes.note: Dominated by the Town Hall/police/court RFEI debate plus water-line, field, dog-park and generator projects.
Repeated clashes over transparency and public input on the RFEI and the ethics-code review.
Gateway/Mariani permit extension, Mianus River Gorge hearing, Eagle Ridge road naming, wetland bond.
Airbnb disturbances, traffic/density fears from new developments, historic-district preservation.
Board committed to drafting an enforceable Airbnb/STR law after the 31 Washington Ave complaints.
Water district interconnect, generator service, and new well/treatment work in District 4.
County $25M shortfall and ConEd delivery-rate hikes; taxpayer cost of the town hall project.
County Executive Jenkins update and the county's ConEd/NYSEG rate-case interventions.
