No members were absent; all five participated (one via Zoom). This is a 2025 meeting, so Jose Berra is on the board and Sonny Vitaj is not.

meetings.meetingSummary: The Town Board opened with a lengthy work session on a proposed local law regulating short-term rentals (Airbnb-type) under Building Code Chapter 127, debating enforceability, an owner-occupancy/overnight requirement, quiet hours, and waiting periods without taking a vote. It then handled a full agenda of resolutions and approvals, including a contested 4-1 resolution supporting the intermunicipal airport master plan task force recommendations (Milim opposed), a contested 4-1 extension of the town hall RFEI deadline (Berra opposed) that triggered a heated Rende-DiGiacinto exchange over the RFEI process, adoption of revised workplace-violence and sexual-harassment policies, a special-use-permit extension for additional horses, event/alcohol permits, and a change order to reconstruct the Clove Road baseball fields. Residents spoke on short-term rentals, sidewalk/trail and crosswalk safety, and the Clove Road field improvements.
meetings.durationNote: All five members present (roll calls named Berra, DiGiacinto, Milim/Milam, Hussain/Hussein, and Supervisor Rende); Hussain participated by Zoom. No absences noted.

cases.name: Local Law to Amend Chapter 127 — Short-Term Rental Regulations
cases.summary: A work session on a draft local law creating a registration/regulation scheme for short-term rentals, prompted by a severe problem property on Washington Avenue in North White Plains. The board reached rough consensus to keep a primary-residence requirement, retain (over Hussain's and Rende's objection) an owner-must-be-present requirement, reduce the waiting period from four years/two years to two years on the CO and one year of residency, and add quiet-hours provisions. No vote was taken; the planner and building inspector will revise the draft, compile an inventory of existing rentals, and bring it back before scheduling a public hearing.
cases.publicComment: Two North White Plains residents (33 and 41 Washington Avenue) urged adoption, citing an overcrowded Airbnb (reportedly ~42 occupants), shared-driveway blockage, and an out-of-state owner; supportive of a protective law.

memberPositions.evidence: Backs the need for legislation but is 'definitely concerned' it will be hard to enforce and a burden on the building department; strongly favors keeping the primary-residence and owner-overnight requirements for fire/safety reasons.

Overall supports legislation; wants quiet-hours/nuisance standards added, opposes the owner-overnight requirement as unenforceable and punitive to legitimate hosts, and pushed to shorten the waiting periods (agreed to 2 years CO / 1 year residency).
Likes the maximum-control draft including owner-presence and holding periods; dismisses enforceability objections with a stop-sign analogy ('you still have the law').
Wants a law 'in short order' to protect residents; sides with Hussain against requiring the owner to stay, saying it would largely eliminate legitimate Airbnb use.

cases.name: Resolution Supporting Intermunicipal Airport Master Plan Task Force Recommendations
cases.applicant: Airport Master Plan Task Force (rep. Michael Pollock, w/ Larry Ruisi)
cases.summary: A resolution joining seven municipalities in support of task force recommendations to the county on Westchester County Airport, covering the terminal use agreement (240-passenger/half-hour limit), FBOs, noise, traffic, and environmental concerns. Task force representative Michael Pollock presented and answered extensive questions about the ~80/20 private-vs-commercial traffic split and legal constraints. Adopted 4-1 by roll call, with Milim voting no because he wanted the resolution to push for a larger commercial-carrier share over time. Rende commended Milim for voting his conviction rather than abstaining.
cases.publicComment: Michael Pollock (appointed task force rep) presented at length; no adverse public comment.

memberPositions.evidence: Voted no; argued the resolution locks in the 80/20 split and would flatten/shrink commercial-carrier availability, which he considers the airport's main value to residents; could not find a way to amend it.
Voted yes; praised Pollock and Ruisi and stressed value of the municipalities acting unanimously to carry weight with the county, while sharing some of Milim's frustration.
Voted aye; 'super supportive' of moving it forward, praised the task force's work, and asked for future focus on the customer/airport-user experience.
Voted aye; engaged on the percentage math, landing-fee economics, and neighbor opposition; grateful for the task force's thorough work.
Voted aye in roll call ('Councilman Berra — Aye'); no substantive remarks recorded.

cases.name: Extension of Town Hall Project RFEI Deadline (Excelsior Housing Group request)
cases.address: 45/15 Bedford Road & town hall parcel, Armonk
cases.applicant: Excelsior Housing Group, LLC (via letter from Patrick Normyle)
cases.summary: Consideration of a letter requesting extension of the deadline to submit an RFEI (Request for Expression of Interest) on the town hall project to Dec 1. After a long and heated debate over the RFEI process itself, the board voted 4-1 to extend the deadline for all respondents to November 10 (aligning with the Nov 12 board meeting). Berra voted no, wanting the process concluded sooner while Milim is still on the board and believing respondents had ample time. The item produced a sharp Rende-DiGiacinto confrontation over whether the RFEI is a political/misleading exercise, with Milim also criticizing DiGiacinto's public messaging as divisive.
cases.publicComment: Keith Rosenthal referenced as a prior prospective respondent; no new resident comment at the vote.

memberPositions.evidence: Voted yes; vigorously defended the RFEI as a free, non-binding information-gathering step that will still go to a townwide referendum, and rebutted DiGiacinto's characterization as misinformation.
Voted no on the extension; said respondents had enough time and wanted the RFEIs reviewed while Milim is still on the board rather than dragging to December.

Voted aye; would have preferred dual-track engineering over an RFEI but backed it as a reasonable compromise, and criticized DiGiacinto's emails as divisive and misleading about residential development.

Voted aye and said she is genuinely interested in Excelsior's plan (fine waiting to Dec 1), yet is the lone RFEI 'no' vote overall, worried about large residential components (Pelham 127 units, Briarcliff 86 units) and wants budget & finance committee involvement.
Voted aye; framed the RFEI as a way to gather ideas and urged residents and colleagues to contribute input rather than criticize the input-collection method.

cases.name: Sidewalks, Trails & Pedestrian Crosswalk Safety (Parks Board follow-up)
cases.address: Main Street/Rt 128, School Street, Wampus Brook Park (Armonk); Nethermont/Virginia Road (North White Plains)
cases.summary: During public comment a Parks Board member followed up on ~2.5-year-old survey recommendations for sidewalk/trail extensions in Armonk and an unsafe CVS-area crosswalk on state Route 128. Rende described reviving a shelved comprehensive sidewalk plan and pursuing a staged, grant-and-bond funding approach, noting a prior grant application was denied. The board discussed prioritizing safety segments and coordinating with NYSDOT on the crosswalk and a possible signal; no formal action was taken.
cases.publicComment: Parks Board member (21 Orchard Drive) pressed for progress on sidewalks/trails and the CVS crosswalk; Randy Levitt, president of Kensico Little League, thanked the board for planned Clove Road field improvements. Tone appreciative but urging follow-through.

memberPositions.evidence: Stressed critical safety need for North White Plains (Nethermont path, Route 22, unbuilt Virginia Road sidewalks) and repeatedly urged involving the budget & finance committee given multi-million-dollar costs and bonding concerns.
Advocated a long-term staged pedestrian plan across hamlets and bonding against the town's AAA rating as favorable to taxpayers; disagreed that a budget & finance committee review is needed.
Asked that funding for this be a consideration in next year's budget planning so the long-stalled project can get moving.

cases.name: Special Use Permit Extension — Additional Horses at 263 Bedford Banksville Road
cases.summary: The board received a letter and adopted a resolution granting a one-year extension of a special use permit for additional horses, given ongoing construction of equestrian buildings and a new residence that will not be completed by the 9/13/2025 expiration. The applicant's attorney reported construction is proceeding smoothly with no issues. Received and extension granted to September 13, 2026 by unanimous voice vote.
cases.publicComment: Attorney Jerry Tortorella presented; board praised the succinct presentation.

cases.name: Local Law to Amend Chapter 263 Special Events — Remove Public Hearing Requirement
cases.summary: The board received a proposed local law updating Chapter 263 (special events) to remove the public hearing requirement and scheduled a public hearing on it for October 22, 2025. Received and public hearing set by voice vote.

cases.name: Code of Ethics Amendments — Close Public Hearing & Schedule Work Session
cases.summary: The board acted on the public hearing opened April 9, 2025 regarding proposed Code of Ethics amendments and set a joint work session with the Ethics Board for the first November meeting (November 12), when the drafting counsel is available. A clean revised draft incorporating minor word changes will be circulated to Ethics Board members by end of week, with the aim of setting a public hearing date after the work session.
cases.publicComment: A resident who attended to hear the ethics update was satisfied by the explanation.

cases.name: Revised Town Workplace Violence Policy
cases.summary: The board adopted a revised workplace violence prevention policy after discussion, prompted by DiGiacinto, over whether it covers elected officials. The Town Administrator and special counsel clarified that under state statute the policy covers municipal employees but not town board members/officers (who are public officers, not employees), whereas the sexual harassment policy covers everyone. A proposed parallel-language tweak was set aside to avoid tabling; adopted by voice vote.

memberPositions.evidence: Questioned whether the policy should also cover complaints between elected officials and noted an omission relative to the sexual-harassment policy; ultimately did not force a change.
Pushed to adopt rather than wordsmith a labor-counsel-drafted policy from the dais, offering to route any change through labor counsel instead.

cases.name: Revised Town Sexual Harassment Policy
cases.summary: The board adopted the revised sexual harassment policy by voice vote. Staff confirmed that, unlike the workplace violence policy, this policy covers all elected officials, appointees, and consultants under state and federal law.

cases.name: Policy for Use of Municipal Vehicles for Highway Emergency Personnel
cases.summary: The board adopted a policy governing take-home/emergency use of municipal vehicles by highway emergency personnel. Adopted by roll call with all five members voting aye. DiGiacinto supported it but asked that the recurring cost be considered in the context of the upcoming budget.

memberPositions.evidence: Supported the highway staff but wanted the recurring expense weighed as part of the coming budget before committing.

cases.name: Change Order #2 — IBM Community Park Turf / Clove Road Baseball Field Reconstruction (Shaw Sports Turf)
cases.address: Clove Road ballfields; IBM Community Park
cases.summary: The board received a letter and approved Change Order #2 to the Shaw Sports Turf agreement to reconstruct the natural-grass Clove Road baseball fields (drainage, regrading, re-cut infields) alongside the IBM Community Park artificial turf project, authorizing the supervisor to sign. Doing the work through the existing co-op contract and reusing stockpiled tested topsoil saved substantial money versus a new bid. DiGiacinto made the motion and thanked longtime advocate Bob Kandrea; received and authorization approved by voice vote.
cases.publicComment: Kensico Little League and Bob Kandrea, longtime advocates, thanked the board.

memberPositions.evidence: 'Definitely' wanted to make the motion and credited Kandrea's decade-plus advocacy for the field improvements.
Detailed the safety need and the cost savings from using the co-op contract and stockpiled topsoil; 'excited about it.'

cases.name: Aquaworks Contract Termination & Emergency Contractor Authorization
cases.applicant: Town Board (docs prepared by Town Attorney Roland's office) / Aquaworks
cases.summary: Add-on items: the board adopted a resolution declaring an emergency condition and authorizing termination of an existing contract, approved the contract termination agreement, authorized the supervisor to sign, and approved the Aquaworks bid proposal to serve as emergency contractor to complete the project. Added on, received, and all items adopted by voice vote.

cases.name: Conservation Board Memo — Major Andre Site Improvements
cases.summary: The board received a memo from the Conservation Board asking to be consulted on projects like the Major Andre site improvements. Rende explained he had responded that referral was not required because the donor-funded work (invasive-plant and dead-tree removal, grass planting) made no substantive change to the wetland/watercourse and, per the planning department, needed no Conservation Board review. Received by voice vote; discussion only.

memberPositions.evidence: Defended not referring the donor-funded improvements to the Conservation Board, saying there was no substantive wetland change, while calling the board's letter respectful and welcoming dialogue.

cases.name: Alcohol Permits & Community Event Approvals
cases.address: Whippoorwill Hall, 19 East Whippoorwill Road; Wampus Brook Park; North Castle Public Library, Armonk
cases.applicant: Katonah Classic Stage; Friends of Frosty; 250th Revolutionary War Committee
cases.summary: The board approved a group of routine permits/event requests by voice vote: an alcohol permit for Katonah Classic Stage receptions at Whippoorwill Hall (Oct 14-Nov 2), use of town roads and Wampus Brook Park for the annual Frosty Day parade and tree lighting (Nov 30), and an alcohol permit for the 250th Revolutionary War Committee opening-night exhibit reception (Oct 20). Rende encouraged residents to attend the Oct 20 exhibit at the Armonk library branch.

cases.name: Appointments & Personnel — Planning Board Appointment and Police Training
cases.summary: The board approved sending Police Officer Matthew Janelli to the NYS Highway Safety Symposium in Oswego (Oct 14-17), appointed Thomas Crespi to the Planning Board for a term ending December 31, 2025, and approved the consensus agenda. All approved by voice vote; DiGiacinto welcomed the Crespi appointment.

cases.name: Approval of Town Board Minutes — September 30, 2025
cases.summary: The board approved the minutes of its September 30, 2025 meeting by voice vote with no discussion.

themes.note: Long work session on a short-term rental local law; enforceability and owner-occupancy split the board.
Town hall RFEI, Clove Road fields, and sidewalk/trail plans dominated the capital discussion.
Repeated procedural clashes and a heated Rende-DiGiacinto exchange over the RFEI and meeting decorum.
Airport master plan resolution adopted 4-1; NYSDOT coordination on crosswalks and Route 22.
DiGiacinto repeatedly pushed budget & finance committee review and bonding scrutiny of capital costs.
Clove Road field reconstruction, dog park fountain, and turf/tennis facility progress.
Policy adoptions plus Planning Board appointment and police training approval.
Fire/overcrowding safety framing for STR law and crosswalk safety concerns.
Event/alcohol permits and the 250th Revolutionary War exhibit; breast cancer awareness note.

Building Inspector; described current enforcement via building code, a new online complaint form, likely commercial-equivalent fees/inspections, and uncertainty about workload; ambivalent about rushing the STR law.

meetings.attributionNote: Roll-call votes explicitly named members (Berra, DiGiacinto, Milim, Hussain, Rende), enabling confident attribution of the two split votes (airport 4-1 Milim no; RFEI extension 4-1 Berra no). ASR mangled surnames (Rendezvous/Rende for Rende, Milam for Milim, Hussein for Hussain, Digesento/Digacinto for DiGiacinto, Barra/Bera for Berra). All five members present; Hussain attended by Zoom.

meetings.meetingSummary: The Town Board opened with a lengthy work session on sidewalk and trail improvements for the Armonk and North White Plains hamlets, presented by Town Planner Adam Kaufman, and reached a consensus to have staff and engineers redesign a comprehensive, more cost-effective sidewalk plan covering both hamlets, with a spirited debate over bonding and tax impact. The board then held and closed a public hearing adopting a local law amending Chapter 263 (Special Events) to remove the public-hearing requirement in favor of staff referral. It approved routine business including meeting minutes, a Water District #4 payment application, a NY Swims grant resolution, receipt of the Water District #9 (Quarry Heights) map/plan/report, a tax-map maintenance agreement, a Hergenhan Recreation Center roof replacement (passed with one abstention), and three personnel appointments. Public comment centered on strong resident support for sidewalks and a call to enforce/revise the temporary political-sign law.
meetings.durationNote: Quorum present; board reopened public session after an executive session. No absences noted. Councilman Jose Berra participated (2025 roster). Note: 'Sonny Vitaj/Vitage' appears here only as a resident/candidate giving public comment, not as a board member.

cases.name: Sidewalk & Trail Improvements — Armonk and North White Plains Hamlets (Work Session)
cases.applicant: Town Planner Adam Kaufman / Recreation & Parks Advisory Board
cases.summary: Adam Kaufman presented a long-planned multi-phase vision for pedestrian connectivity: filling sidewalk gaps on North Broadway with a mid-block crossing, a Virginia Road sidewalk, and multi-use paths connecting schools and neighborhoods in the Armonk hamlet. The board learned the Greenway grant for the School Street-to-Sands Mill path was denied a second time, prompting discussion of self-funding via a bond given the town's AAA rating. Consensus was to close the work session and direct staff/engineers to redesign a comprehensive, lower-cost sidewalk plan serving BOTH hamlets (substituting cheaper trails/gravel paths and a Route 128 sidewalk for expensive boardwalk options), then bring back cost estimates. No formal vote to spend money was taken; the board also weighed the plan against other big-ticket projects (town hall, highway garage).
cases.publicComment: Strongly supportive. PRAB chair Carl Hendricks urged 'safety over Taj Mahal' and to keep the ball rolling, citing pedestrian accidents on School Street; PRAB member Norma Hill warned that delay only raises costs; resident/candidate Sonny Vitaj recommended making paths plow-width and noted state funding inequities; a resident (Michael Akivan) added context. Overall the public pressed the board to act.

memberPositions.evidence: Pushed hard to stop procrastinating ('you can't steal second with your feet on first'), willing to bond given the AAA rating and favorable rates rather than 'roll up the plans and put them on the shelf again.'
Supports sidewalks in principle but repeatedly asked for ballpark cost/tax-impact figures across all three big projects and warned against 'mortgaging our residents' future' with debt.

Framed sidewalks as a high-value quality-of-life item, suggested proceeding without grants, and supplied debt-service math (~$550k/year per $10M over 30 yrs) plus context that the town controls only ~15% of the tax bill.

Asked clarifying questions on the Lombardi Park path and said he loves the ideas but wants 'the most bang for the buck' — prioritizing sidewalks where people otherwise walk in the street over paths through parks.
Added scope suggestions: improving the Nethermont path with solar lighting and railings in North White Plains, and repaving the poor-condition west-side Main Street sidewalk pavers.

cases.name: Local Law Amending Chapter 263 (Special Events) — Remove Public Hearing Requirement
cases.summary: The board opened and held a public hearing on a local law to remove the public-hearing requirement for special-event permits, replacing it with a staff referral while keeping safety protocols and the 250-ft neighbor-notification requirement. Staff explained the change reduces burden on applicants (e.g., Troy's Nursery Easter event, corporate car shows) and aligns special-event permits with the town's event-permit process. The board received the required documents (public notice, affidavits, negative declaration, EAF Parts 1-2), closed the hearing, adopted the negative declaration, and adopted the local law, all by voice vote (aye). Matt Milim probed whether notice should exceed 250 ft and use town envelopes/certificates of mailing, but the board opted to keep the existing 250-ft standard.
cases.publicComment: Resident/candidate Sonny Vitaj asked for a plain-language explanation and welcomed retaining the 250-ft neighbor notification; a resident (Michael Akivan) suggested wider notice for high-traffic events like car shows. Tone constructive.

memberPositions.evidence: Explained the change makes the process less burdensome while preserving police/staff due diligence to deny permits that create hazards.
Supported the law but questioned whether notification should extend beyond 250 ft and whether town-envelope/certificate-of-mailing rules should apply; deferred when others preferred the status quo.

cases.name: Approval of Town Board Meeting Minutes — October 8, 2025
cases.summary: The board approved the minutes of its October 8, 2025 meeting by voice vote (aye). Routine, no discussion.

cases.name: Payment Application No. 2 — Papito Construction (Water District #4 Well Site Work)
cases.summary: The board approved payment application No. 2 to Papito Construction for site work on the Water District #4 well project. Described as 'pretty straightforward'; Water/Sewer superintendent Sal was available for questions but none were raised. Passed by voice vote (aye).

cases.name: Resolution Authorizing NY Statewide Investment in More Swimming (NY Swims) Grant
cases.summary: The board adopted a resolution authorizing participation in the New York Statewide Investment in More Swimming (NY Swims) grant program. Passed by voice vote (aye) with no substantive discussion.

cases.name: Receipt of Map, Plan & Report — Proposed Extension of Water District #9 (Quarry Heights)
cases.summary: The board voted to receive the AI Engineers map, plan and report for a proposed extension of Water District #9 to serve the Quarry Heights area of North White Plains. Supervisor Rende explained this is the first formal step to bring safe public water to roughly 44 of 55 homes whose private wells have suffered drought-related dry-ups and high PFAS levels; the work is costly due to heavy rock, and the town will pursue grants (enlisting the visiting Governor's office representative). A well-attended, generally positive informational meeting was held the prior evening, and a landing page with Sal's presentation was created. Passed by voice vote (all in favor).
cases.publicComment: Referenced from the prior evening's informational meeting in North White Plains: residents were generally positive but expressed many concerns about the project and costs.

memberPositions.evidence: Championed the extension to deliver safe drinking water to wells impacted by PFAS and drought, and pressed the Governor's office representative to help secure grants to make it affordable.

cases.name: Proposal from Cartographic Associates (CAI) — Tax Map Maintenance for 2026 Data
cases.summary: The board approved a proposal from Cartographic Associates, Inc. for tax-map maintenance processing data recorded in 2026, and authorized the Supervisor to sign the agreement. A member began raising roof-warranty questions before realizing they had jumped ahead to a later item; the tax-map item itself passed by voice vote (aye).

cases.name: Hergenhan Recreation Center Roof Replacement — ELQ Industries via Gordian Cooperative
cases.summary: The board approved an ELQ Industries proposal (through the Gordian state-bid cooperative) to replace the leaking Hergenhan Recreation Center roof at about $194,000, paid from fund balance. Extensive discussion centered on a 20-year shingle warranty and the flat-roof/shingle junction that had failed; one member wanted the cost of stepping up to 25/30-year shingles and asked that the Town Attorney review the manufacturer's warranty. Staff explained the steep pitch makes higher-rated shingles unnecessary and that the cooperative bid limits material choices. The motion passed with one abstention (the member seeking more warranty/cost information); Supervisor Rende voted yes, glad to 'finally get the roof fixed' after years of leaks.

memberPositions.evidence: Urged voting tonight given the season and worsening leaks; 'proud to vote yes to finally get the roof fixed at the Hergenhan center that's been leaking' for at least two years.
Repeatedly questioned the 20-year shingle warranty, wanted the added cost of 25/30-year shingles and a Town Attorney review of the warranty, and abstained on the roll call pending that information.

cases.name: Personnel Appointments — Librarian, Library Clerk, and Recreation Supervisor
cases.summary: The board adopted three personnel actions effective November 10, 2025: the probationary/promotional appointment of Diana Wendell to full-time Librarian; the provisional promotional appointment of Michelle McDavid to full-time Library Clerk; and the provisional appointment of Kimberly Williams to Recreation Supervisor (Senior Citizens). Rende wished Williams luck and acknowledged the work of the outgoing Liz Duffy (staying on part-time). The librarian and clerk positions were noted as budgeted for 2025. All passed by voice vote (aye).

cases.name: Temporary Political Signs / Sign Law Enforcement & Revision (Discussion)
cases.summary: Prompted by resident and former highway employee Mike Giaccio, the board discussed the proliferation of temporary political signs and inconsistent enforcement of the existing sign code. Members broadly agreed the situation is 'out of control' and that the sign law is ambiguous and should be revised, recalling prior unsuccessful work sessions. Rende favored requiring each candidate to register a responsible contact with the Clerk so violating signs can be flagged for removal rather than having town staff pull them; Barbara urged candidate self-restraint on timing and quantity and prompt post-election cleanup; Matt stressed that rewriting the ambiguous law is necessary to enable fair, non-selective enforcement. No formal action taken.
cases.publicComment: Resident/former highway employee Mike Giaccio was pointed and frustrated, arguing the town fails to enforce its own sign code, offered a simple front-of-property rule, and warned of trip hazards at School Street/Route 128 for Halloween.

memberPositions.evidence: Agreed signs are out of control and proposed a candidate-registered contact system so violators are asked to remove signs rather than having town staff pull them.
Called for candidate self-restraint limiting the time period and number of signs and prompt next-day cleanup; noted she only places signs with permission on private property.
Agreed it is out of control but stressed the sign law itself must be rewritten because its ambiguity fuels perceptions of selective enforcement.

cases.name: Driveway / Highway Bond Permit Process Simplification (Discussion)
cases.summary: During liaison/updates, Barbara DiGiacinto raised that residents doing driveway work can face two separate permits (building department plus a highway bond when work touches the curb cut/right-of-way). Rende noted the town had already met with the building and highway departments and posted clarifying notes on the website, and explained the highway bond is required only when work affects the curb cut in the right-of-way. Barbara asked to check whether the process can be further simplified to a single permit. No action taken.

memberPositions.evidence: Flagged that a resident had to obtain two permits despite not affecting the road area and asked the town to simplify the driveway permit process.

themes.note: Sidewalks/trails, rec-center roof, and water-district projects dominated the agenda.
Extended debate over bonding vs. tax impact for sidewalks, town hall, and highway garage; AAA rating cited.
Water District #4 well payment and the Quarry Heights (WD9) extension addressing PFAS/dry wells.
Trails, rec-center roof, dog park ribbon-cutting, turf and Clove Road field projects.
Special-events local law, sign-law ambiguity, transparency landing pages, permit simplification.
Sidewalk safety and out-of-control political signs drove public comment.
Papito payment app, CAI tax-map agreement, ELQ/Gordian roof contract.
Three routine library/recreation appointments adopted.
Governor's office rep Luke Powell introduced; county/state grant and road-condition asks.

staffInput.summary: Town Planner; presented the sidewalk/trail plans for both hamlets, reported the Greenway grant denial, and outlined cheaper alternatives (Route 128 sidewalk vs. costly boardwalk over wetlands) and available cost estimates.

cases.name: 2026 Budget Tax-Cap Override and 4.81% Tax Increase Discussion
cases.summary: Receipt of the budget prompted a lengthy, at times heated debate over the proposed 4.81% property tax increase, which would override the state's 2% tax cap for the first time in town history. Councilman Milim asked the Comptroller to explain how the tax cap works; Abbas explained it is a state-calculated levy limit (lower of 2% or inflation) with no penalty for exceeding it, effectively an alert to the public. The Supervisor, Milim, and Berra argued the cap is arbitrary/a 'red herring' given roughly 4-4.5% cost inflation (healthcare ~8%, retirement) on ~$37M of spending against only ~$22M of property-tax revenue, and that years of flat taxes had meant deferred maintenance (town hall, Hogan, pool, fields), an oversized fund balance, and budgeting for unfilled police/other positions. DiGiacinto and Berra voiced concern about breaking the cap and about development's impact on schools, and DiGiacinto requested the Budget & Finance Committee review the budget before the next meeting. The exchange grew adversarial, with Rende accusing DiGiacinto of politicizing the tax-cap issue for electoral advantage and she countering that receiving the budget at a special meeting without disclosing the cap override was itself political. No vote; discussion only, deferred to the November 19 hearing. Meeting adjourned as the Supervisor had to leave.
cases.publicComment: A Zoom attendee was invited to comment but declined; DiGiacinto noted North White Plains residents at her Saturday gathering first learned of the potential cap override from her.

memberPositions.evidence: Argued the 4.81% increase is reasonable and the 2% tax cap is 'totally irrelevant, a red herring'; blamed prior years of deferred maintenance, oversized fund balance, and budgeting for ~6-7 unfilled police officer positions; framed opposition as political fodder.

Shared concern about breaking the tax cap for the first time and about the 4.81% increase; disputed that the town 'padded' budgets; requested the Budget & Finance Committee review the proposed budget for objectivity before the next meeting.

Asked Abbas to explain the tax cap; concluded it has no real enforcement threshold ('effectively like a guidance'), and argued 2% on ~$22M of property-tax revenue cannot cover ~4.5% inflation on ~$37M of spending, so the cap is largely irrelevant.

Urged tightening the belt and voiced concern about the numbers and development's impact on schools/capital costs, but agreed prior years of not even taking the allowed 2% was bad financial planning and emphasized productivity/technology (Tech Task Force) to improve efficiency.

themes.note: Dominant topic: receiving the 2026 budget and debating the 4.81% increase and 2% tax-cap override.
Deferred maintenance on town hall, Hogan, pool, fields, and roofs cited as driving current costs; rising repair estimates over time.
Police staffing (28 sworn vs. budgeted 34) framed as a key underinvestment and rationale for the increase.
Dispute over transparency of the special meeting and whether the cap override was adequately disclosed; request for Budget & Finance Committee input.
Trade-offs between tax increases, service levels, and development discussed at length.

staffInput.summary: Explained the tax cap as a state-calculated maximum levy (lower of 2% or inflation) based on the prior year's levy, with no penalty for overriding; noted the levy limit is about $600,000 higher than the proposed levy and that the cap applies to all taxing districts including school and fire districts.
Confirmed that certain budgeted positions (e.g., under water/sewer superintendent Sal, building department) went unfilled because civil-service lists lacked suitable or available candidates.

meetings.meetingSummary: After an executive session, the board devoted most of the evening to a lengthy work session on proposed Ethics Code amendments, focusing on treating campaign loans as contributions, defining 'business associate,' the effective date of a new contribution-based recusal rule, and Section 5's applicant-disclosure requirements. The board then moved through a full regular agenda of routine resolutions and agreements: a conservation easement, wetland bonds, a water-district payment, a local law to override the tax levy limit (with a public hearing set for Dec 10), several intermunicipal agreements with Westchester County, library website/branding contracts, parking-lot change orders, telecom and payroll software contracts, and highway personnel appointments. cases.name: Ethics Code Amendments — Work Session
cases.summary: Continuation of a multi-year effort to revise the town Ethics Code, held as a work session on a rewritten draft prepared by special counsel Bob Spolzino with Board of Ethics input. Key debates: adding a sentence so a campaign loan (even if repaid) is treated as a contribution; broadening the 'interest' definition to cover an applicant's relative, partner, or business associate (with concern that 'business associate' is undefined and legally vague); the effective date of a new $500 contribution-triggered recusal rule; and Section 5, which would force land-use applicants to disclose campaign contributions to board members. The board reached rough consensus to keep the loan/business-associate language, adopt a rule-of-necessity/abstention fix (moving the recusal cross-reference), and rework Section 5 so F1 disclosure applies only to Town Board applications while F2 (interest-based) applies to all boards. No vote taken; counsel will redraft and the item will be placed on a future agenda to schedule a public hearing.
cases.publicComment: Board of Ethics members (chair/Mr. Summers, Brett, and others) presented and answered questions; they were largely satisfied with the rewrite and urged adoption with minor supplements. Planning Board chair Chris Carthy had submitted written objection to the applicant-disclosure provision. A Scout troop and two students attended and later led the Pledge.

memberPositions.evidence: Called the requirement that land-use applicants disclose contributions 'extremely offensive' and an 'overreach'; argued it injects politics into routine applications, presumes a quid pro quo, and could drive dark money; favored existing disclosure-plus-elections mechanism.

Found the applicant-disclosure and recusal proposals irrelevant and inappropriate, 'a violation of applicants' rights,' hard to enforce; said it would deter people from running and lamented to the visiting students that no one would run after such a debate.

Framed the changes as 'embedding trust into the community,' said constant, visible disclosure would make him more confident as a resident; supported an immediate effective date and trusting the ethics board's discretion on 'business associate.'

Brokered the compromise to delete/limit Section 5 F1 to Town Board applications ('I like it because everybody hates it'); agreed disclosure at non-town-board land-use boards injects politics, but wanted to finish and move to a hearing.
Backed treating forgivable loans as contributions ('held over the head'), proposed the Romanette wording so F1 captures town-board contributions; warned that fully deleting F1 'would lose my vote.'

cases.name: Work Session — Route 22 Bridge Replacement over Armonk Road Connector
cases.address: Route 22 over Armonk Road connector, North White Plains
cases.applicant: Westchester County Department of Public Works / HVA Engineers (design consultant)
cases.summary: County DPW and HVA Engineers presented the design for replacing the structurally deficient, county-owned Route 22 bridge, backed by over $12 million in federal funds within a roughly $17.5 million project. The preferred alternative slides a precast concrete arch beneath the existing structure to minimize traffic impact, eliminates the accident-prone stop sign by converting the ramp into a free-flow merge lane, and reuses the original stone facade. The board and residents raised safety, bicycle/pedestrian access, fire-truck clearance, environmental (Kensico Reservoir/DEP wetlands), and communication questions; construction is targeted for spring 2027. No vote was taken; the board committed to send a formal letter of concerns urging the county/state not to delay broader Route 22 improvements.
cases.publicComment: Resident Fred Cohen raised specific ramp-striping/merge safety concerns; resident Sonny Vitaj (a firefighter/EMS volunteer) urged wider shoulders for bicyclists and worried about ladder-truck clearance; residents Carolyn Hoffman and Ed Loberman commented, with Loberman vehemently opposing any North White Plains bike lanes. Generally supportive of the replacement.

memberPositions.evidence: Commended the county and federal funding, pressed hard that the bridge work must not delay long-overdue Route 22 corridor repairs (citing two recent fatalities and hazardous conditions), and pledged a formal board letter of concerns.

Called the presentation very helpful, probed whether federal funding could be pulled (told it is already earmarked) and asked about the duration of ramp closures and the Bronx River Parkway on-ramp merge.

cases.name: Public Hearing — 2026 Town and Special Districts Preliminary Budgets

Numerous residents objected to exceeding the tax cap and to reliance on reserves, arguing for deeper spending cuts; the board defended the plan as a fiscally responsible pivot away from years of over-hoarded reserves and deferred maintenance (citing one-off 2025 costs for roofs, salt domes, police radios, and lawsuits). No vote was taken; the board adjourned the public hearing to December 10 and agreed to hold additional public budget work sessions to look for cuts.
cases.publicComment: Heavy resident participation, largely critical: Ed Loberman argued at length against overriding the 2% tax cap and against using fund balance; Carolyn Hoffman, Julie DeFilippo, Nora, and Mariana Pandora voiced fixed-income and affordability concerns and asked for a five-year forecast; Brett Summers (former school board member) contextualized that town taxes are a small share of total bills; Fred Cohen was supportive of the town's shift toward budgeting to actual.

memberPositions.evidence: Defended the preliminary budget as fiscally responsible, argued prior boards artificially kept taxes flat by overusing reserves and 'ghost' unfilled positions, said breaking the cap was the honest choice over a politically easy 0% increase, but pledged openness to further cuts.

Called the shift a crucial strategic pivot, saying the town had been 'hoarding' money while infrastructure deteriorated; endorsed using savings to soften the tax hit and strongly backed creating a five-year capital plan.

Pushed to 'tighten our belts' and get down toward the tax cap, emphasizing recurring savings; floated ending condo-tax abatements on new projects, questioning a proposed HR hire, and forming tech/procurement committees.

Reviewed the budget line-by-line until midnight, flagged unchanged/duplicate line items, and pressed for another public budget work session, for department heads to identify non-essential cuts, and for reactivating the Budget & Finance Committee.

cases.applicant: Police Chief Peter Simonson / Town Board
cases.summary: The board received Police Chief Peter Simonson's memo recommending amendments to town code Chapter 325 to designate Crossroad North as one-way westbound because the steep grade at Old Mount Kisco Road causes vehicles to bottom out and creates a sight-distance hazard. After the chief explained that Crossroad South already serves the alternate movement and rebuilding the grade would be too costly, the board voted to receive the memo and to schedule a public hearing for December 10 to draft the local law.

memberPositions.evidence: Said the location is essentially her neighborhood and agreed the sharp grade is 'a disaster,' noting she had nearly had trouble turning there and endorsing the one-way fix given Crossroad South serves the same purpose.

cases.name: Settlement — Andrew Verboy v. Town of North Castle
cases.summary: The board approved a settlement in the matter of Andrew Verboy v. Town of North Castle by motion, second, and voice vote. Supervisor Rende afterward asked counsel whether the vote could be revisited off-camera; counsel advised it was the insurer's decision and unlikely given minors were involved and were supervised by town employees.

cases.name: 2026 Agreement with Verde Electric Maintenance Corp — Traffic Signal Maintenance
cases.address: Bedford Road & Maple Avenue; four flashing beacons on Route 22, Armonk
cases.summary: The board authorized the Supervisor to sign a 2026 agreement with Verde Electric Maintenance Corporation for traffic-signal maintenance at the Bedford Road/Maple Avenue intersection and four flashing-beacon assemblies on Route 22 in Armonk. The motion passed by voice vote after Supervisor Rende disclosed that principals of Verde Electric had made contributions to his past campaigns.

memberPositions.evidence: Proactively disclosed for the record that Verde Electric principals had contributed to his campaigns before the board voted to approve the maintenance agreement.

cases.name: Resignation for Retirement — Police Chief Peter Simonson
cases.summary: The board accepted Police Chief Peter Simonson's letter of resignation for retirement after 36 years, effective end of 2026. Board members expressed extensive appreciation for his professionalism, leadership, and outside utility contacts; the motion was made 'with deep regret and appreciation' and passed 'regrettably' by voice vote.

memberPositions.evidence: Called Simonson among the department heads he most enjoyed working with, praised his professionalism and his department's admiration, and wished him well in retirement.
Praised the chief's connections and effectiveness with ConEd and Verizon during storms and his professionalism, asking for his contacts before he leaves.
Said his overwhelming feeling was delight that the chief had earned the break, expressing sadness to see him go and appreciation for his and his department's work.

cases.name: Proposed Code of Ethics Amendments and Public Hearing Scheduling
cases.summary: A late-added item to receive proposed Code of Ethics amendments (drafted with special counsel Bob Spolzino and the Board of Ethics) and schedule a December 10 public hearing triggered a heated dispute. DiGiacinto objected that she received a revised draft only at 4:27 p.m. and accused Berra of overreaching by directing the attorney's edits; Rende said the law 'stinks,' was drafted for the wrong reasons, and that incoming member Sonny Vitaj should weigh in. After agreeing to delete one disputed provision, the motion (Berra/Hussain in favor) failed on a 2-2 roll call (Berra aye, Hussain aye, DiGiacinto no, Rende no; Milim absent), a tie constituting denial.
cases.publicComment: Brett Summers of the Board of Ethics earlier thanked the board for placing the item on the agenda; during the debate he attempted to speak on the drafting but was not recognized.

memberPositions.evidence: Defended the draft as the product of back-and-forth with the Ethics Board, characterized his edits as minor fixes to items counsel missed, and moved to receive it (with one deletion) and set the December 10 public hearing.
Wanted the one erroneously added provision removed and to move forward, saying the board had already agreed on the substance and pleading to stop spending precious time re-litigating it; voted aye.
Voted no, citing receipt of the document at 4:27 p.m. and 'lack of process,' and repeatedly accused Berra of a pattern of last-minute changes and overreaching his liaison role.

Voted no, saying he was prepared to reject it regardless of quorum, that the law 'stinks' and was drafted for the wrong reasons with no evidence of the abuses it claims to prevent, and that incoming member Vitaj should help evaluate it.

cases.name: Consensus Agenda
cases.summary: The board approved the consensus agenda by motion, second, and voice vote (all in favor).

themes.note: 2026 preliminary budget hearing dominated the meeting: 4.81% increase, tax-cap override, heavy resident pushback and internal debate over cuts vs fund balance.
Route 22 bridge replacement, deferred maintenance (roofs, salt domes), and calls for a five-year capital plan recurred throughout.
Process fights over the Code of Ethics amendments and calls for more public budget work sessions.
Route 22 corridor safety, the Crossroad one-way local law, and traffic-signal maintenance contract.
Water District No. 9 established; special-district financing, Quarry Heights and School Street waterline projects discussed.
Police radios, bridge fire-truck clearance, and Chief Simonson's retirement.
Verboy settlement plus ethics-law and multiple 2025 lawsuit costs referenced.
Police chief retirement and budget debate over new HR/staff hires.
County-owned bridge, federal funding, and coordination with NYSDOT on Route 22.
Holiday events and 914 Cares charity drive announcements.

staffInput.summary: Delivered the 2026 preliminary budget presentation, explaining the $43.7M budget, 4.81% tax-rate increase, tax-cap override, fund-balance use, and how the state tax cap is calculated; answered extensive resident questions on the cap, fund balance, and internal loans to special districts.
Police Chief; submitted and explained the memo recommending Crossroad North be made one-way westbound due to grade/sight-distance hazards, and separately submitted his retirement letter.

Handled meeting logistics, screen-sharing of budget documents, coordinated public/Zoom comment, and delivered community announcements (toy drive, closures, Frosty Day Parade, shredder event, December 1 town hall presentation).

Water/Sewer superintendent; explained that water and sewer are separate special districts with their own budgets and debt, described the internal 4.25% loan financing from the general fund, and detailed Water District 4, Quarry Heights, and School Street pipeline projects.
Special counsel who drafted the proposed Code of Ethics amendments with the Board of Ethics; circulated revised versions the day of the meeting, flagging certain highlighted changes as substantive.

Sitting town attorney; advised on the settlement revote question and cautioned board members about the Open Meetings Law and foilable documents when circulating budget-savings ideas ahead of a work session.

Assistant to the Town Administrator, filling in for absent Administrator Kevin Hay; tasked with coordinating a project landing page for the bridge project and scheduling additional budget work sessions.

meetings.attributionNote: Speakers were generally identifiable: roll-call votes named each member (Water District 9 4-0; Ethics 2-2), and the Supervisor, Berra, DiGiacinto, and Hussain spoke distinctly on major items. Matt Milim was absent all evening (out-of-town business, no Zoom), so no positions are attributed to him despite residents quoting his prior statements. Sonny Vitaj appears only as a resident/EMS volunteer (he does not join the board until 2026) and is placed in publicComment, not memberPositions. ASR mangled names (Rende as 'Rendez/Endy/Randy', DiGiacinto as 'Digacinto/Digisonto', Berra as 'Barra/Bearer/Vera', Hussain as 'Hussein') were normalized. One board voice agreeing on the Crossroad item was attributed to DiGiacinto with medium confidence; a bridge-communication question could not be confidently attributed and was omitted.

meetings.meetingSummary: A specially called Town Board meeting held so the two responders to the town's RFEI (Request for Expression of Interest) could present ideas for redeveloping North Castle's municipal facilities (town hall, police, court, and highway department). Michael Ferrari's team presented an ambitious ~$70M comprehensive plan (new police/court on the Mariani/45 Bedford Road site, expanded town hall, relocation of highway and school-bus operations to 215 Business Park Drive, new parks/fields/amphitheater, and conversion of 333 Main Street to ~40 residential units), while Keith Rosenthal ('Citizens of North Castle') presented a lower-cost ~$40-45M plan keeping everything on the existing town-owned 9.4-acre site with a village green. Residents and board members then gave feedback; no decisions or votes were taken beyond opening and closing the meeting.
meetings.durationNote: Special meeting; quorum present. Supervisor Rende plus council members present in person; Councilman Saleem Hussain participated via Zoom; Councilman Milim stepped out briefly during the public comment period.

cases.name: RFEI Presentations — Municipal Facilities Redevelopment (Town Hall / Police / Court / Highway)
cases.address: Town Hall & Highway Department site, Bedford Road, Armonk
cases.applicant: RFEI responders: Ferrari Companies (Michael Ferrari, with Torti Gallas & Croco architecture) and Keith Rosenthal / 'Citizens of North Castle'
cases.summary: The board convened a special meeting to receive two responses to its RFEI for modernizing the town's municipal facilities. Ferrari presented a comprehensive ~$70M vision acquiring the Mariani (45 Bedford Rd) and 215 Business Park Drive properties, relocating highway/bus operations, and adding extensive parkland, fields, an amphitheater, and ~40 residential units at 333 Main St; Rosenthal presented a ~$40-45M plan confined to the existing town-owned site with phased, interconnected buildings and a village green. Both plans notably contained NO commercial development of town land, addressing prior resident fears. The board stressed these are conceptual ideas, not proposals, and that any final plan would go to a full town-wide referendum (they committed to a full vote rather than relying on permissive referendum). No vote or decision was taken; the board signaled more meetings and likely a steering/expert committee to develop concrete A/B or single-bond options with real cost estimates.
cases.publicComment: Heavy public participation (in person and on Zoom). Residents broadly praised the effort and creativity of both plans; tone was constructive but cost-cautious. Recurring themes: urge fiscal prudence and phasing/'a la carte' sequencing, skepticism of eminent domain and of the Ferrari plan's optimistic cost/tax assumptions, concern that $400/yr means groceries for less-affluent North White Plains families (Diane Borgia), doubts about needing more sports fields and a dog park, and worry over the accuracy of the tax-impact estimate. A minority (Sharon, others) urged boldness — 'build, build, build.' One resident (Stefan Martinovic) argued the tax hit could be lower due to corporate taxpayers and ample fund balance/borrowing capacity.

memberPositions.evidence: Presided; framed the RFEI as an idea-gathering exercise, repeatedly stressed the urgent, long-recognized NEED (code-deficient offices, no ADA access, highway crews working outdoors), committed to a full town referendum, and favored preserving town land as open/green space while getting real cost figures before deciding.

Gave a detailed needs-vs-wants financial framework (~$1,000/sf build cost, each $25M ≈ 1% property-tax increase), urged urgency, but was skeptical of costly land acquisitions — called eminent domain of Mariani (~$12-20M risk) and 215 Business Park Drive (sold 2022 for $36M) poor value; favored maximizing use of existing town land and evaluating build-new-on-site vs 333 renovation.

Described herself as very conservative with money and 'scared' of the true cost (soft costs, construction, ongoing maintenance/staffing); worried taxes could rise 'beyond comprehension' and force residents out; advocated keeping the highway department on-site and screening it with landscaping/evergreens rather than buying new land.

Joined via Zoom; agreed with the urgency ('a burning situation'), said he is still in listening mode wanting resident and town-employee input, urged residents to react to specific ideas rather than pick one plan, and called for being bold long-term but frugal on immediate needs over the next one to two years.

Referenced secondhand by Supervisor Rende as taking the lead on legislation to limit condominium tax treatment on future development (to protect the school-tax base); not clearly heard speaking on the redevelopment item itself at this meeting.

cases.name: 333 Main Street — Proposed Rezoning from Commercial to Residential (~40 units)
cases.applicant: Michael Ferrari and partners (owners of 333 Main Street)
cases.summary: The 333 Main Street property (the Boyes law-firm building, owned in part by presenter Michael Ferrari) had been targeted a year earlier by the town for possible eminent-domain acquisition as a new town hall, drawing opposition; Ferrari included it in his RFEI concept as a conversion to ~40 residential units and disclosed he is separately filing a rezoning petition (to be completed the next day) to change it from commercial to residential, independent of any town-hall decision. Board members clarified this is a separate matter a future town board would decide, and that a private rezoning is not protected by permissive referendum — the board can grant or deny it. Whippoorwill Hills residents (a 150-home HOA adjacent via Log Cabin Way) voiced concern about traffic, construction disruption, and sightlines. No action was taken; the petition was not yet before the board.
cases.publicComment: Elisa Brickell (president, Whippoorwill Hills HOA, 150 homes) pressed on whether 333 would be rezoned/built regardless of the town-hall outcome and raised traffic/construction/sightline concerns; others (Jeff Sotolano, Sue Oakland) questioned the residential inclusion or opposed added density/school impact, while some accepted residential as a better use than a boarded-up office. Ferrari argued residential is the highest-and-best use and that office space would otherwise go dark.

memberPositions.evidence: Said his initial reaction is that he does not like the idea of 333 being rezoned to residential and that it is a separate decision for a future town board, which has every right to deny the petition.

Noted the 2018 comprehensive plan calls for more residential but is stale (should be updated every 2-3 years); said no rezoning proposal is formally before the board and that he'd like public input on whether 333 should stay office or become residential.

themes.note: Core purpose — modernizing/consolidating town hall, police, court and highway facilities long identified as deficient.
Dominant concern: ~$40M vs ~$70M plans, tax-impact estimates (~$400/household disputed), fund balance and AAA borrowing capacity, needs vs wants.
333 Main St rezoning petition, Mariani (45 Bedford Rd) acquisition, and eminent-domain risk debated.
RFEI (not RFP) framing; commitment to a full town-wide bond referendum; debate over a steering/charrette committee and process speed.
Village green/open space widely liked; skepticism about added soccer fields, amphitheater cost, and a dog park.
Relocating vs screening the highway garage/salt domes and bus operations; poor working conditions for highway crews.
Proposed ~40 residential units at 333 Main St and the entitled 34-townhouse Mariani site; school-enrollment and traffic concerns.

staffInput.summary: Explained permissive referendum (30-day publication, 5% electorate petition) and that a bond referendum requires a maximum cost figure taken to voters ('you've got to have the maximum cost'); confirmed the town's right of first refusal on the American Legion property; required a notary on Ferrari's rezoning petition.
Managed the public sign-up sheet, called speakers in order, and coordinated in-person and Zoom participants.

meetings.attributionNote: Raw ASR with no speaker labels. Supervisor Joseph Rende (presiding) and the two outside presenters (Michael Ferrari, Keith Rosenthal) and numerous named residents were readily identifiable. Board comments at the end were attributable: Barbara DiGiacinto explicitly named 'Matt' for the detailed financial-analysis remarks, so those are attributed to Matt Milim (confidence lowered to medium because that speaker twice said he 'won't be here' for future decisions, which is unusual given the roster and could indicate a different member); Barbara DiGiacinto's own remarks (conservative-with-money, North White Plains, keep highway on-site) are high confidence; Saleem Hussain identified himself on Zoom. Jose Berra (still on the board through 2025) was not clearly heard on the redevelopment item and is attributed only low-confidence via Supervisor Rende's secondhand reference to him leading condo-taxation legislation at a prior budget meeting. Sonny Vitaj not attributed (2026 only).

meetings.meetingSummary: The Town Board opened by honoring retiring Police Chief Peter Simonson (35 years) with county, state, and town proclamations, and recognized departing Councilman Matt Milim, whose term was ending. The board then made several appointments (interim Police Chief Reagan Huffnagel, animal warden/parking officer Mary Madsen, two building department staff), held public hearings adopting a Chapter 325 traffic law (Crossroad North one-way), a local law overriding the tax levy limit, and the 2026 town budget (both 4-1 with DiGiacinto opposed). It handled a contentious late-added $5M pool bond resolution and pool structural-engineering authorization, Lombardi Park water-extension change orders (demolition change order split 4-1), receipt of a Ferrari Companies rezoning petition, and a discussion to redraft the EV charging law to permit Level 3 fast charging. The meeting began at 5:30 with an executive session to interview police chief candidates and ran past midnight.
meetings.durationNote: Full five-member board present (Rende, DiGiacinto, Hussain, Milim, Berra); quorum met, no absences. Meeting opened at 5:30 p.m., recessed to executive session for police-chief interviews, reconvened late and ran past midnight. Incoming councilman Sonny Vitaj attended as a resident/audience member (not yet seated).

cases.name: Proclamations Honoring Retiring Police Chief Peter Simonson
cases.applicant: Town Board / County Legislator Margaret Kunzio / Senator Shelley Mayer
cases.summary: County Legislator Margaret Kunzio presented a Westchester County proclamation declaring December 11 'Chief Peter Simonson Day,' Senator Shelley Mayer sent a state proclamation, and Supervisor Rende read a town proclamation recognizing Simonson's 35 years of service (1990-2025), including his rise through the ranks to chief in 2014. Every board member spoke at length in tribute to his leadership, mentorship, and community impact. Members of the public, including former secretary Mindy Berard reading a statement from former Supervisor Michael Schillero, also offered praise. Purely ceremonial and universally supportive.
cases.publicComment: Mindy Berard (former confidential secretary) read a laudatory statement from former Supervisor Schillero; deeply appreciative, emotional tone.

memberPositions.evidence: Read the town proclamation and said he was 'blessed' to work with Simonson and would miss his counsel.
Praised Simonson's principled, family-based, mentoring leadership that 'enables the next generation of leadership.'
Called him an example 'absent of any ego,' recalled his professionalism handling a personal matter.
As PD liaison, praised his dedication and self-effacing work that will have 'a lasting impact.'
Said the whole town would agree on Simonson's positive impact and the legacy and culture he built.

cases.name: Certificate of Recognition for Departing Councilman Matt Milim
cases.summary: The board presented a certificate of recognition to Councilman Matt Milim, whose four-year term was ending (this being his last meeting), thanking him for his service and specifically for resurrecting the Armonk Lions Club and the Folderol festival. Each colleague spoke warmly about his intelligence, independence, and willingness to embrace debate and dissent. Supervisor Rende and Chief Simonson noted their close working relationships. Ceremonial and universally supportive; incoming councilman Sonny Vitaj was acknowledged as his successor.
cases.publicComment: County Legislator Margaret Kunzio and incoming councilman Sonny Vitaj (as a resident) thanked Milim for his service, especially reviving the Folderol.

memberPositions.evidence: Called it a 'bittersweet night,' thanked Milim's 'voice of reason' and professionalism over two years.
Praised how Milim 'leans into people that dissent' and his curiosity, saying he'll miss him dearly.
Thanked him for resurrecting the Folderol and doing the town-board 'balancing act' well.
Recalled having praised Milim before he joined as 'the real deal,' smart, independent and free of conflicts.

cases.name: Provisional Appointment of Mary Madsen — Animal Warden/Parking Enforcement Officer
cases.summary: Police Chief Simonson recommended the provisional appointment of Mary Madsen as Animal Warden/Parking Enforcement Officer, filling a vacancy left by Angel Morales's January 2025 retirement. He detailed her 11+ years as a dog control officer and veterinary background and a completed background investigation. The board voted unanimously to appoint her effective January 5, 2026, and Rende then swore her in with family present.

memberPositions.evidence: Welcomed Madsen warmly, joking about her snapping turtle and bull terriers; congratulated her.

cases.name: Appointment of Reagan Huffnagel as Interim Police Chief
cases.summary: The board appointed Reagan Huffnagel to interim Police Chief effective January 1, 2026, to succeed the retiring Chief Simonson. The motion passed unanimously by voice vote with congratulations from the board. (The meeting had opened with an executive session interviewing three candidates from the police chief list.)

cases.name: Local Law Amending Chapter 325 — Crossroad North One-Way and Prohibited Left Turn
cases.address: Crossroad North between State Route 128 and Old Mount Kisco Road, Armonk
cases.applicant: North Castle Police Department / Highway Department
cases.summary: A public hearing was held on a local law amending Chapter 325 to make Crossroad North one-way westbound and to prohibit left turns onto Old Mount Kisco Road, after Highway General Foreman Jamie Norris flagged that vehicles were bottoming out on the steep grade. Lt. Tom McCormick presented site photos, including a September 25 incident where a vehicle got hung up and needed a tow. The board closed the hearing and adopted the law unanimously, combining both changes into one local law.
cases.publicComment: Resident Elisa Brickell (Whippoorwill Hills) supported the change and separately raised potholes on Route 128; Rende explained 128 is a state road being addressed with NYSDOT Region 8.

memberPositions.evidence: Said it 'makes complete sense,' the road is very steep and a good case was made.
Lives nearby; 'there but for the grace of God,' has seen cars there and appreciated the work.
Appreciated the 'thoughtful planning' that went into it.
Agreed it will be 'a much safer situation this way.'

cases.name: Local Law to Override the Tax Levy Limit (Tax Cap)
cases.summary: A public hearing was held on a local law to override the tax levy limit established in General Municipal Law 3-c. Resident correspondence was received into the record. The board framed the override as unavoidable given ~8% healthcare and retirement inflation on a budget dominated by employee costs. It was adopted 4-1 on a roll call vote (Milim, Berra, Hussain, Rende in favor; DiGiacinto opposed), the first time in the town's history the cap has been overridden.
cases.publicComment: Correspondence received from residents Judy Corticelli, Yolanda Cumming, the Jacobs family, John Junker, Holly Maggio and Betty Sangarico.

memberPositions.evidence: 'I don't view this as having a choice'; after ~20 hours of work sessions no idea would avoid the cap; explained only 15% of the tax bill is the town portion.
'Troubled by taxes going up this much' but said it would be irresponsible not to enact the override given the consequences.
Voted no, saying she would explain during the budget; wanted expense cuts attempted first.
Voted yes; described it as the first override in town history, driven by real inflation, not discretionary spending.

cases.name: Adoption of the 2026 Town and Special Districts Preliminary Budget
cases.summary: After a lengthy public hearing, the board adopted the 2026 budget (total appropriation just under $44M, town-portion tax increase 4.81%) on a 4-1 roll call vote (Milim, Berra, Hussain, Rende yes; DiGiacinto no). Comptroller Abbas and Milim defended a multi-year 'glide path' to structurally balance revenues with expenses and wean the town off drawing on a fund balance that had ballooned to ~$25M. DiGiacinto objected that the board rejected her requests for 8-10% departmental cuts, a hiring freeze, and review of long-vacant positions, noting the county had trimmed its increase to ~3%. Berra voted yes 'with regret,' pressing on declining interest income, condo taxation, overtime, and missing quarterly reports.
cases.publicComment: Resident Michael Akivan (58 Chestnut Ridge Rd) strongly supported the budget ('$165/year is well worth' funding police/school resource officers). Incoming councilman Sonny Vitaj spoke as a resident supporting breaking the cap but questioning the magnitude, asking about the current ~$16.5M fund balance and suggesting a smaller 3% increase.

memberPositions.evidence: Argued 'price is what you pay, value is what you get'; only marginal item was a full-time HR person; cutting services (e.g. a smaller police force) is the alternative.
Called it a 'sound budget,' said pushing 0% would be politically expedient but wrong; rejected any accusation of reckless spending.
Said the increase was made 'very cautiously,' deeply discussed, not a 'hand-wavy gesture.'
Voted yes 'with regret'; real concerns over value, ~$500K decline in interest income, condo taxation for new development, and wanting quarterly financial reports.
Voted no; disappointed the board wouldn't direct department heads to cut 8-10%, freeze hiring, or examine vacant positions; said the county did better under the cap.

cases.name: Approval of Town Board Minutes (Nov 19 and Dec 1, 2025)
cases.summary: The board approved the minutes of its November 19, 2025 and December 1, 2025 meetings by unanimous voice vote. Routine procedural item.

cases.name: Receipt of Ferrari Companies Petition to Rezone 333 Main Street for Residential Use
cases.summary: The board voted only to RECEIVE (not consider or refer) a petition from Ferrari Companies to rezone 333 Main Street to permit residential use, after special counsel Bob Spolzino distinguished the ministerial act of receiving from the discretionary act of considering. The receipt passed on a roll call (DiGiacinto, Hussain, Milim, Rende aye; Berra abstained). Milim, who is leaving the board, opined that the rezoning does not fit the comprehensive plan given already-approved units (Airport Campus 175, Mariani 34, Lumberyard 20, Summit Club). Berra's abstention triggered a sharp exchange with Rende over whether a member may abstain without stating a reason under Robert's Rules.

memberPositions.evidence: Voted to receive but called pursuing the rezoning 'really dangerous for our town'; said it ignores facts on the ground and prior approved development.
Abstained, saying he wouldn't comment on the merits and wasn't 'willing to expose the town to liability.'
Voted to receive; argued a member shouldn't abstain without giving a reason, citing Robert's Rules.

cases.name: Proposed Local Law to Permit Level 3 (Fast) EV Charging Stations
cases.applicant: Town Planner / prompted by IBM application
cases.summary: Town Planner Adam Kaufman presented a proposed amendment to Section 355-4 to permit Level 3 fast EV charging (currently limited to Levels 1-2, capped at 20% of parking), prompted by an IBM application at its gated corporate campus. Councilman Hussain recused himself because he works at IBM. The board received the related documents (items 1-5) and debated how to avoid parking/congestion problems, converging on Milim's idea that EV spaces not count toward off-street parking minimums, restricting the exclusion to Level 3, and adding EV charging as a minor site-plan category. No vote on the law; Kaufman will redraft for the January 14 meeting to then set a public hearing.
cases.publicComment: IBM representatives Seth Wasserman (head of real estate) and counsel Meredith Black advocated for gated-access Level 3 charging; incoming councilman Sonny Vitaj, an EV owner, spoke supporting Level 3 and cautioning about clustering/parking.

memberPositions.evidence: Argued Level 3 chargers would bring commerce into town and government is pushing EVs; 'forward thinking.'
'I want the level three charging. It just makes sense,' warning against restrictive legislation.
Supportive but wary of parking/congestion; proposed EV spaces not count toward off-street minimum and limit to Level 3.
An EV owner; explained Level 3 chargers site off highways and won't cluster, favoring allowance with parking safeguards.

cases.name: Sidewalk Improvement Bond Release and Escrow — 873 North Broadway
cases.summary: On a memo from KSCJ Consulting, the board released the NYS sidewalk improvement bond held for four years from the prior owner (873 Holding Company LLC) and established a new escrow agreement with the new owner (873 LLC) for the improvements to be completed by June 2026, authorizing the supervisor to sign. Members briefly discussed making the release contingent on the new escrow; staff advised the documents would handle it simultaneously and the new owner cannot get a building permit without escrowing. Both items passed unanimously by voice vote.

memberPositions.evidence: Asked whether the release should be contingent on receiving the new escrow first.

cases.name: Payment Application #4 — Papatio Construction, Water District #4 New Well
cases.summary: The board approved payment application #4 from Papatio Construction Company Inc. for site work performed at the Water District #4 new well project. Passed unanimously by voice vote with no questions.

cases.name: Bond Resolution — $5M Financing for Town Pool Improvements
cases.summary: A late-added bond resolution authorized up to $5M (15-year) in financing for town pool improvements so that design/engineering costs could be rolled into the bond rather than paid from fund balance. It provoked extended debate led by Berra over Section 5's broad delegation of the town board's powers (bond terms, form, credit enhancements) to the supervisor; Milim and special counsel Spolzino argued the terms are largely market-driven and the board retains authority over expenditures. It passed 4-1 on a roll call (Milim, Hussain, DiGiacinto, Rende aye; Berra no) and is subject to permissive referendum.

memberPositions.evidence: Voted no; the broad delegation of bond terms to the supervisor 'scares the heck out of me' and felt like abdicating board responsibility, especially on a same-day resolution.
Called the delegation fairly standard and market-driven; wants the pool renovated and sees no material discretion abused.
Pushed the late resolution so design costs could be captured in the bond rather than fund balance.
Preferred to move forward with the delegation as written rather than revisit details later.
Voted aye but shared Berra's discomfort, saying delegating terms to bond counsel 'scares the heck out of me.'

cases.name: Pool Structural Engineering (Macri Consulting) and Authorization to Bid
cases.summary: The board hired Macri Consulting for structural engineering of the pool deck (~$26,300) and authorized the town to go out to bid for the construction work, subject to Macri's specifications, to keep the project on schedule (bids by mid-February) to reopen the pool by early June. Members debated confusing agenda wording and whether they should review the bid specs before publication; staff explained professional services aren't bid and specs are published (Jan 6) before board review. The Macri hiring (5A) passed by voice vote; the authorization to bid (4E) passed on a roll call, with Berra voting yes despite wanting to see the plans.

memberPositions.evidence: Said the pool-deck work is technical repair, not subjective design, so authorizing the bid now saves time.
Wanted to see the plans and felt he lacked information, but voted yes to avoid a month's delay to the pool.
Preferred to move forward on both the engineering and the bid to keep the work going.

cases.name: Chabad Hanukkah Menorah Lighting at Wampus Park Gazebo
cases.applicant: Chabad of Armonk, Chappaqua and Pleasantville
cases.summary: The board approved a request from the Chabad of Armonk, Chappaqua and Pleasantville to hold its annual Hanukkah menorah lighting ceremony at the Wampus Park gazebo on December 16. Passed unanimously by voice vote.

cases.name: Aqua Works Change Orders — Lombardi Park Water District Extension
cases.summary: The board approved three change orders on the John A. Lombardi Park water district extension. Change Order #1 (concrete removal/disposal at $130/cubic yard, verified by the engineer) and #2 (air release valve chamber) passed unanimously. Change Order #3 — an added ~$115,000+ to demolish an old, asbestos-containing, oil-heated building and reroute the water connection so the town stops heating it — passed 4-1 (Milim, Hussain, Berra, Rende yes; DiGiacinto no). DiGiacinto and Berra objected that a building demolition should have been a bid item and an agenda item, not a change order, and complained information arrived late; Milim, Hussain, and Rende defended it as an efficient, money-saving addition to the same contract.

memberPositions.evidence: Voted no on CO#3; said demolition isn't a change order, was never an agenda item voted on, and lacked process/transparency.
Voted yes but said it should be bid, he couldn't evaluate cost, and he isn't getting information early enough.
Called it an efficient way to do needed work without an elongated, costlier process.
Questioned CO#1 pricing but supported using the on-site contractor as an efficient, money-saving addition.
Proposed the demolition change order to save the town money vs. heating a doomed building and paying to re-mobilize a demolition contractor.

cases.name: Sewer District #2 Bid Awards — Sludge Hauling and Methanol Supply
cases.applicant: Wind River Environmental LLC / Solvents and Petroleum Service Inc.
cases.summary: The board awarded two 2026 fiscal-year Sewer District #2 contracts, sludge hauling to Wind River Environmental LLC and methanol supply to Solvents and Petroleum Service Inc., and authorized the supervisor to sign both agreements. Both passed unanimously by voice vote.

cases.name: Agreement with Arc Westchester — Main Street Armonk Maintenance 2026
cases.summary: The board authorized the supervisor to sign a 2026 agreement with Arc Westchester for maintenance of Main Street, Armonk. Passed unanimously by voice vote.

cases.name: Probationary Appointments — Building Department (Segmuller, Henriquez)
cases.summary: The board made two probationary appointments effective December 11, 2025: William Segmuller as Assistant Building Inspector and Yvonne Henriquez as Office Assistant (Automated System). Both passed unanimously by voice vote.

cases.name: Receipt of Retirement/Resignation — Lisa Larson, Parks & Recreation
cases.summary: The board received, with regret, a letter of resignation for retirement from Lisa Larson, Senior Office Assistant in Parks and Recreation, effective January 23. Passed unanimously by voice vote; Rende thanked her for the advance notice.

memberPositions.evidence: Thanked Larson for a nice conversation and for giving the town so much advance notice of her retirement.

cases.name: Consensus Agenda (Including Litigation Dismissal)
cases.summary: The board adopted the consensus agenda by unanimous voice vote. Milim confirmed with special counsel that the Pacamon/EFG litigation had been dismissed with no further liability to the town.

memberPositions.evidence: Confirmed the Pacamon/EFG litigation was dismissed with no more liability: 'I'm satisfied.'

themes.note: 2026 budget (4.81% town increase, ~$44M) and first-ever tax-cap override both adopted 4-1; DiGiacinto opposed, Berra voted yes reluctantly.
Extended, universally warm tributes to retiring Chief Simonson and departing Councilman Milim.
$5M pool bond (4-1) and pool engineering/bid authorization advanced despite delegation-of-authority concerns.
Multiple bids/agreements approved; Lombardi Park demolition change order split the board over process.
Lombardi Park water extension change orders, WD#4 well payment, and Sewer District #2 contract awards.
Interim chief, animal warden, and two building-department appointments; one retirement received.
Discussion to redraft the EV charging law to permit Level 3 fast charging, with parking safeguards.
Friction over Berra's abstention, transparency/timeliness of information, and delegation of bond authority.
Ferrari 333 Main Street rezone petition received-only; Milim called pursuing it dangerous.
Crossroad North one-way/no-left-turn safety law adopted unanimously.
Chief transition (Simonson retirement, Huffnagel interim appointment) handled positively.

staffInput.summary: Read hearing correspondence and legal notices into the record; delivered community announcements (toy/coat drives, menorah lighting, record 124-car shredder event, holiday office/library closures); reminded the board of the missed personnel agenda item.
